The assets on which tax is payable in respect of any income arising from the transfer are listed securities or unit or zero coupon bond. If the asset is not a share or debenture, the residents and non-resident assessees are allowed computation of capital gains on the basis of indexation. In respect of units and zero coupon bonds, which are other than shares or debentures, all the assessees, whether residents or non-residents, are eligible to the benefit of indexation in the computation of capital gains arising on their transfer. However, the 3rd proviso denies the benefit of indexation to bonds or debentures. While applying the proviso to section 112(1) to determine the tax payable, the computation mechanism includes such assets. There is, thus, no dichotomy in the proviso to section 112(1) and the 3rd proviso to section 48. Section 48 is a section which governs mode of computation of income whereas section 112 determines the tax payable on such income. It may be important to keep in mind that the application of the proviso is based on the capital asset to which the provisions of 2nd proviso to section 48 apply. If it is the case that it applies to the 1st proviso meant for a non-resident assessee, then the proviso would have made a mention of it. One cannot read anything more in the statute than what is stated therein. [Para 25]

It is averred that the mandate of the phrase in the proviso to section 112(1) is not to let the indexation formula enter into the computation process and is not a condition that unless an assessee is eligible to apply the indexation formula, only then the reduced rate of 10 per cent prescribed by the proviso to section 112(1) can be applied. In this regard, it may be stated that the indexation formula already enters into the computation in the first limb where it is mentioned that 'tax payable in respect of any income arising from the transfer of long-term capital asset' is to be determined. In fact, there is no issue on this part of proviso whether the 2nd proviso to section 48 enters into the said computation or not. The issue that arises lies in the second limb of the proviso starting with the phrase 'ten per cent of the amount of capital gains before giving effect to the provisions of the second proviso to section 48'. This cannot be read to mean 'deny the concessional rate of tax to the category of assessees who are not eligible to have the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition under the second proviso of section 48'. It only conveys how a particular amount is to be determined. Any other meaning would tantamount to rewriting this part of the proviso of section 112(1). [Para 26]

As the indexation on the zero coupon bond is available by virtue of 2nd proviso, it will affect the computation of capital gains under section 48 on which tax is payable under the first limb of the proviso and, thus would not go out of the purview of the proviso to section 112(1). The zero coupon bond on which indexation is available will get the benefit of the lower rate of tax at 10 per cent under the proviso. The exclusion from application of 1st and 2nd provisos to section 48 while calculating the amount of Income-tax on the income by way of long-term capital gains in the cases of non-residents and allow them the benefit of lower tax rates of 10 per cent also find mention in sections 115AC(3) and 115AD(3). The Act has taken care when, where, and how the 1st and the 2nd provisos to section 48 are to be excluded. The long-term capital gains on the sale of shares of the listed companies are otherwise exempt from tax under section 10(38) if the sale of the shares takes place through the recognized stock exchange on which security transaction tax is paid. However, in the instant case, such exemption is not available as the shares of the listed company CIL are sold in the off-market mode. [Para 27]

headnotes.text: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Assessee held certain shares of company ‘G’ and was also managing agent of said company - During relevant accounting year, one ‘T’ made offer to assessee to purchase of aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ held by assessee also managing agency rights of assessee - Assessee accepted aforesaid offer and thereafter wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting his resignation from office of managing agents and further recommended ‘T’ to be appointed as managing agents in his place - Company ‘G’ accepted said letter - Whether resignation by assessee of managing agency and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, was nothing but mode of performance of agreement to sell managing agency arrived at between assessee and, therefore, provisions of section 12B of 1922 Act were attracted - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessee - company was managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies and also held majority of their conversion shares - 'D' company made an offer to assessee to purchase conversions share of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency - Assessee accepted said offer - Subsequently, agreement was modified and as per new agreement, assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in favour of 'D' company, resigned from it - Revenue authorities brought to tax under section 12B of 1922 Act amount of compensation received by assessee-company on account of resigning managing agency agreement - Whether since transaction in its true legal character was relinquishment of managing agency and was neither a sale nor transfer thereof, High Court rightly held that assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1947-48 and 1948-49 - Whether levy of tax on capital gains under section 12B of 1922 Act is ultra vires Government of India Act, 1935 - Held, no - Whether expression "distribution of capital assets" in third proviso to section 12B(1) of 1922 Act means distribution in specie and not distribution of sale proceeds - Held, yes

SECTION 80L OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-DEDUCTIONS-INTEREST ON CERTAIN SECURITIES AND DIVIDENDS-ASSESSEE’S INCOME INCLUDED INTEREST 
ON PROVIDENT FUND IN EXCESS OF PRESCRIBED RATE-FUND HELD IN TRUST 
AND TRUSTEES EARNED INTEREST FROM INVESTMENTS IN BANK-WHETHER ASSESSEE WAS ENTITLED TO DEDUCTION QUA SUCH INCOME UNDER SECTION 
8OL-HELD, YES

Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 12B of the Indian  Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1948-49 - Assessee was partner in a firm - Said firm sold shares of a company together with its managing agency rights at an amount calculated at Rs. 65 per share though market value of share was Rs. 46 only - Whether full value must be true value and not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset and, hence, for purposes of section 12B of 1922 Act sale price of shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. at 65 per share - Held, yes

Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of Indian Income-tax Act 1922] - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1947-48 - Assessee-firm sold certain share and securities held by it to company on 28-2-1947 which was admitted as partner in firm with 99 per cent share in goodwill and profits of firm for certain consideration - Whether since section 128 was incorporated into Act with effect from 1-4-1947, at time sale transaction took place section 12B was not part of Act and so first proviso to section 12B(2) of 1922 Act was not attracted on facts of case - Held, yes

Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1960-61 - Whether for purpose of taking fair market value, to be value on basis of which capital gains are to be computed, two conditions as required by first proviso to section 12B(2) of 1922 Act should be fulfilled and these conditions are cumulative - Held, yes - Whether if on computation made these is capital loss then there cannot be any liability for capital gains under section 12B of 1922 Act - Held yes

Section 50 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Computation in case of depreciable assets - Assessment year 1959-60 - Whether if consideration for transaction has been honestly agreed upon, with a view to benefit purchaser and out of love and affection on account of relationship, or with reference to particular circumstances, there will be no justification for imputing a motive to vendor to avoid or reduce tax liability and as such, in such a circumstance, proviso to section 12B(2) of 1922 Act can not be invoked - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Whether expression 'Transfer' in section 12B of 1922 Act includes not only a permanent transfer but also a temporary transfer of title to property and lease of mines for any period would fall within ambit of section 12B of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether a lease of land is transfer of interest in land and creates a right in rem and there is a transfer of title in favour of lessee though lessor has right of reversion after period of lease terminates - Held, yes - Whether legislation enacted in section 12B of 1922 Act is in pith and substance legislation relating to tax on capital value of assets and enactment of section 12B is constitutionally a valid piece of legislation - Held, yes

Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1982-83 - Assessee trust sold certain quantity of gold and claimed that net consideration of sale being kept in fixed deposit and utilized for acquiring new capital asset, capital gain on sale of gold would be exempt under section 11(1A) - Assessee's claim was rejected on ground that it had lent sale proceeds on interest - Whether since it was not clear whether assessee advanced loans out of income from fixed deposits or invested net consideration in fixed deposits, matter should be remanded back to Tribunal for fresh consideration - Held, yes

SECTION 11(1A)  OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CHARITABLE OR RELIGIOUS TRUST-EXEMPTION OF INCOME FROM PROPERTY HELD UNDERASSESSEE, A CHARITABLE TRUST, SOLD CERTAIN LANDS AND OUT OF SALE CONSIDERATION, ASSESSEE INVESTED A SUM IN FIXED DEPOSIT WITH MAHARASHTRA STATE ROAD TRANSPORT CORPORATION-WHETHER INVESTMENT IN FIXED DEPOSIT WITH MAHARASHTRA STATE ROAD TRANSPORT CORPORATION AMOUNTED TO ACQUIRING ANOTHER CAPITAL ASSET WITHIN MEANING OF SECTION 11(1A) SO AS TO ENTITLE ASSESSEE TO EXEMPTION IN RESPECT OF CAPITAL GAIN ARISING ON ACCOUNT OF TRANSFER OF LAND-HELD, NO

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gain - Chargeability as - Assessment year 1961-62 - Assessee, electricity company was called upon to sell its undertaking to State Government in terms of section 5(d) and (g) of Indian Electricity Act and possession of same was handed over on 3-5-1944 - Since compensation offered by State Government was subjected to controversy, Arbitrator by its award dated 15-7-1960 increased amount of compensation - ITO made addition of capital gain from said transactions in relevant assessment year - Whether since price which State Government offered to pay to assessee as sale price was value of undertaking on 30-5-1944, incurred sum which was directed by arbitrator would undisputedly be price of undertaking as on 30-5-1944 - Held, yes - Whether therefore, no capital gain was liable to tax under section 12B of Act of 1922 in relevant assessment year - Held, yes
Section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 [Corresponding to Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961] - Capital gain - Chargeable as

Section 47 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B(1) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Transactions not regarded as transfer - Whether expression ‘possessed by assessee’ used in second proviso to section 12B(1) of 1922 Act means possessed juridically and not actual possession - Held, yes - Whether where juridical possession of concerned property was not with assessee, but with assessee along with his sons who were coparceners and who constituted joint and undivided Hindu family at material time, case of assessee would not fall within second proviso to section 12B(1) of 1922 Act - Held, yes
Section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 [Corresponding to section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961] - Capital gain - Chargeable as
Section 12B of the Indian Income-Tax Act, 1922 [Corresponding to section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961] - Capital gain - Chargeable as

Section 48, read with sections 45(6) and 80CCB, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital Gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1996-97 - Whether second proviso to section 48 has no role to play in ascertainment of capital gains in context of section 45(6) and, therefore, indexed cost cannot be adopted in respect of repurchase of units of mutual funds specified in section 80CCB(2) - Held, yes

proviso to section 12b(2) of the indian income-tax act, 1922 [corresponding to section 52(1) of the income-tax act, 1961]-capital gains-transfer in cases of understatement-assessee-firm sold buses and routes to a company in which its partners were shareholders-revenue failed to prove any understatement of consideration qua sale of buses or routes but computed notional capital gains and sought to tax the same-whether revenue's action justified-held, on facts, no

Section 48 of the Income-tax, Act 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1992] - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1959-60 - Whether capital loss for assessment year 1951-52, when tax on capital gains was not in force, could be carried forward and set off against capital gains for assessment year 1959-60 - Held, no - Whether in absence of relevant material enabling Income-tax Officer to determine fair market value of asset as on 1-1-1954, benefit of third proviso to section 12B(2) of 1922 Act could not be given merely because there was possibility of increase in value of shares on account of increase in earning capacity of company - Held, yes

Section 45 of the income-tax Act, 1961-Capital gains-Chargeability of-Assessee, holder of two-third shares of a company and also managing agent of said company, sold its entire shareholding in one block to a third company gaining some profit and  surrendering said managing agency-No finding on record that assessee was a dealer in managing agency and transaction was a colourable one-Whether surplus realised out of sale of shares was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains-Held, on facts, yes

Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1960-61 - Whether incidence of charge being on capital gains actually received by assessee, in order that transfer was one with object of avoiding or reducing liability of assessee under section 12B it must be a case where consideration mentioned in deed has been understated and actually transferor has received more than what was stated in document - Held, yes - Whether, where, assessee transferred shares in a company to a person connected with him, for much less than fair market value of shares, first proviso to section 12B(2) was not applicable - Held, yes

Section 45,  read with section 256 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B, read with section 66 of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Assessee purchased certain shares of company with a view to obtain managing agency and control of company - Tribunal found that shares were not stock-in-trade - Whether mere fact that assessee took loan for purchase of said shares and subsequently sold part of shares would not by itself go to show that it was purchase of stock-in-trade - Held, yes - Whether conclusion of Tribunal being based upon relevant material could not be interfered with in reference under section 66 of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether therefore, profit made on sale of said shares constituted capital gain chargeable to income-tax under section 12B of 1922 Act - Held, yes

Section 12B(1) of the indian income-ax act, 1922 [corresponding to section 45 of the income-tax act, 1961]-Capital gains-assessee-firm transferred shares held by it to partners at a profit-Whether tribunal's view that it does not result in trading profit to the firm was correct-Held, no

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Whether Indian Income-tax and Excess Profits Tax (Amendment) Act, 1947 which amended 1922 Act, by enlarging definition of term income in section 2(6C) of 1922 Act and introducing a new head of income in section 6 of 1922 Act and inserting new section 12B, was intra vires powers of Central Legislature acting under entry 54 in List I of Seventh Schedule of Government of India Act, 1935 - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessee owned certain coal mines - Later, he formed a company along with family members and transferred entire management of coal mines to company - Company agreed to pay assessee a royalty and certain amount in respect of goodwill - Whether, in instant case, there was no transfer, sale or exchange of capital asset as all that was done was to give management of that asset to someone else - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee in effecting transfer of management of coal mines to company did not make any capital gain - Held, yes

Section 50C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains -  Special provision for computation of full value consideration (Applicability of) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was a charitable society - It sold a property and invested entire sale consideration in other capital asset - Assessing Officer invoked section 50C and made additions on account of capital gains on sale of property - Commissioner (Appeals) deleted additions on grounds that section 11(1A), which lays down a complete system of taxability of capital gains in respect of an institution approved by Commissioner under section 12A, is a complete code - He, thus, held that as section 11(1A) had specifically defined meaning of "net consideration" for purposes of capital gains and same shall prevail over deemed sale consideration as provided under section 50C - Whether since Commissioner (Appeals) adjudicated issue in accordance with law, no interference was to be called for - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]INCOME TAX : Where assessee-charitable society sold an immovable property, since section 11(1A) specifically defined meaning of "net consideration" for purposes of capital gains and provides a complete system of taxability of capital gains in respect of an institution approved by Commissioner under section 12A, in such case section 50C couldnot be invoked

Section 45, read with section 2(14), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B, read with section 2(4A) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment years 1960-61 and 1961-62 - During relevant assessment year, assessee sold a land with building and trees thereon - ITO computed capital gains and made assessment - Case of assessee was that land was agricultural land and therefore, not assessable under section 12B - Whether, property in question was a capital asset as defined in section 2(4A) of 1922 Act, even though, there were few trees thereon yielding some income - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, profits or gains derived from sales of such land would be assessable under section 12B of 1922 Act - Held, yes

While extracting the statement of objects and reasons of the amended SARFAESI Act, the Division Bench arrived a conclusion that “Inclusion of section 31-B does not change the position insofar as primacy of claim under the provisions of the EPF Act is concerned. The mention of Government dues which would include revenues, taxes, cesses and rates due to the Central Government, State Government or local authority would not take into its fold, the first charge created by operation of law in the form of section 11 (2) of the EPF Act”. Accordingly, the Division Bench came to the conclusion that “what is sought to be recovered by the petitioner-Bank from respondent No. 2 is its debts which are included in section 11(2) of the EPF Act and therefore, there is no hesitation in holding that the Provident Fund Organisation was within its power to issue the order dated 9.8.2016.”

Section 15 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 7(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Salaries - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1953-54 - Assessee was employed in 'B' Ltd. as a manager - As per terms of employment, appointment was liable to be terminated on twelve month's notice on either side - After a dispute between assessee and employer assessee decided to resign service and accordingly in terms of employment gave a notice of twelve months to employer - This letter of resignation was accepted by employer and thereafter instead of allowing assessee to come to office and work, employer had paid twelth month's salary and provident fund to assessee - Assessee's claim that said twelve month's salary and provident fund was compensation for loss of employment was rejected by revenue and same was brought to tax as salary - Whether since payment of sum consisted of 12 month's salary and provident fund of that period to which assessee was entitled under terms of employment, same was liable to be taxed as salary in hands of assessee - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] – Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 – Whether on facts stated under head 'Deemed dividend', section 12B of 1922 Act would not apply to amount received by assessee as it was not profits or gains arising from sale of any capital asset of his but from sale of capital assets of company – Held, yes

Section 50C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains -  Special provision for computation of full value consideration (Applicability of) - Assessment year 2008-09 - Assessee was a charitable society - It sold a property and invested entire sale consideration in other capital asset - Assessing Officer invoked section 50C and made additions on account of capital gains on sale of property - Commissioner (Appeals) deleted additions on grounds that section 11(1A), which lays down a complete system of taxability of capital gains in respect of an institution approved by Commissioner under section 12A, is a complete code - He, thus, held that as section 11(1A) had specifically defined meaning of "net consideration" for purposes of capital gains and same shall prevail over deemed sale consideration as provided under section 50C - Whether since Commissioner (Appeals) adjudicated issue in accordance with law, no interference was to be called for - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]

SECTION 11(1A)(a) OF THE INCOME-TAX ACT, 1961-CHARITABLE OR RELIGIOUS TRUST-EXEMPTION OF INCOME FROM PROPERTY HELD UNDER TRUST-ASSESSEE-
 TRUST INVESTED CAPITAL GAINS DERIVED ON SALE OF INVESTMENTS IN INTE-
REST-BEARING DEPOSITS OF ANOTHER TRUST-WHETHER THIS WOULD AMOUNT 
TO ACQUISITION OF ANOTHER CAPITAL ASSET SO AS TO ENTITLE ASSESSEE TO EXEMPTION FROM TAX ON CAPITAL GAINS-HELD, NO

Section 12B of the indian income-tax act, 1922 [corresponding to section 45 of the in-come-tax act, 1961]-Capital gains-Assessee is a owner of certain land and used the same for agricultural purposes yielding agricultural income-In 1949 state government requisitioned assessee's land and allotted same to landless people who used land for agricultural purposes and derived agricultural income there from-Whether amount of compensation received by assessee in 1959 was liable to capital gains tax in spite of fact that assessee was prevented from earning agricultural income from land due to requisition-Held, no

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1955-56 - Under will, assessee along with other trustees was empowered to invest sale proceeds of certain properties left by testator in certain securities and to vary said investments from time to time in best interests of trust - In relevant assessment year, trustees sold shares in four blocks, two of which were sold within three years of their purchase and others beyond three years - ITO treated entire surplus as income while AAC treated surplus on shares sold within three years as income from dealing in shares and remaining surplus as capital gains - Tribunal treated entire surplus as capital gains - Whether Tribunal was right in its conclusion that assessee could not be held to be dealer in shares and surplus realised was not income but capital gains as there was no proof that trustees had any intention to make profits when they purchased shares - Held, yes

Section 10(11) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, read with section 2(e) of the Provident Fund Act, 1925 - Provident fund, payment from -  Assessment years 2001-02 to 2004-05 - Whether interest income, that has accrued on credit balance maintained by employees of Punjab State Electricity Board in their provident fund governed by Provident Fund Act, 1925 after their retirement, would continue to qualify for exemption from income-tax - Held, yes

Section 11(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1982-83 - Assessee-trust sold shares of certain companies which formed corpus of trust-fund and utilised net sale consideration for acquiring new capital assets in form of fixed deposits with public sector undertakings and units of UTI - Whether investment or deposit in any public sector company was one of permitted forms or mode of investment or deposit under section 11(5), and in view of section 2(14), such investment or deposit could be treated as investment in capital asset, entitling assessee to claim exemption in respect of capital gains - Held, yes - Whether where investment in Unit Trust had been made during accounting period, fact that units were issued after expiry of accounting year would disentitle assessee to exemption - Held, no.

Section 69B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Undisclosed investment - Assessee purchased 3814 grams worth of National Defence Gold Bonds, 1980 on 4-1-1980 at the rate of Rs. 750 per ten grams, which was market price prevailing in June 1979 as against rate of Rs. 1,450 per ten grams quoted at Bombay Stock Exchange on 4-1-1980 - Assessee sold said bonds at the rate of Rs. 1,500 per ten grams on 9-1-1980 and claimed difference amount as capital gains which was exempt - ITO accepted assessee’s claim without investigation - In revisionary proceedings under section 263, assessee contended that bonds had been purchased on basis of agreement entered into with seller in June 1979 - Commissioner rejected this contention as said agreement was not produced and held that amount claimed as capital gain was nothing but undisclosed
 income of assessee for relevant year - Whether Commissioner was justified in treating amount claimed as capital gains by assessee as his undisclosed income under section 69B - Held, yes

Section 13, read with section 11, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Denial of exemption - Assessment years 1971-72 to 1973-74 - Assessee, a public charitable trust, had seven subscribers to memorandum of association of whom three, ‘SR’, ‘BR’ and ‘CR’, constituted Board of trustees - CR and BR donated to assessee-trust in all 290 shares of BRCRP Ltd. against which 870 bonus shares were issued to assessee - Percentage of shares held by relatives of BR and CR, who were founder members of trust and were treated by revenue as ‘excluded persons’ in terms of section 13(3)(b), in BRCRP Ltd., came to 56.79 per cent as against 5.8 per cent held by trust - Tribunal held that assessee was not covered by section 13(2)(h) or any other provision of section 13 and, therefore, allowed its claim for exemption of its dividend income under section 11 - Whether fundamental requirement of section 13(2)(h) is that there must be investment of funds of a trust and if any expanded meaning is given to include assets other than money in hand or cash or credit balance in a bank account, such assets, unless converted into money or cash, would be incapable of being invested as such - Held, yes - Whether expression ‘invest’ connotes a positive act on part of trust whereby trust funds are laid out or committed in any particular property or business or transaction with object of earning a profit or financial advantage or return - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, on facts of instant case, Tribunal was justified in its views - Held, yes
Words & phrases - words ‘funds’ and ‘invested’ occurring in section 13(2)(h) of the Income-tax Act, 1961

Section 2(29B) , read with section 2(29A) and 2(42A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Long-term capital gains/assets - Assessment year 1992-93 - Assessee, a share broker, was a member of Bombay Stock Exchange - He, with a view to acquire membership of Bangalore Stock Exchange Ltd., acquired business of one ‘G’, who held share in Bangalore Stock Exchange Ltd., on 15-3-1990 along with his business assets - However, assessee could not get SEBI’s permission to trade in more than one exchange and, therefore, he sold business of ‘G’ on 18-12-1991 to one ‘V’ - Whether since what was virtually sold by assessee to ‘V’ was mainly share in Bangalore Stock Exchange Ltd., which answered description of shares held in a company within meaning of proviso to section 2(42A) and, moreover, said share was sold after a gap of more than 12 months, profit arising from sale of share was taxable as long-term capital gains within meaning of section 2(29B), read with sections 2(29A) and 2(42A) - Held, yes

Section 11(1A) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption in respect of property held under - Assessee, a charitable trust, sold shares of certain companies held by it - Under sale agreement, part of consideration was allowed to be kept as interest bearing fixed deposit with purchaser and rest, received in cash, was invested in bank deposit - Whether Tribunal was justified in exempting capital gains resulting from sale of shares under section 11(1A) as assessee had invested consideration in fixed deposits with purchaser and in bank and could be, thus, said to have utilised sale proceeds in acquiring another capital asset - Held, yes

Section 11(1A)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - In accounting year relevant to assessment year in question, assessee-trust sold shares of certain companies held by it - Proceeds so realised were reinvested in fixed deposits with different parties - Whether ‘fixed deposits’ were property and would, therefore, constitute ‘capital asset’ within meaning of section 2(14) and, thus, utilisation of capital gain which arose on sale of said share by assessee was for charitable purpose - Held, yes

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1961-62 - Whether compulsory acquisition of property by State amounts its to transfer within meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act, and profits and gains arising to assessee from such compulsory acquisition must be held to be capital gains under that section - Held, yes - Whether amount of solatium forms part of compensation received by expropriated owner for compulsory acquisition of property and same would have to be taken into account in computing capital gains arising to assessee from such compulsory acquisition - Held, yes

II. Section 43B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 read with West Bengal Power Development Corporation Ltd. Employees (Death-Cum-Retirement) Benefit Regulation, 1992 and article 12 of the Constitution of India - Business disallowance - Certain deductions to be allowed only on actual payment (GPF) - Assessment years 2007-08, 2009-10, 2012-13 and 2014-15 - Assessee-West Bengal Power Development Corporation Ltd (WBPDCL) maintained two types of funds namely Contributory Provident Fund (CPF) and General Provident Fund (GPF) - CPF was a fund maintained by assessee-company and all contributions towards CPF were accounted for on accrual basis and remitted regularly to CPF Trust - Similarly GPF was a separate Fund maintained by assessee-company as per West Bengal Power Development Corporation Ltd. Employees (Death-Cum-Retirement) Benefit Regulation, 1992 - This fund was maintained for only those employees who opted for defined benefit plans under WBPDCL regulation - Assessing Officer on noticing that employer's contributions to pension fund had remained unpaid till due date of return of income under section 139(1) disallowed same under section 43B - Whether since assessee was a wholly owned State Govt undertaking set up by Govt of West Bengal under Companies Act 1956 solely and exclusively for generating electricity in State of Bengal for development of power in state, in view of article 12 of Constitution assessee was to be treated as State - Held, yes - Whether since GPF was created by notification in Official Gazette under PF Act, 1925 and since, GPF being a fund under PF Act, 1925, it was excluded from ambit of provisions of Recognized Provident Fund by virtue of PART A of Fourth Schedule of Income-tax Act, 1961 and therefore, there was merit in arguments of assessee that provisions of Income-tax Act were not applicable in case of GPF as established by assessee under PF Act - Held, yes - Whether in view of these facts, provisions of section 43B would not be applicable to assessee and even in worse case scenario, provisions of section 43B were to be applied, then contribution would be considered as paid as account was maintained by WBPDCL which was extended arm or instrumentality of State Government only - Held, yes [Paras 26, 30 and 31] [In favour of assessee]

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section  12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Whether though expression “any distribution of capital assets” as occurring in third proviso to section 12B(1) of 1922 Act governs not only partition of an HUF but also dissolution of a firm and other AOP or liquidation of a company, but same does not cover case of a company where there is no distribution of capital asset as such but only a distribution among its shareholders of amount of sale proceeds of a capital asset realised in liquidation proceedings by liquidator - Held, yes - Assessee-company went into voluntary liquidation and its capital assets were sold by liquidator - Sale proceeds realised were distributed among shareholders - Whether profits realised by sale of plant, machinery and buildings by assessee was exempt from capital gains tax under third proviso to section 12B(1) - Held, no - Whether profit realised by sale of that portion of buildings which was used for assessee’s business was exempt from capital gains tax under second proviso to section 12B(1) - Held, no

II. Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessee had its own provident fund scheme known as ‘DCM Employees Provident Fund Trust’ which was recognized under Employees Provident Funds Act, 1952 - Trust was required to declare same rate of interest for its members as was declared by Central Government under EPF Scheme, 1952 - On termination of services of its employees on closure of one of its units, when provident fund dues were required to be paid, assessee approached Regional Provident Fund Commissioner to obtain approval for sale of Government securities in order to make payment to employees - Commissioner granted permission with a caveat that in event of any deficiency on sale of securities, burden would have to be borne by assessee in order to ensure that employees would get rate of interest equivalent to rate paid by Central Government - There was a loss on sale of securities and, accordingly, assessee had to incur an expenditure to make good that loss - Assessing Officer disallowed assessee’s claim for deduction of said amount by applying provisions of section 14A - Whether expenses incurred by assessee were towards its employees and loss on sale of securities was only a trigger based on which such expenses had to be incurred by assessee and, therefore, provisions of section 14A had no applicability whatsoever - Held, yes - Whether, on facts, Tribunal was justified in allowing assessee’s claim - Held, yes

The manner, in which the Provident Fund Authorities have encashed and appropriated the term deposits of the Bank, is wholly illegal. In any event, since nothing is due to any of the employees of the Bank on account of provident fund dues, there could be no occasion for the Provident Fund Authorities to take such action, particularly when such money belongs to the poor investors and is not even the Bank’s money. Mr. Agrawal, learned Advocate for the respondent Authorities, disputes such contention.

Section 143 read with section 80CCB, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Prima facie adjustments - Assessment year 1997-98 - Whether issue as to whether benefit of indexation is to be allowed for purpose of computation of capital gains on units referred to in section 80CCB, does not fall under limited purview of section 143(1)(a) as it cannot be considered as beyond pale of debate or discussion - Held, yes

Section 45, read with section 28(i), of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Chargeable as (Profit from sale of shares) - Assessment years 2006-07, 2008-09 - Assessee-company engaged in business of finance and films, took a loan and had invested borrowed funds in shares through Portfolio Management Scheme of 'M' - Assessing Officer held income/profits earned on sale and purchase of shares, as 'business income' - Appellate authorities held same as 'Capital gain' of assessee - Whether where funds lying with assessee was always be invested in shares for earning higher returns either directly or through professionally managed Portfolio Management Scheme and by doing so, it would not mean that assessee was carrying on business of investment in shares - Held, yes - Whether Tribunal was justified in ascertaining profit from sale of shares, as capital gains - Held, yes [Para 11] [In favour of assessee]IT : Excess borrowed funds lying with assessee can always be invested in shares for earning higher returns or through professionally managed Portfolio Management Scheme; it would not mean that assessee was carrying on business of investment in shares

Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] read with section 47 of the Registration Act, 1908 and section 8 of the Transfer of property Act, 1882 - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Assessee a private company, carrying on business in different lines, entered into agreement for sale of the undertaking including all moveable and immovable properties and assets to a public company which effect from 1-12-1946 and in pursuance thereof possession of entire properties was delivered but conveyance deed in respect of immovable properties could not be executed until 26-2-1949 - ITO sought to assess assessee to capital gains tax in respect of such income as accrued to it by sale of its properties having taken place on 1-12-1946 - Whether since word ‘sale’ is not defined in Act, one must in order to find out legal implication of ‘sale’, resort to Transfer of Property Act in case of immovable property and to sale of Goods Act for movable property - Held, yes - Whether under section 8 of Transfer of property Act, even though assessee had parted with immovable properties to all intents and purposes as from 1-12-1946, in law ownership continued in it until 26-2-1949 and, therefore, sale of immovable properties having thus been effected on 26-2-1949, capital gains tax was not chargeable under section 12B - Held, yes - Whether since one sixth of properties in instant case was tenanted, same would be exempt from charge under section 12B and as no part of depreciation could be allowed in respect of tenanted portion, entire depreciation had to be deducted under provision of third proviso to section 12B(2) from fair market value only of portion which was used for business purposes - Held, yes

Section 43B of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business disallowance
¨ Where assessee State Financial Corporation had established Employees’ Provident Fund Scheme duly approved by RBI and Government and while contributing to that Fund assessee had maintained a separate management fund where two directors were responsible to hold and manage fund, disallowance of amount contributed on ground that there was no actual cash payment by employer was not justified
The assessee-State Financial Corporation had established Employees’ Provident Fund Scheme duly approved by RBI and the Government and while contributing to the said fund the assessee had maintained a separate management fund where two directors were re­sponsible to hold and manage the fund. The Assessing Officer did not allow the amount contributed by the assessee on the ground that there was no actual cash payment by the employer.
Held that the assessee-corporation was excluded from the clutches of provident fund authorities under the State of Orissa under the Employees’ Provident Fund Act and Rules as per the prior approval and sanction of the RBI and the State Government of Orissa com­bined together. So certainly it was a special case of its own nature where the general treatment of the revenue authorities could not be applicable to the assessee-corporation as it had a separate regulation of its own for administration of EPF. Even regarding interest paid on outstanding provident fund dues there was no relevance of either section 43B or section 2(24)(x) or section 36(1)(va) as that was also made by the assessee-corporation on investments made from the fund held by the corporation and utilized for the purpose of financing the industrial unit. In that backdrop of the case both factually and legally the assessee-corporation appeared to have a sound case whereas the objections raised by the revenue were general in nature without any specific finding as to any irregularity. The revenue’s treatment of the fund maintained by the assessee-corporation in general terms was not sustainable in view of the specific exception clause applicable to the assessee-corporation in the light of the analysis and observation made above. Therefore, the disallowance of contribution to PF was not justified.

facts.text:
The assessee co-operative society invested the funds of the provident fund accounts of its employees in Government securities and earned interest income by this investment. It claimed deduction from its 'income from interest' of the amount of interest payable by it to its employees on the balance of their provident fund accounts. The ITO found that the case was not covered by section 19(ii) because it was not a case of money borrowed from any one and, therefore, he dismissed the claim of the assessee. The AAC held that the provident fund amount was invested by the assessee in Government securities and it paid interest to its employees on the amount deducted from their salaries and, therefore, it was entitled to claim deduction. The Tribunal held that the assessee could be said to have borrowed moneys for the purpose of making investment in the Government securities within the meaning of section 19(ii) and, therefore, upheld the order of the AAC allowing the assessee's claim of deduction.

On reference :

The assessee and one ‘G’ were partners in three partnership concerns and those concerns were managing agent of there different mills. As per partnership deeds they were free to sell or mortgage their shares in the partnership. The assessee transferred his shares in one company to ‘G’ and as a condition of transfer ‘G’ paid Rs. 1,00,000 in cash in addition to the shares held by him in other two firms to assessee. The department treated this sum as capital gains liable to tax under section 12B. The assessee appealed without success. The assessee contended that the right of a partner in a partnership which had a managing agency was not a capital asset as defined by section 2(4A) and even if it was a capital asset, the requirements of section 12B were not satisfied, because there was no sale, exchange or transfer.

On reference:

While processing the return under section 143(1)(a), benefit of indexation on section 80CCB investment, as claimed by the assessee, had not been allowed for calculating capital gains for the assessment year 1997-98 as per the second proviso to section 48. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal :

In 1954, the assessee-company had purchased certain shares of a company. During accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1959-60, the assessee sold these shares to three ladies at a lower price. On 11-11-1959, the directors of the assessee resolved that the difference between the cost price and sale price of the shares might be treated as a gift to the purchasers. However, the ITO invoked first proviso to section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act and treated the difference between the cost and the market prices, as a capital gain on the sale of the shares made during the year of account. The Tribunal found as a fact that the sale was a real transaction which was given effect to and acted upon by the parties thereto and that further it was not made with the object of avoidance or reduction of tax liability but made for the purpose of benefiting the ladies and as a matter of fact, the motive for the sale might have been the natural love and affection for and desire to provide the ladies. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the second condition for application of the proviso to section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act had not been satisfied and that, therefore, the proviso could not be invoked.

On reference:

The assessee was joint with his brother prior to 1932. There was a partition in the year 1932 and the property in question came to the share of assessee. As assessee had sons, it became the joint property of the assessee and his sons. There was a partition between the assessee and his sons on 9-6-1944 and the concerned property came to the share of the assessee. The assessee sold it in 1947 and earned profits. The assessee claimed exemption from capital gains tax on the ground that his case fell within the second proviso to section 12B(1). But the Tribunal did not agree.

On reference:

The assessee-company was the managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies. The assessee held majority of conversion shares of those companies. 'D' company wrote a letter to the assessee mentioning that it wanted to purchase conversion shares of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency.

In a meeting of board of directors of the assessee-company, offer of 'D' company was accepted and it was stated in its minutes that out of the total amount received from the sale of the shares, a sum of Rs. 1 crore should be paid to the assessee company as compensation for the loss of the managing agency of the two mills. Subsequently, 'D' company wrote a letter to assessee wherein it was mentioned that assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in their favour, should resign it so that at the time of delivery of shares, managing agency would have come to an end. The assessee, accordingly, wrote to the 'M' and 'S' companies that it had decided to resign the office of the managing agency and tendered its resignation. ITO brought to tax the amount received in lieu of waving managing agency. The AAC as well as Tribunal held that the assessee company had sold the managing agency and therefore the profits or gains arising from that sale were capital gains within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court, however, held that there was neither a sale nor a transfer of the managing agency within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

The assessee, a public charitable trust realised capital gains on sale of shares held by it. After allowing an admissible deduction at 65% the ITO included the balance in the total income of the assessee.

On appeal, the assessee contended before the AAC that though it had a substantial interest in the company of which shares were sold, the income arising from the said capital gain was exempt under section 11. The AAC rejected the contention having regard to the provisions of section 13 and dismissed the appeal.

On second appeal, the Tribunal taking a view that the charge to capital gains arose from the transfer of a capital asset and not merely from the holding of the capital asset, held that the income form capital gains could not be considered to be income arising from the investment and could not be included in the total income of the assessee.

On reference:

The assessee-trust sold gold certain quantity of, received by way of a corpus donation in the preceding year and made certain profit. The assessee claimed that the net consideration of the sale was kept in fixed deposit with the bank, and was thus utilized for acquiring a new capital asset. It was claimed that the capital gain was, therefore, exempt under section 11(1A). The ITO found that the sale proceeds of gold were lent on interest to two concerns which were subsequently repaid and credited in the assessee's bank account and out of the amount received from the said parties, the assessee trust again gave a loan to 'B'. The ITO, therefore, did not accept the assessee's contention and, accordingly, did not allow exemption in respect of capital gains under section 11(1A). The AAC allowed the exemption to the assessee. The Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC.

On reference:

The assessee’s income included interest from a provident fund, the quantum of which was in excess of the statutory rate as prescribed by the Government. The assessee’s contention that the said interest was eligible for deduction under section 8OL, since the trustees of the provident fund earned interest from bank on its investments, was rejected by the ITO and the AAC, on the basis of a Special Bench decision of the Tribunal.

On second appeal :

In the relevant accounting year, the assessee, a charitable trust, sold certain lands resulting in capital gain. The assessee invested a part of sale consideration in fixed deposit with the Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC). The assessee claimed that the capital gains arising on account of transfer of the aforesaid land would not be included in its total income, as the investment in fixed deposit with MSRTC amounted to utilisation of the consideration for acquiring another capital asset to be held wholly for charitable purpose and, as such, the said amount would be deemed to have been applied for charitable purposes as laid down in section 11(1A). In support of its claim, the assessee relied upon Instruction No. 883 dated 24-9-1975 issued by the Board. The ITO rejected the assessee’s claim holding that the fixed deposit was not a capital asset and, as such, the provisions of section 11(1A) were not attracted. The AAC upheld the ITO’s order.

On second appeal :

The deceased left a will by which a bank was appointed executor of his estate. The bank gave the power of attorney to the appellant. The appellant made an application to the High Court under section 24I (sic) of the Indian Succession Act and on that application obtained letters of administration with a copy of the will annexed. In the course of administration of the estate of the deceased, the appellant sold certain shares and securities belonging to the deceased for the purpose of distributing the assets amongst the legatees. The sale of these shares and securities realised more than their cost price. The excess of the sale price over the cost price was treated by the ITO as capital gain under section 12B of the 1922 Act. These amounts of capital gain were brought to tax for the relevant assessment years along with certain dividend and interest income which had accrued or had been received in the relevant years of account. Not satisfied with these assessments, the appellant preferred appeal to the Tribunal and urged three points in support of his contention that the assessments were invalid: firstly, that section 12B of the 1922 Act imposing a tax on capital gains is ultra vires the Government of India Act, 1935; secondly, that under section 24B of the 1922 Act, the appellant was only liable to pay tax which the testator would have been liable to pay and as these capital assets were not sold by the testator, there was no liability upon the appellant; and thirdly, that the sale of the shares and securities by the appellant under the will of the deceased came within the purview of the third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act and, therefore, was not to be treated as a sale of capital assets under section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act. The Tribunal repelled the first two contentions, but accepted the third as correct and in that view allowed the two appeals in part. It directed the ITO to delete from the assessed income the capital gains made by the sale of shares and securities. On reference, the High Court decided against the appellant.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

The trustee under the trust deed, were to hold the property of the trust for the purposes of meetings, dramatic or other entertainments or other objects of like nature, in which the public may be interested as also private entertainment baring political meetings. The trustees were not bound to charge a rent, but in cases they might charge a reasonable rent. They had discretion to let rooms for private entertainment and to charge a rent. Further the trustees had no obligation to apply the income derived from the letting to any specifies charitable objects. They were free to utilize the monies subject only to their obligation to invest the surplus in the securities authorised by section 20 of the Indian Trusts Act. It was no doubt open to them to utilize the income and also the excess amount, if any available with them for creating the depreciation reserve as also for meeting the expenses of periodical renewal. It was also open to them to utilize those monies to constitute a provident fund for the employees of the trust.

According to the Tribunal the assessee-trust was not entitled to exemption under section 11.

On reference :

The assessee-firm acted as the managing agent of a company year received a larger commission. Out of its commission, the assessee purchased shares of that company on 23-5-1955, for the total price of Rs. 7,15,399. On 26-4-1956, the assessee transferred the aforesaid shares to the various partners in proportion to their shares in the firm at book value , i.e., actual cost. The Income-tax Officer, however, found that the market value of the shares on 26-4-1956, was Rs. 8,03,080. He held that the transaction was made in order to avoid the tax liability on the assessee; both capital gains tax as well as the tax on registered firm; that this transaction was a device when the shares were transferred at cost and that to this transaction the provisions of section 12B(2) applied.

He therefore, held that the difference of Rs. 87,681 was capital gain of the assessee and included this amount as income in computing the tax liability of the assessee for the assessment year 1957-58.

On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner affirmed the action of Income-tax Officer.

On second appeal, the Tribunal held in favour of the assessee-firm that a transfer was not involved in the transaction as required under the provisions of section 12B(2).

On reference :

The assessee held certain shares of Company ‘G’ and was also the managing agent of said company. On 31-8-1946 one ‘T’ made on offer to assessee to purchase aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ and also offered pay certain amount for getting the rights of the managing agency. The assessee adopted the said offer. On 7-1-1947, the assessee wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting their resignation from the office of managing agents of the company, and, further recommending that ‘T’ be appointed as managing agents in their place. The registration of managing agents was accepted by company ‘G’ and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agent was also accepted. For the assessment year the ITO computed the capital gains and assessed it in the hands of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. Before Tribunal the assessee contended that the AAC was in error in holding that the assessee had made any capital gain as a result of the transfer of managing agency as the transaction between the assessee and ‘T’ was not of either sale or transfer the AAC had found that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in loss and that the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. The Tribunal, however, in its order observed that the finding of the AAC that there was capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares was not correct, and for the reasons stated by it in its order, the Tribunal held that having regard to the various aspects of the case, the value of the shares of company ‘G’ as on 1-1-1939, could not be more than 60 per cent of what it was at the time of the sale.

On reference :

The assessee, a public charitable trust, was entitled to exemption under section 11. During the previous year ending on 31-3-1981 relevant to the assessment year 1981-82 it sold shares of companies for a total sum of Rs. 63,52,565. A capital gain of Rs. 40,27,099 arose therefrom. The assessee made a fixed deposit of Rs. 31,75,000 within the previous year with a scheduled bank for a period of 60 days. As the assessee-trust did not receive the entire sale proceeds during the said previous year, it exercised the option of applying a part of the capital gain in the following previous year as provided in the Explanation 2 to section 11. The assessee claimed that no tax could be charged on the capital gains arising out of sale of said shares, as it had acquired another capital asset during the previous year and for the balance sum it had exercised its option to utilize the same in the following previous year. The ITO held that the fixed deposit with the banks did not constitute a capital asset and the benefit under section 11(1A) could not be claimed. He, therefore, rejected the claim of the assessee. He also rejected the assessee's claim of having exercised the option to invest the remaining sum in the following year. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO. On further appeals by the department and the assessee, the Tribunal held that the investment in the said fixed deposit amounted to acquisition of a capital asset within the meaning of section 11(1A) and that the trust had also exercised an option to invest the balance capital gains in the following year. It, therefore, held that the capital gains could not be assessed in the hands of the assessee-trust.

On reference :

In the accounting period 1-4-1980 to 31-3-1981 relevant to the assessment year,1981-82, the assessee-trust sold the shares of certain companies held by it. The proceeds so realised were invested in fixed deposits with different parties. The assessee claimed that the net consideration of capital gain arose out of the sale of shares deemed to have been applied for charitable purpose since it had acquired ‘another capital asset’ within the meaning of the aforesaid term occurring in section 11(1A). The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim and held that the capital gain arose on sale of shares was assessable as its income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal:

The assessee was a member of an approved provident fund constituted by his employer and recognised by the Commissioner under section 58B(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922. One of the rules governing the fund and its administration provided for the investment of the funds received by the trustees and for the payment of interest realised thereby to the members. For the assessment years 1975-76 and 1976-77 the assessee received interest from the investments made out of the amounts belonging to the fund and the interest received in excess of the limit prescribed under rule 6(b) of Part A of the Fourth Schedule was assessed under the head 'Salaries' in the hands of the assessee. On appeal before the AAC, the assessee claimed deduction under section 80L in respect of the excess interest amount so added to his income. The AAC, however, disallowed the assessee's claim on the ground that by virtue of section 17(1)( vi) and rule 6 of Part A of the Fourth Schedule, the amounts were rightly assessed under the head 'Salaries', and, therefore, there was no question of permitting any deduction under section 80L. On second appeal, the Tribunal held that the interest amounts paid to the assessee were 'salary' only for limited purposes and would not partake of the nature of 'salary' and that the trustees were the owners of the fund and the investment of the funds was for the benefit of the beneficiaries and not on their behalf and that as the interest was paid to the assessee and others only on behalf of the trustees of the fund, such interest did not emanate from any of the sources mentioned in section 80L and, therefore, the deduction under section 80L was not available to the assessee.

On reference:

The assessee, a society registered under section 12AA, was running an educational institution.

During the assessment year under consideration, the assessee sold a land for certain amount. The purpose of sale was to use the sale proceeds for expansion of the educational activities. However, the amount was advanced to a limited company AIPL in which trustee and his wife were directors.

The Assessing Officer treated the income from sale of land as income of the assessee and also denied exemption under section 11 as the amount advanced to AIPL was not an approved investment under section 11(5) and, thus, provisions of section 13(1)(c) were attracted. The income of the assessee was computed as 'AOP' under section 164(2).

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) held that condition of section 13(3) was not fulfilled as the Assessing Officer had not proved as to what benefit accrued to the specified person from the advancement of amount in question to AIPL. Regarding denying the exemption under section 11 and assessing the assessee under section 164(2), the Commissioner (Appeals) had given a finding that there was valid registration under section 12AA and since this was not cancelled or withdrawn by the Commissioner, benefit of section 11 could not be denied. Further, he observed that the capital gain arising out of transfer of capital asset was to be assessed as per section 48 and the rate was to be applied as per section 112 and not at the maximum marginal rate as suggested by the Assessing Officer.

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee, entered into an agreement with ‘C’ on 8-2-1960. Under the agreement the assessee was to convey certain property in favour of the purchaser for a sum of Rs. 4,35,000. A further stipulation between the parties was that the sale deeds should be executed either in favour of ‘C’ or his nominees. A sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was paid and there remained a balance of Rs. 3,35,000 which was to be paid before 31-5-1960. The balance was paid on two dates, 15-9-1960, and 13-11-1960. As per the stipulation, sale deeds were executed in favour of the nominees of ‘C’, the first of which was on 15-3-1961, and the last on 20-10-1962. On 24-11-1961, the assessee purchased some other bungalow for his residential purpose for Rs. 94,850. The assessee, on that basis, claimed the benefit of section 12B(b). The benefit claimed by the assessee was disallowed in the first instance on the view that the sale was not finalised as maintained by the assessee in December, 1960, and that the full payment for the transactions had been received by 13-11-1960. The ITO thought that the transfer took place long before December 1960, particularly because the ‘M’ Limited, which by an arrangement with ‘C’ paid the balance of consideration, was arranging to let out the property. The AAC took, however, a different view. He considered that the sale of the property was not completed by the end of the accounting year and therefore, no question of capital gains arose. On a departmental appeal, which was dismissed, the Tribunal accepted the contention for the assessee that the property could be said to have been transferred only when a sale deed was executed, and that as the purchase of the property in December, 1961, was sufficiently within the time during which the sale deeds were executed in relation to parcels of the property, the assessee would be entitled to the benefit of section 12B(4)(b).

On reference :

The assessee-society was registered under section 12A. The main activities of the society were educational in nature.

The assessee disposed of some of its investments giving rise to capital gains of Rs. 68.88 lakhs and that it made further investments. It was the assessee's contention that the investments disposed of being its capital assets held under Trust wholly for charitable purposes and the net consideration from such disposal having been utilized for acquiring other capital assets held under Trust wholly for charitable purposes, the capital gains arising from such disposal of the original investments were required to be treated as applied to charitable purposes in terms of section 11(1A) to the extent specified there under.

The Assessing Officer accepted the assessee's contention to the extent of Rs. 67 lakhs. However, in respect of reinvestment which was not held as capital asset up to the end of the year, i.e., 31-3-2007, the Assessing Officer denied the assessee's claim.

On appeal, same was affirmed by Commissioner (Appeals).

On second appeal:

The petitioner, who belonged to the Indian Civil Service, took a loan of Rs. 65,000 from his provident fund as a non-refundable advance in 1958-59 and spent it along with his own Rs. 13,000 in buying and reconstructing a house He sold the said house for Rs. 1,25,000 without obtaining the prior permission of the Government. As the petitioner parted with the possession of the house contrary to rule 7E(1) of the Indian Civil Service Provident Fund Rules, the sum withdrawn by him became payable together with interest thereon amounting to Rs. 27,932 by him as the subscriber to the fund under rule 7E(2). The petitioner paid the amount with interest to his fund accordingly. In calculating income-tax payable on 'capital gains' under section 48 the petitioner deducted from the sale proceeds of the house the interest of Rs. 27,932, as expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer of the house in addition to the cost of acquisition of the said house stating that this interest was compulsorily payable on the sale of the house, so that the capital gain by selling the house could not possibly be earned without making this payment of the Government. The ITO assessed the income-tax on 'capital gains' solely on the basis of the representation made by the petitioner. Subsequently a notice under section 148 was issued to the petitioner by the ITO stating that the ITO got information from audit department that interest was not compulsorily payable, that it became payable only because this house was sold in contravention of the provision of rule 7E of the I.C.S. Provident Fund Rules and since deposit in the provident fund including the interest accruing thereon belonged to the depositor, only repayment was deferred, and thus payment of this interest could not be treated as expenditure.

On writ petition to quash the notice, the petitioner contended that ( 1) No income had escaped assessment within the meaning of section 147 because the interest paid by the petitioner on the loan taken from his provident fund was paid to the Government; that it became a part of the Consolidated Fund of India, that is, the property of the Government and was, therefore, expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with the transfer of the house within the meaning of section 48(1).(2) that even if the interest was paid into the petitioner's own account in the provident fund and thus continued to belong to the petitioner without becoming the property of the Government, this information was known to the ITO at the time of the assessment and did not become known to him subsequently and the said officer thus had no jurisdiction to make the reassessment under section 147(b).

The Canara Bank floated through Canstar Mutual Fund, the Canstar Scheme, 1990 which offered; two types of units, namely, CG Canstar and 80L Canstar. Under both the schemes interest not less than 12.5 per cent accrued each year, but there was no disbursal as the income so declared was ploughed back for investment purposes. In the case of 80L Canstar holders a certificate was given for purposes of filing the income-tax return, but in the case of CG Canstar holders, such a certificate was not given as the payment was to be made on the termination or at the time of re-purchase of the Canstar. In other words, the only difference between the two schemes was that in the case of 80L Canstar the interest income was declared every year whereas in the case of CG Canstar the payment was made at the time of the repurchase.

On the aforesaid facts, the issue was whether the interest income, which accrued to the CG Canstar holders but was postponed for payment, became an accretion to the capital value of the investment for purposes of capital gains or whether the same was a revenue receipt distinct and separate from the capital invested by the assessee.

There was a difference of opinion between the Members and a reference was made under section 255(4) to the Third Member.

The assessee purchased in 1959, a plot of land with a building and some trees thereon for Rs. 67,000. He sold portions of the land in the accounting periods relevant to the assessment years 1960-61 and 1961-62. The ITO computed the capital gains at Rs. 5,500 for the assessment year 1960-61 and at Rs. 10,500 for the assessment year 1961-62. The case of the assessee was that the land concerned was agricultural land and that as a result the provisions of section 12B of 1922 Act were not attracted to the profits or gains arising from the sales he made.

The Commission in his order under section 33B held that the land concerned was not agricultural in character but a "capital asset" within the meaning of that expression as defined in section 2(4A) of the 1922 Act.

On petition :

The assessee-company purchased vacant land with an object to grow herbs and plants for medicinal purposes and to construct a warehouse for stocking its goods. The land was, however, compulsorily acquired by the State Government and the assessee obtained a sum as compensation and, made a profit out of the purchase of said land.

The assessee claimed exemption from tax on this amount on the ground that section 12B(1) of 1922 Act was not applicable. The ITO held that the land was a 'capital asset' within the meaning of section 2(4A) of 1922 Act, and therefore, section 12B of 1922 Act was attracted. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order of AAC.

On reference:

The assessee purchased some plots of cultivable land. Subsequently, assessee entered into an agreement with a school committee to construct a building for use as a school. The committee occupied the building and paid rent. Later on, the committee decided to buy the property and after some negotiations the assessee sold the land and building for profit. The assessee claimed that all the land, except that actually occupied by the building in use as a school house, was held by him as agricultural land, and that any profit made by the sale of such agricultural land was excluded from the operation of section 12B as agricultural land was not a capital asset as defined by section 2(4A). However, the department assessed the profits to capital gains tax which was upheld by the Tribunal .

On reference :

interpret the crucial provision, namely, the proviso to section 112(1) with reference to the supposed intention of the legislature when such intention is not clearly ascertainable. The best course would be to go by the plain language which is to be understood in the manner in which we have explained earlier. The objective is to be inferred from the language itself. The interpretation we are placing does not run counter to the language employed nor does it lead to any absurdity or anomaly.

ITAT’s decision 14. Now we shall turn our attention to the order of the ITAT, "H" Bench, Mumbai in ITA No. 2552 of 2005 on which strong reliance has been placed by Revenue. The learned Members of the Tribunal held that the Legis- lature never intended to give the benefit of proviso to section 112(1) to those cases where long-term capital gain is required to be computed under the first proviso to section 48. The Tribunal purported to reach the con- clusion on a literal construction of the proviso, the language of which, the Tribunal acknowledges, is unambiguous. With due respect to the lear- ned Members of Tribunal, we find it difficult to appreciate the observation that the literal construction of proviso leads to the meaning it has attributed to the provision. The Tribunal failed to note that there are no words of exclusion of the assessees like the applicant governed by the first proviso to section 48. Nor can they be inferred by necessary implication. It appears that the Tribunal’s views is based on the premise that the legislature did not intend to provide two reliefs to a non-resident assessee - one under the proviso to section 48 and another under the proviso to section 112(1). As already discussed in the preceding para, no such legislative intention can be imputed to the legislature except by way of some guess work or a priori reasoning. The assumption of the Tribunal that it was giving effect to literal construction as well as legislative intent is incorrect. The further observation of the Tribunal that if the legislature intended to cover the cases falling under the first proviso to section 48, it would not have used the words ‘second proviso to section 48’ [in the proviso to section 112(1)] is based on a wrong premise. One does not follow from the other. The second proviso to section 48 should necessarily be mentioned in the proviso to section 112(1) as the tax rate of 10 per cent should be calculated without reference to the indexation formula that is applicable to the resident assessees. Hence, the reference to 2nd proviso to section 48 cannot be avoided. The only question is about the connotation of the expression "before giving effect to the second proviso to section 48" - whether those words have the effect of excluding those who cannot avail of the indexation benefit under the 2nd proviso, that is to say, the non-residents including foreign companies. We are of the considered opinion, for the reasons already set out, that the crucial phrase in the proviso to section 112(1) does not have such effect.

14.1 The learned Members of the Tribunal placed much reliance on sub-section (3) to section 115AD by way of contrast with the language of the proviso to section 112(1). Section 115 AD, inter alia, provides that where the total income of a foreign institutional investor includes income by way of capital gain arising from the transfer of securities, the amount of income-tax calculated on the said income shall be at the rate of 10 per cent. Sub-section (3) says nothing contained in the first and second provisos to section 48 shall apply for the computation of capital gains arising out of the transfer of securities...’. After referring to sub-section (3), the Tribunal makes an observation that "if the legislature had intended to give benefit of marginal relief of tax to all non-residents, it could have easily used the words ‘first and second provisos of section 48’. The Tribunal missed to note that by adding the words ‘first proviso’, the intended result will not be achieved. On the other hand, the position of non-resident will be worse. For these reasons, we have no hesitation in differing with the view taken by the Tribunal.
