16A.1

INTRODUCTION

Capital gains, being the fourth specie of total income of an assessee, are covered in sections 45 to 55AA of the Income-tax Act (the Act) and are contained in Chapter IV-E of the Act. Though these sections numbering about 25 form approximately 7 to 8% of the entire Income-tax Act, capital gain issues occupy nearly 15 to 20% of the cases reported in various tax journals and websites. One of the main issues which should engage the attention of the Legislature is prohibiting an assessee from making a claim in respect of investments in an altogether different name or in the name of distant relative as, in the considered opinion of the author, it is not the intention of the Legislature. The proviso to section 54F of the Act imposes certain restrictions with regard to holding and acquiring properties and so if the investments in different names are permitted to be made, the provisions of section 54F of the Act may get defeated/ diluted and the issue may go out of the purview of the Revenue as the assessee, if given an option, may invest in the name of another person thereby making way for probable escapement of income. In this article case laws pertaining to investment made in the names different relatives have been analyzed. The various decisions rendered by the judicial authorities have not been grouped in one or two paragraphs but have been covered in different paragraphs in order to highlight the issues covered in those decisions by these judicial authorities.

32.4

CAPITAL GAINS KEPT IN FIXED DEPOSIT IN BANK

In CIT v. Hindustan Welfare Trusts [1993] 70 Taxman 93 (Cal.) the assessee sold shares in limited companies resulting in capital gain being Rs. 40.27 lakhs. The assessee trust made a fixed deposit with a scheduled bank for a period of 60 days. In the next financial year, the assessee trust encashed the fixed deposit and gave loans to various parties. The assessee received a portion of sale consideration in the next previous year and the trust exercised the option of applying the capital gains in the following previous year as provided in Explanation 2 to section 11(1).

The Assessing Officer taxed the entire amount of capital gain as income of the trust and held that the fixed deposit is not a capital asset and hence the benefit of section 11(1A) could not be claimed by the trust. The first appellate authority viz. CIT (Appeals) upheld the order of Assessing Officer saying that the fixed deposit is not equivalent to acquisition of capital asset. The Tribunal however held that the fixed deposit is an investment which amounted to acquisition of capital asset and hence the benefit of section 11(1A) must be given to the assessee.

The Court held that making deposit in a bank would amount to acquisition of capital asset and therefore eligible for the exemption under section 11(1A). The decision was given in favour of the assessee holding that fixed deposit in banks are capital assets. Also, the Court held that "no minimum duration of the deposit can be set forth as the determinative criterion to decide whether a bank deposit in a bank takes on the colour of an asset of a specie separate from cash fund from the sale of an asset". CBDT's Instruction No. 883 clarifying that only fixed deposits with bank for 6 months or mere would be capital asset for section 11(1A) was held to be without any legal basis.

8.14

Scope of Part B of ICDS-VIII (Revised) dealing with Securities held by a Scheduled Bank or Public Financial Institution

Para 1 of Part B of this ICDS clarifies that this part deals with securities held by the following entities:

a scheduled bank or

public financial institutions formed under a Central or a State Act or so declared under the Companies Act, 1956 or the Companies Act, 2013

Unlike Part A, this Part (Part B) deals with securities held by Scheduled banks or public financial institutions. Therefore, this Part will not apply to securities held by mutual funds, banks other than scheduled banks, insurance companies and financial institutions other than Public Financial Institutions.

Part A deals with securities held as stock-in-trade while this Part is silent on this aspect. A question, therefore, arises whether this Part will also apply to securities held as investments. Securities held as stock-in-trade are excluded from the definition of 'capital asset' in section 2(14) of the Act while securities held as investments are very much capital assets. Therefore, profits and gains from sale/transfer of securities held as investments will be taxed as capital gains. ICDSs do not apply to computation of income under the head "Capital Gains". Therefore, Part B also applies only to securities held as stock in trade.

The classification of securities by bank as stock-in-trade or as investment should be made according to RBI Guidelines and norms. CBDT's Circular No. 665, dated 5 October, 1993, clarifies as follows:

"The question whether a particular item of investment in securities constitutes stock-in-trade or a capital asset is a question of fact. In fact, the banks are generally governed by the instructions of the Reserve Bank of India from time to time with regard to the classification of assets and also the accounting standards for investments. The Board has, therefore, decided that the Assessing Officers should determine on the facts and circumstances of each case as to whether any particular security constitutes stock-in-trade or investment taking into account the guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India in this regard from time to time."

Part B of ICDS is also silent on provision regarding recognition of income on securities (interest/dividend etc.). Therefore, computation of income from such sources would be as per normal provisions of the Act read with ICDS IV(Revised)- Revenue Recognition.

The following provisions may be noted:

Income in the hands of investment fund, other than income from profits and gains of business, shall be exempt from tax. [Section 10(23FBA)]

AE, 44B, 44BBA and 44BBB provide that notwithstanding anything contained in sections 28 to 43C/44, etc., (as the case may be as per the relevant section), a certain amount calculated on the basis of specified percentage of the specified base would be deemed to be income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'.

Such deemed profits would be included in total income of the concerned company when its Normal TI is computed. Even in such cases, if Normal TI is less than 30% of book profits, section 115JA of the Act would apply and such book profits would constitute its total income.

This is because:

◆ Section 115JA of the Act affects total income computed under normal provisions of the Act which include the aforesaid sections.

◆ The field of operation of section 44AD, etc. is different and restricted. They deem a certain amount as profits chargeable under the said head and not total income.

1.14-6 Capital gains and rate of tax - In case of a company engaged in investment business, in respect of investments held as capital assets, under the Act, income on sale of such assets would be chargeable as capital gains. For the purpose of computing capital gains, prescribed method of arriving at cost of acquisition or cost of improvement are to be applied. As a result, the capital gains may be substantially lower then the profits which are booked in the accounts. Even, in such a case, provisions of section 115JA of the Act may apply and the company may be liable to pay tax on 30% of its book profits.

For the purpose of levy of tax on long term capital gains, section 112 prescribes a concessional rate, which, in the case of a company, with effect from assessment year 1997-98 is 20%.

In the above case, the issue is; what is the rate of tax chargeable ?

There could be two possible views, which are discussed hereinafter in little detail.

As per one view, the effect of section 115JA of the Act is as follows :

◆ Section 115JA deems a certain part of book profits as total income. Such computation is irrespective of the head. The provision does not prescribe any rate of tax.

◆ Sub-section (4) of section 115JA provides that save as otherwise provided in that provision, all other provisions of the Act would apply.

◆ Accordingly, the deemed total income is computed. Section 2(45) defines 'total income' to mean as total amount of income referred to in section 5, computed in the manner laid down in this Act. In the context of section 115JA, it would therefore mean income referred to in section 115JA and computed in the manner laid down in that section.

◆ Section 4 creates a charge on total income. The charge is to be determined with reference to rate or rates of tax as may be prescribed by a Central Act.

◆ The rate of tax is prescribed by a Finance Act. For assessment year 1997-98, the rates for the purpose of advance tax are prescribed by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1996. The provisions are contained in section 2(7) of the said Finance Act and Part III of the First Schedule to the said Act prescribes the rate of tax, which includes the rate of tax prescribed under Chapter XII of the Act in respect of any income chargeable to tax under Chapter XII. Section 112 forms part of Chapter XII and prescribes rate of tax on long term capital gains.

◆ The said provisions read as follows :

'Where the total income of an assessee includes any income..., chargeable under the head 'Capital gains", the tax payable by the assessee on the total income shall be the aggregate of,—

(a) …………..

(b) in the case of a domestic company—

(i) The amount of income-tax payable on the total income as reduced by ... such long term capital gains,....; and

(ii) The amount of income-tax calculated on such long term capital gains at the rate of twenty per cent.'

◆ As is evident from section 4 read with above provisions prescribing the rate, the tax is on total income. Section 112 of the Act lays down the manner in which tax is computed where total income includes any income arising from transfer of a long term capital asset. The said provision applies to section 115JA also.

◆ 30% of the books profit also includes the amount embedded in book profits, which are chargeable under the head 'Capital gains'. Accordingly, to the extent of profit which represents income chargeable under the head capital gains, it is taxable at the rate prescribed by section 112.

The other view could be :

The moment Normal IT is ignored, by applying section 115JA of the Act, manner of computation and charge under different heads, etc., are nullified.

◆ Accordingly, when 30% of book profits is total income on which tax is payable, this is a total income as computed under section 115JA of the Act and not the one computed as per normal provisions.

3.7-1 Receiving gifts in the form of impermissible investments

A question that arises is whether a charitable institution can accept gift of impermissible investments. This is explained separately for shares and other assets.

3.7-1a Other impermissible assets

So far as assets other than shares are concerned, the relevant clause reads as follows:

"…any income thereof, if for any period during the previous year-

(i) any funds of the trust or institution are invested or deposited after the 28th day of February, 1983 otherwise than in any one or more of the forms or modes specified in sub-section (5) of section 11;

…

to the extent of such deposits or investments referred to in sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iii).

Thus, the clause applies in respect of funds invested or deposited otherwise than in permissible modes. It has been held in a series of decisions that when a charitable institution receives a gift, its funds are not invested or deposited within the meaning of the aforesaid sub-clause [Auditor Dasaradha Rami Reddy Charities v. CIT [1989] 44 Taxman 453 (Mad.); CIT v. Birla Charity Trust [1987] 34 Taxman 504 (Cal.); CIT v. Sir Shri Ram Foundation [2001] 116 Taxman 113 (Delhi)]. Hence, the amendment does not affect the taxation of other impermissible assets received as a gift. Incidentally, such assets could have been held by the institution even under the pre-amendment law without losing any exemption; however, after the amendment, if the income of the charitable institution is actually invested or deposited in impermissible modes (say, debentures of a private company) the amount of income so invested in making such investment will not enjoy exemption under section 11(1) and be liable to tax under section 13(1)(d).

3.7-1b Shares

So far as shares are concerned, under the pre-amended law, shares could not be held by a charitable institution, even if they were donated to the institution. After the amendment, the exact language of the amendment is "to the extent of such deposits or investments referred to in sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iii)". It is pertinent that sub-clause (iii), which deals with shares does not at all use the expression "such deposits or investments." On the other hand, income is not invested if shares are received as a gift and hence, on a plain reading, in such a case, no part of income can be regarded as invested.

The matter is not very clear, but it appears that:

(a)

income invested in shares is taxable under section 13 (1)(d)

(b)

shares received as gifts are not taxable.

As mentioned above, the aforesaid view is also supported by the Explanatory Memorandum, reproduced in para 3.7 above.

The law is silent on the income from such impermissible investment. It appears that such income (including capital gains) qualifies for exemption under section 11(1)(a) and is entitled to the benefit of the deemed application under Explanation 1(2) or secondary accumulation for 5 years under section 11(2). Further, the capital gains from investment should also qualify for benefit under section 11(1A).

Proviso (iia) to section 13(1)(d) provides that nothing in the section shall apply if the impermissible investment is not held beyond the expiry of one year from the end of the previous year in which such impermissible investment is acquired. This proviso continues to apply even after the amendment. Hence, income shall not be taxable under the amended section 13(1)(d) if the impermissible investment is liquidated on or before the expiry of the year subsequent to the year in which it is acquired. To illustrate, suppose an assessee buys preference shares in a company on 15th March 2023. If it transfers the shares on or before 31st March 2024, no part of its income will be taxable. On the other hand, if it transfers the shares on 4th April 2024, the income to the extent of the cost of shares will be taxable under section 13(1)(d).

The amount of taxable income is not liable to penalty under section 271AAE (please see para 11).

ADVANCE RECEIPT OF SALE PROCEEDS USED FOR REGULAR OBJECTS

In Trustees of Shri Ramnagar Trust v. Third ITO [1985] 13 ITD 426 (Bom. - Trib.) the trust entered into a sale agreement and received sale proceeds in instalments over a period of years and later executed the sale deed. The amounts received in instalments prior to transfer were applied towards achieving the objects of the trust. The assessee contended that the application made already must be taken as deemed application within the meaning of section 11(1). The Court held that section 11(1) does not specify the point at which the income has to be spent. Accordingly, it was held that the assessee had adjusted the advances against the sale consideration. Hence, the income of the assessee by way of capital gains had been applied in a manner entitling it to claim exemption under section 11(1) of the Act.

In Gurparshad Trust v. Dy. CIT [2005] 93 TTJ (Chd. - Trib.) 1103 the issue for consideration was whether the trust was eligible for exemption under section 11 even when the sale proceeds of the capital asset were utilized for the purpose for which the trust was created. The assessee sold a land for Rs. 22.58 lakhs and had income computed at Rs. 22.48 lakhs. The amount spent towards the objects of the trust was claimed as exempt which the Assessing Officer denied. The Revenue contended that section 11(1A) has been specifically incorporated and if the conditions therein were not complied with, the assessee was not entitled to exemption in respect of the capital gains derived on sale of immovable property. The assessee contended that section 11(1A) was incorporated for enlarging the benefit of exemption, so as to enable the charitable trust to purchase capital asset in lieu of capital gains derived from the sale of trust property. The assessee also gave donation to yet another trust. The Tribunal held that the expenses were incurred on the maintenance of the trust property which were attached to the trust and being utilized for charitable purpose, the trust was eligible for exemption as it has applied its income for the objects for which it was created. The issue was thus decided in favour of the assessee.

Proviso to section 112 - If proviso to section 112(1) is applied, then almost all the assessees covered by the 1st proviso to section 48 would be liable to pay tax @ 10% only and not @ 20% on LTCG. This appears to be correct and a logical consequence of the proviso to section 112(1) but this cannot be a ground to contextually read the proviso to section 112(1) differently. The said proviso is applicable to listed securities (excluding units) or zero coupon bonds. LTCG is not payable on listed securities sold through stock exchanges as STT is payable. 1st proviso to section 48 is applicable on sale of shares or debentures in Indian company, whether or not the said shares or debentures are listed or not. Thus, proviso to section 112(1) is more restrictive and will not necessarily apply in all cases covered by the 1st proviso to section 48. Secondly, the proviso to section 112(1) is not applicable to debentures. Nevertheless, the proviso to section 112(1) is applicable to zero coupon bonds, which are not covered by the 1st proviso to section 48 [Cairn UK Holdings Ltd. v. DIT [2013] 38 taxmann.com 179/[2014] 220 Taxman 230 (Delhi)].

CONCESSIONAL TAX RATE OF 10% NOT APPLICABLE TO LONG-TERM CAPITAL GAINS FROM UNITS OF GETFs/DEBT-ORIENTED MUTUAL FUNDS [SECTION 112(1)]

Section 112 relates to tax on long-term capital gains. The existing provisions contained in section 112 provide for tax payable in the case of income arising from the transfer of a long-term capital asset. The proviso to sub-section (1) provides that where the tax payable in respect of any income arising from transfer of a long-term capital asset, being listed securities (other than a unit) or unit or zero-coupon bond exceeds ten per cent of the amount of capital gains without indexation adjustment, such excess shall be ignored.

The benefit of concessional rate of tax of 10% in the proviso shall not be available to long-term capital gains from units of debt-oriented mutual funds.

The Finance Minister explained as under the rationale for not allowing concessional rate of 10% to long-term capital gains from units of debt - oriented mutual funds:

"205. In the case of Mutual Funds, other than equity-oriented funds, the capital gains arising on transfer of units held for more than a year is taxed at a concessional rate of 10% whereas direct investments in banks and other debt instruments attract a higher rate of tax. This allows tax arbitrage opportunity. This arbitrage has hardly benefited retail investors as their percentage is very small among such Mutual Fund investors. With a view to remove this tax arbitrage, I propose to increase the rate of tax on long term capital gains from 10 per cent to 20 per cent on transfer of units of such funds. I also propose to increase the period of holding in respect of such units from 12 months to 36 months for this purpose."

INTEREST ON PROVIDENT FUND LOAN - WHETHER DEDUCTIBLE

In Vashist Bhargava v. ITO [1975] 99 ITR 148 (Delhi) the assessee took a non-refundable advance from his government provident fund account for buying and reconstructing a house. Later, when he sold the house, he was obliged to repay the advance with interest. Under the rules governing the relevant prov-ident fund, the interest so paid was to be credited to the asses-see's provident fund account. The Court held that the money paid by the petitioner by way of interest went into his own account in the provident fund and remained his own money. There was thus no expenditure at all incurred by him in making the said payment. The payment into the petitioner's account in the provident fund did not amount to a payment to the Government and was not "an expenditure incurred in connection with the transfer" within the meaning of section 48.

CAPITAL OF THAT CONCERN - SECOND PROVISO [AS IT STOOD AT RELEVANT TIME]

1317. CWT v. Lallubhai Gordhandas Charitable Trust [1999] 102 Taxman 174/239 ITR 448 (Guj.)

The expression 'capital of that concern' which occurs in the second proviso to section 21A is intended to take within its sweep all types of concerns in which the trust could invest its funds. The word 'capital' will, therefore, take colour from the type of concern to which it is applied.

The capital of a company, therefore, would mean share capital in the context of the provisions of the second proviso to section 21A and the meaning of the word 'capital' cannot be made mercurial by attaching it to all the assets that the company may own, nor can it include the reserves of the company,which can at any subsequent time be distributed as dividend. The expression 'capital employed' stands on a different footing in the context of the provisions of section 80J of the Income-tax Act, read with rule 19A of the Income-tax Rules framed thereunder and cannot be projected in the expression 'capital of that concern' occurring in the second proviso to section 21A.

ARE PORTFOLIO MANAGEMENT CHARGES ALLOWABLE UNDER SECTION 48?

The ITAT Mumbai Bench in the case of Mateen Pyarali Dholkia v. Dy. CIT [2018] 94 taxmann.com 294/171 ITD 294 (Mum. - Trib.) held that while computing capital gain on sale of shares kept under Portfolio Management Scheme (PMS), assessee could not claim deduction of PMS fee as same neither fell under category of transfer fee, nor cost of acquisi-tion/improvement.

The ITAT Pune Bench in the case of Dy. CIT v. KRA Holding & Trading (P.) Ltd [2012] 26 tax-mann.com 48/54 SOT 493 (Pune - Trib.) held that Portfolio man-agement fee paid by assessee was to be allowed as deduction while computing capital gains arising from sale of shares. The Pune Bench in this case followed its earlier order in the case of the same assessee in KRA Holding & Trading (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2011] 46 SOT 19/11 taxmann.com 250 (Pune - Trib.) and noted that the Mumbai Bench in the case of Homi K. Bhabha v. ITO (International Taxa-tion) [2011] 48 SOT 102/14 taxmann.com 165 (Pune - Trib.) struck a different note.

The ITAT Mumbai Bench in the case of Krishnamurthy Thiagarajan v. ACIT [2024] 164 taxmann.com 550 (Mum. - Trib.), following precedents, held that where assessee paid management fee to a company for sale of securities and reduced same from short-term capital gains, since management fee was linked to earning of short-term capital gain arising from transfer of securities, same was to be allowed as deduction under section 48 of the Act.

The Tribunal also noted that "there are contrary deci-sions of the Tribunal on allowability of Management Fee under sec-tion 48 of the Act." The Tribunal also observed that "It is a well settled proposition that when two views are possible, the view in favour of assessee should be preferred [CIT v. Vegetable Products Ltd. [1973] 88 ITR 192 (SC)]."

The appeals of the Revenue were thus dismissed.

Taxability of zero coupon bonds (ZCB)

3.4 The taxation of deep discount bonds (DDB) is not clear. The CBDT has issued clarifications explaining the taxability of DDBs and the tax deduction provisions for the issuer. [Circular No. 2/2002, dated 15-2-2002 and Press Release, dated 20-3-2002]

In order to clear doubts regarding the taxation of similar bonds issued by certain entities and satisfying certain conditions, the Finance Act, 2005 has introduced certain provisions. Broadly the provisions are as follows :

TAX TREATMENT IN HANDS OF INVESTOR

The provisions apply to specified Zero Coupon Bonds ('ZCB') (See para 3.4-2 )

Maturity or redemption of ZCB is a 'transfer' [Section 2(47)(iva)] (See para 3.4-5)

ZCBs are long term asset if held for more than 12 months [proviso to section 2(42A)] (with effect from 1-4-2006)

Income received on transfer of long term ZCBs is taxable as capital gains @ 10% (plus surcharge and cess) [proviso to section 112(1) read with section 2(9) & 2(11) of the Finance Act, 2005] (with effect from 1-4-2006)

There is no income-tax on the year-to-year appreciation of ZCB held as capital assets

TAX TREATMENT IN HANDS OF ISSUER

Issuer of ZCBs is eligible for a deduction of the discount on pro rata basis calculated as per prescribed method [Section 36(1)(iiia)] (Seepara 3.4-3)

No tax is to be deducted under section 194A in respect of income payable on 'specified' ZCBs [Section 194A(3)(x)] (Seepara 3.4-3A)

Accretion to capital does not become income merely because the original capital was invested in the hope or expectation that it would in due course of time, rise in value. And if it does so rise, the realisation does not partake the character of income. The true character of the transaction would depend upon all the facts and circumstances of a’ case. In the instant case, it was not disputed that the assessee was an investment company. By its very nature of that character, the assessee, in normal course, might reasonably be looked at as acquiring various assets with a view to earn interest income therefrom. In that sense of matter, the number of purchases or the frequency in making investments could not be viewed with suspicion. Then, the assets involved were gold bonds, which did not fall within the categories of ‘capital asset’ as defined in section 2(14)(iv). Gold bonds are not items of trade and according to the scheme of the Act annual payments on them is not to be taxed as provided under section 10(15)(ia). It was also the established position that the department never treated the gold bonds as stock-in-trade of the assessee. The gold bonds were always projected as investments in the balance sheets from year to year. Surplus realisation on their sales was transferred to capital reserve account and was never made available for distribution. Annual payment for their holding and retention at one stage or the other of the relevant assessment proceedings, was treated by the department as exempt from tax under section 10(15)(ia).

The position of their sales was this that initially the assessee had received 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds on 1-8-1977 not as stock-in-trade but as capital. After a retention for about 13 months 20 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold on 31-8-1978 and the surplus taken to capital reserve account Then 5 Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased on 15-4-1978 and 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold on 30-3-1979. The surplus realisation was again transferred to capital reserve account. 10Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased on 13-4-1979 and no sales were effected in that year. It was on 11-7-1980 that the entire balance holding of 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds was sold and the surplus realisation transferred to capital reserve account. It might be noted that during the duration of three years there were two instances of sales. The frequency in sales was not such as might justify the conclusion that it was in the direction of undertaking adventures in the nature of trade. On each sales the surplus realisation was taken to capital reserve account and not distributed as income. The revenue had brought no evidence on record to prove that the profits earned by the assessee on the sales of gold bonds had not resulted in capital accretions and were revenue receipts of the assessee.

Therefore, the sales of the gold bonds by the assessee during the previous year relevant to the assessment year in question were not adventures in the nature of trade and as such did not bring taxable profits to the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 2(13)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Adventure in nature of trade - Assessment years 1979-80 and 1981-82 - Assessee-company was an investment company - Assessee had received 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds on dissolution of a partnership firm as capital - After a retention for 13 months, 20 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold and surplus taken to capital reserve account - Then 5 Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased and 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold - Surplus realisation was again transferred to capital reserve account - Again 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased on 13-4-1979 and no sales were effected - It was on 11-7-1980 that entire balance holding of 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds was sold and surplus realisation transferred to capital reserve account - Whether, it could be said that sale of aforesaid bonds by assessee was an adventure in nature of trade and, therefore, excess realisation on sale of such bonds was assessable as assessee’s Income - Held, on facts, no

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1979-80 - Assessee-company made contributions to provident fund, which was a new account applied for - On asking Code No. Provident Fund Commissioner informed that it was not covered within definition of establishment - Aforesaid contributions made were returned and paid to employees as additional salary - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of such contributions to provident fund - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was earning income from rendering various kinds of services to certain companies and interest income on its investments and holdings. It maintained its accounts on mercantile system. It had received 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds on 1-8-1977 on dissolution of a partnership firm as capital. For the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee had claimed exemption in respect of the amount respresenting profit realised on sale of National Defence Gold Bonds worth 10 Kg. gold. This amount had been credited to the profit and loss account and therefrom transferred to the ‘capital reserve account’. The assessee had claimed exemption on the ground that the gold bonds sold were not capital assets under section 2(14)(iv ). The ITO held that the sale of 10 Kg. worth gold bonds by the assessee was an adventure in the nature of trade and, therefore, the excess realisation on the sale of aforesaid bonds was the assessee’s taxable income. He, therefore, proposed to include the aforesaid realisation in the total Income of the assessee and sought necessary directions under section 144B from the IAC. The IAC noted that prior to the sale of 10 Kg. of gold bonds the assessee possessed 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds out of which 20 Kg. worth of gold bonds had been purchased. The IAC held that during the year in question the assessee had become an investment trading company and the profit made by it on sale of 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds was required to be assessed as its income. He, therefore, accepted the proposal of the ITO and directed the ITO to add the aforesaid amount to the assessee’s total income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition.

On second appeal:

HELD: No hard and fast rule, principle or test may be laid down to determine the character of a transaction being adventure in the nature of trade or not. A number of factors like the income-earning regular activity of the assessee, the nature of the asset involved, the intention of the assessee of acquiring it, the treatment given to the profit on sale thereof, the period of retention thereof, the circumstances attending on and leading to the sale of the asset etc., are required to be taken into account before the transaction is held to be an adventure in the nature of trade. A capital investment on resale thereof would not lose its capital nature merely because resale was foreseen and contemplated by the assessee when investment was made and the possibility of enhanced value motivated the investment. Accretion to capital does not become income merely because the original capital was invested in the hope or expectation that it would in due course of time, rise in value. And if it does so rise, the realisation does not partake the character of income. The true character of the transaction would depend upon all the facts and circumstances of a’ case.

the legislature in section 12B of the 1922 Act a transaction clothed with all its legal formalities. What is to be seen is what actually was the contract between the parties. The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction. It is clear that what is vital and what is determinative is the nature of the transaction as embodying in the documents in which the parties have chosen to embody, the terms of the transaction, and not the mode by which it is performed. In the instant case, the documents in which the parties had embodied the transaction between them was only the offer of purchase made by ‘T’ by their letter of 31-8-1946, and its acceptance by the assessee on 22-9-1946, and, on the construction of these two documents, there could not be any doubt that the transaction between the parties was one of sale or transfer of the share as well as the managing agency. Further, the steps taken by the assessee also left no doubt that this agreement between the parties had been performed by the assessee by tendering their resignations simultaneously with the appointment of T as managing agents. The consideration had been received by the assessee. It was thereafter that on 7-1-1947, the resignation had been tendered by the assessee of their managing agency. It had to be kept in view that all the shares of the managed company were held by the assessee. The managing agency firm consisted of only two persons as partners.

Within two days the assessee ceased to be managing agents, and ‘T’ became managing agents of the managed company simultaneously. This exactly was the result which the agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ contemplated. The resignation by the assessee of the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, therefore, was nothing but the mode of performance of the agreement to sell the managing agency arrived at between the assessee and ‘T’. That being the position, the income-tax authorities were justified in holding that the provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act were attracted to the facts of the case.

The subject-matter of appeal would get confined to the limits of the grounds specifically raised in the memorandum of appeal, the new grounds raised by the appellant with the previous permission of the Tribunal and the grounds urged by the respondent in support of the decree passed in his favour, even though the decision of the Court, against which the appeal is filed, is against him. It is thus clear that the Tribunal will have no jurisdiction to found its decision on grounds which have not been raised before it by any of the parties at all. In other words, it would not be open to the Tribunal to make out a new case for either the appellant or the respondent. The finding of the AAC was that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital loss and the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. Deducting the capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares, the total figure of the capital gain was arrived at, and from the total gain, the capital gain falling to the share of the assessee was computed at. In this context, it would not be reasonable to assume that by raising this ground the appellant was challenging the finding which was already in his favour, but it would be reasonable to hold that he was challenging the finding which was only against him, and that finding was that the value of the managing agency as on 1-1-1939, was nil. In dealing with this ground, the Tribunal itself observed that the said contention of the assessee related to the capital gains computed by the department.

It was thus clear that this was the only contention of the assessee, and this was the only ground of attack as regards the computation of the capital gains made by the AAC. It was indeed true that the Tribunal had gone into the question of determining the capital gains on the transaction of sale of shares. But nowhere from the order it appeared that the departmental representative had raised any contention before the Tribunal or tried to support the order of the AAC on the ground that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital gain. From the order of the AAC also, it did not appear that at any time it was the case of the ITO that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital gains. These being the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was neither competent nor justified in interfering with the finding of the AAC as regards the transaction of sale and holding that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in capital gains. The assessee's contention that the managing agency had value as on 1-1-1939, had been accepted by the Tribunal, and in view of this finding of the Tribunal, and in the light of the observations herein made, the amount of capital gains would have to be computed afresh.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the revenue.

TR 758. This question was not, therefore, pressed. The question under section 24B was also not seriously pressed. The view of the High Court that section 24B of the 1922 Act does not limit the liability of the administrator or executor to the cases referred to under that section was correct; because the appellant was as much an assessee under the Act as any other individual and if he made capital gains, he was as much liable to pay tax as any other individual. Section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act is the substantive provision which levies a tax in respect of profits or gains arising from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset effected during a specified period. The admitted position in this case was that the appellant sold the shares and securities, which constituted capital asset, within that period and thus clearly came within sub-section (1) of section 12B of the 1922 Act. Section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act states how the amount of capital gain shall be computed, and it allows certain deductions from the full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange or transfer of capital assets is made.

Section 12B(3) of the 1922 Act refers to a capital asset which became the property of the assessee by succession, inheritance or devolution or under any of the circumstances referred to in the third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act and states what deductions the assessee is then entitled to. In one case, the assessee may be the administrator or executor who has himself sold the capital assets; in another case the assessee may be the person who has got the capital assets by succession etc. or under any of the circumstances referred to in the third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act, and if in the latter case the assessee sells the capital assets, he brings himself within section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act but is entitled to a deduction of the actual cost to the previous owner in accordance with the provisions of section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act; where however, the cost to the previous owner cannot be determined, he is entitled to a deduction of the fair market value at the date on which the capital assets became the property of the previous owner. This in effect is the scheme of the three sub-sections. Manifestly, the intention of the legislature is to tax the profits made by the sale, exchange or transfer of capital assets and the incidence of the taxation falls at the time of the transfer. If the sale is made by the administrator or executor, the liability under section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act falls on him; if, however, the sale is made by a person who got the capital assets inter alia in any of the ways mentioned in section 12B(3) of the 1922 Act, he becomes liable to tax as and when he sells the capital assets and makes the profits therefrom. The third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act states in effect that under certain circumstances mentioned therein a transfer of capital assets shall not be treated as a transfer for the purposes of the section. The circumstances enumerated are: (a) compulsory acquisition of property for public purposes, (b) distribution of capital assets on the total or partial partition of a Hindu undivided family, (c) distribution of capital assets on the dissolution of a firm or other association of persons, or on the liquidation of a company, and (d) distribution of capital assets under a deed of gift, bequest, will or transfer on irrevocable trust. In the instant case the question concerned was whether there had been a distribution of capital assets by the appellant under a will so as to bring him within the ambit of the third proviso. If the appellant comes within that ambit, then the sales which he made of the shares and securities would not be treated as transfer within the meaning of section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act.

HEADNOTE: Section 50 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Computation in case of depreciable assets - Assessment year 1959-60 - Whether if consideration for transaction has been honestly agreed upon, with a view to benefit purchaser and out of love and affection on account of relationship, or with reference to particular circumstances, there will be no justification for imputing a motive to vendor to avoid or reduce tax liability and as such, in such a circumstance, proviso to section 12B(2) of 1922 Act can not be invoked - Held, yes

FACT: In 1954, the assessee-company had purchased certain shares of a company. During accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1959-60, the assessee sold these shares to three ladies at a lower price. On 11-11-1959, the directors of the assessee resolved that the difference between the cost price and sale price of the shares might be treated as a gift to the purchasers. However, the ITO invoked first proviso to section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act and treated the difference between the cost and the market prices, as a capital gain on the sale of the shares made during the year of account. The Tribunal found as a fact that the sale was a real transaction which was given effect to and acted upon by the parties thereto and that further it was not made with the object of avoidance or reduction of tax liability but made for the purpose of benefiting the ladies and as a matter of fact, the motive for the sale might have been the natural love and affection for and desire to provide the ladies. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the second condition for application of the proviso to section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act had not been satisfied and that, therefore, the proviso could not be invoked.

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Assessee held certain shares of company ‘G’ and was also managing agent of said company - During relevant accounting year, one ‘T’ made offer to assessee to purchase of aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ held by assessee also managing agency rights of assessee - Assessee accepted aforesaid offer and thereafter wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting his resignation from office of managing agents and further recommended ‘T’ to be appointed as managing agents in his place - Company ‘G’ accepted said letter - Whether resignation by assessee of managing agency and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, was nothing but mode of performance of agreement to sell managing agency arrived at between assessee and, therefore, provisions of section 12B of 1922 Act were attracted - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee held certain shares of Company ‘G’ and was also the managing agent of said company. On 31-8-1946 one ‘T’ made on offer to assessee to purchase aforesaid shares of company ‘G’ and also offered pay certain amount for getting the rights of the managing agency. The assessee adopted the said offer. On 7-1-1947, the assessee wrote a letter to Company ‘G’ submitting their resignation from the office of managing agents of the company, and, further recommending that ‘T’ be appointed as managing agents in their place. The registration of managing agents was accepted by company ‘G’ and appointment of ‘T’ as managing agent was also accepted. For the assessment year the ITO computed the capital gains and assessed it in the hands of the assessee. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. Before Tribunal the assessee contended that the AAC was in error in holding that the assessee had made any capital gain as a result of the transfer of managing agency as the transaction between the assessee and ‘T’ was not of either sale or transfer the AAC had found that the transaction of sale of shares had resulted in loss and that the entire sale price of the managing agency was a capital gain. The Tribunal, however, in its order observed that the finding of the AAC that there was capital loss on the transaction of sale of shares was not correct, and for the reasons stated by it in its order, the Tribunal held that having regard to the various aspects of the case, the value of the shares of company ‘G’ as on 1-1-1939, could not be more than 60 per cent of what it was at the time of the sale.

On reference :

HELD: In the instant case, there was no material or an iota of evidence that the original agreement of sale had undergone any change or was modified or was altered. The only circum stances on which reliance was placed was that there was no sale deed executed by the assessee in favour of ‘T’, but, on the other hand, the assessee company had resigned itself the managing agency. In the absence of any evidence or any material that the resignation was the consequence of any agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ altering the terms of the original contract, that circumstance would make no difference, but it would only amount to the mode of performance of the contract of sale. In what form, by what mode, the contract is performed is not to be determined in accordance with the general provisions of law, but in construing section 12B of the 1922 Act one must not give to the expression 'sale or transfer' its technical meaning, nor must one attribute to 'sale or transfer' as used by the legislature in section 12B of the 1922 Act a transaction clothed with all its legal formalities. What is to be seen is what actually was the contract between the parties. The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction.

any difference to the rights of the parties. The position might have been different if the market value of the shares could not be ascertained. Then it might be said that it was difficult to put a proper value upon the shares and to put a proper value for the consideration of the assignment or relinquishment of the managing agency. But when the market value was available and when it was known for what price these shares could be purchased or sold, there was no difficulty whatsoever in the apportionment. It was not the case of the Department and it had never been their case that the capital asset in respect of which capital gain was made by the assessee and which was sought to be taxed was the shares and the managing agency. The whole of the reference was based upon the fact that the only capital asset concerned with was the shares and not the managing agency. Therefore, one must separate the managing agency from the shares in considering what was the value to be put upon the shares. The parties had put upon the shares a value which was much higher than the market value. Admittedly, it was an artificial value and it was artificial because the value put upon the shares was not the value of the shares alone but it was the composite consideration paid by the purchasers for obtaining the shares and also acquiring the managing agency. Under the circumstances, for the purposes of section 12B(2) the sale price of the shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. 65 per share.

Note : The case was decided in favour of assessee.

For this purpose capital value of such units means ‘any amounts’ invested by the assessee in the units referred to in section 80CCB(2). For the chargeability of capital gain in respect of units referred to in sub-section (2) of section 80CCB, no separate modus of computation of capital gain was set out in this section. According to the second proviso of section 48, for computing the long-term capital gains cost of acquisition as in clause(2)(ii) of section 48 shall be taken to be as indexed cost of acquisition. Section 45(6) provides that the difference between there repurchase price of the units and the amount invested therein shall be deemed to be the capital gains arising to the assessee in the previous year in which such repurchase takes place, etc. and taxed accordingly. It is a trite law that if you are bidden to treat an imaginary state of affairs as real, you must surely, unless prohibited from doing so, also imagine as real the consequences and incidents which, if the putative state of affairs in fact had existed, must inevitably have flowed from or accompanied it. By virtue of section 45(6) difference between the repurchase price of the units and the amount invested therein is deemed to be a capital gain once it is deemed to be a capital gain, all the provisions relatable to the competition of capital gain to be applied for ascertaining the true capital gain or loss. If other sub-sections of section 45 are analysed, it is seen that they are merely charging sections. From this it appeared that section 45 lays down the tenets for the charge of capital gains tax. The computation of that tax is to be done in accordance with the modus prescribed under section 48. The benefit of indexation of cost of such units should, thus, be made available on repurchase or redemption of such units.

It was, therefore, held that the benefit of indexation of cost was allowable in respect of the computation of capital gains chargeable under section 45(6).

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessee - company was managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies and also held majority of their conversion shares - 'D' company made an offer to assessee to purchase conversions share of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency - Assessee accepted said offer - Subsequently, agreement was modified and as per new agreement, assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in favour of 'D' company, resigned from it - Revenue authorities brought to tax under section 12B of 1922 Act amount of compensation received by assessee-company on account of resigning managing agency agreement - Whether since transaction in its true legal character was relinquishment of managing agency and was neither a sale nor transfer thereof, High Court rightly held that assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was the managing agent of 'M' and 'S' companies. The assessee held majority of conversion shares of those companies. 'D' company wrote a letter to the assessee mentioning that it wanted to purchase conversion shares of 'M' and 'S' companies with managing agency.

In a meeting of board of directors of the assessee-company, offer of 'D' company was accepted and it was stated in its minutes that out of the total amount received from the sale of the shares, a sum of Rs. 1 crore should be paid to the assessee company as compensation for the loss of the managing agency of the two mills. Subsequently, 'D' company wrote a letter to assessee wherein it was mentioned that assessee-company instead of transferring managing agency in their favour, should resign it so that at the time of delivery of shares, managing agency would have come to an end. The assessee, accordingly, wrote to the 'M' and 'S' companies that it had decided to resign the office of the managing agency and tendered its resignation. ITO brought to tax the amount received in lieu of waving managing agency. The AAC as well as Tribunal held that the assessee company had sold the managing agency and therefore the profits or gains arising from that sale were capital gains within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On reference, the High Court, however, held that there was neither a sale nor a transfer of the managing agency within the meaning of section 12B of 1922 Act.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: Two conditions must be fulfilled before the transaction under consideration can come within the purview of section 12B of 1922 Act. The first condition is that the profits or gains must arise from the sale, exchange or transfer of a capital asset; and the second condition is that the sale, exchange or transfer must be effected after 31-3-1946. There is no doubt that the transaction in instant case was effected after 31-3-1946. There was also no dispute that the managing agency of the two mills which the assessee company held was a capital asset.

The 'D' Company offered to purchase (1) certain shares in the two mills and (2) the managing agency, on payment of a certain consideration, and the assessee-company accepted that offer, in law, this was merely an agreement to sell and purchase the shares together with the managing agency on payment of the consideration, etc. However, before any such sale could take place, the agreement was modified and instead of 'selling' the managing agency the assessee company agreed to resign or relinquish the managing agency.

The High Court, thus, correctly held that whereas under the original contract the 'D' company wanted the managing agency to be transferred, which meant that it wanted the benefit of that contract to be vested in it and was also prepared to accept the burden of the obligations that went with that contract, under the substituted contract, the 'D' Company did not want the managing agency to be assigned to it; on the contrary, it wanted the assessee-company to relinquish its rights in the managing agency of the two mills by resigning. On a true interpretation, the letter written by 'D' company-substituted a new contract, a contract of relinquishment rather than a contract of sale, so far as the managing agency was concerned.

Thus, the transaction in its true legal character was a relinquishment of the managing agency and was neither a sale nor a transfer thereof. Consequently, the High Court correctly held that the assessee-company did not make capital gain within meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

In the result, the appeal failed and was to be dismissed.

Note : Decision was in favour of assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922) - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1960-61 - Whether incidence of charge being on capital gains actually received by assessee, in order that transfer was one with object of avoiding or reducing liability of assessee under section 12B it must be a case where consideration mentioned in deed has been understated and actually transferor has received more than what was stated in document - Held, yes - Whether, where, assessee transferred shares in a company to a person connected with him, for much less than fair market value of shares, first proviso to section 12B(2) was not applicable - Held, yes

FACT: During the accounting period relevant to the assessment year 1960-61, each of the three assessees sold certain shares in a company to persons directly or indirectly connected with either of them at the uniform price of Rs. 125 per share while the face value of each share was Rs. 100. The ITO took the view that the provisions of the first proviso to section 12B were attracted. he, accordingly, computed the value of the shares at Rs. 375 on the basis of the balance sheet of the company as on 31-10-1959. While arriving at the above value, the ITO rejected the deductions claimed by the assessees on account of provision for taxation and the proposed dividend.

On appeal, the AAC took the view that the balance sheet as on 30-10-1958 which had been published prior to the date of sales alone could be taken into consideration and not the balance sheet as on 31-10-1959. He further held that the provision for taxation as claimed by the assessee, had to be deducted in computing the net wealth of the company, while the proposed divident could not be deducted. he accordingly, computed the fair market value of the shares at Rs. 171.50 each. On second appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the ITO's view regarding the fair market value of shares to be computed as per the balance sheet as on 31-10-1959 which was nearer to the dates of sales in question. However, the question of deductions, Tribunal upheld the AAC's order. In this view of the matter, the Tribunal directed that the capital gain could be computed on basis that fair market value of share was Rs. 264.

On reference :

HELD: The charging provision is to be found in sub-section (1) of section 12B and the incidence of charge is on any profits or gains arising from the sale of a capital asset. Sub-section (2) and the first proviso thereto being machinery sections, cannot either control or enlarge the scope of incidence of tax as indicated in section 12B(1). The first proviso does not make any provision for levying incidence of tax on fictional or deemed capital gains which ought to have been received by the assessee. The incidence being on the capital gains actually received by the assessee, the only possible manner in which the second condition mentioned in the proviso could be satisfied would be by showing that the actual consideration received by the transferor is higher than the one mentioned in the transfer deed itself. In other words, it must be a case of under stating the consideration in the transfer deed and the transferor receiving higher consideration than mentioned in the transfer deed.

It is quite possible that though the fair market value of a particular capital asset may be high, the transferor may transfer the capital asset to the transferee who is related directly or indirectly to him for more than one reason and such reasons cannot partake of the object mentioned in the second condition.

HEADNOTE: Section 143 read with section 80CCB, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Assessment - Prima facie adjustments - Assessment year 1997-98 - Whether issue as to whether benefit of indexation is to be allowed for purpose of computation of capital gains on units referred to in section 80CCB, does not fall under limited purview of section 143(1)(a) as it cannot be considered as beyond pale of debate or discussion - Held, yes

FACT: While processing the return under section 143(1)(a), benefit of indexation on section 80CCB investment, as claimed by the assessee, had not been allowed for calculating capital gains for the assessment year 1997-98 as per the second proviso to section 48. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal :

HELD: The issue as to whether benefit of indexation is to be allowed for the purpose of computation of capital gain on the units referred to in section 80CCB, does not fall under the limited purview of section 143(1)(a). Section 143(1)(a) confers a limited and restricted power for making disallowances by the Assessing Officer in respect of only prima facie inadmissible items. The issue involved in the instant case could not be considered as beyond the pale of debate or discussion. Therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be reversed and the assessee’s appeal was to be allowed.

K.R. Manjani for the Appellant. Rajul Awasthi for the Respondent.

HEADNOTE: Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 12B of the Indian  Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1948-49 - Assessee was partner in a firm - Said firm sold shares of a company together with its managing agency rights at an amount calculated at Rs. 65 per share though market value of share was Rs. 46 only - Whether full value must be true value and not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset and, hence, for purposes of section 12B of 1922 Act sale price of shares should be taken at Rs. 46 per share and not Rs. at 65 per share - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee was a partner in a firm. The said firm by agreement dated 7-9-1946 sold shares in a company together with the managing agency right of said company which it was holding to another firm for an amount calculated at Rs. 65 per share, though the market value at the time was Rs. 46 per share. The department held that for purposes of computation of capital gains of assessee partner, the sale price of each share should be taken at Rs. 65 while the assessee contended that the market value of Rs 46 should be taken into account. The Tribunal upheld the decision of the department.

On reference:

HELD: The Tribunal had found as a fact, and there could be no dispute about it, that the main object or rather the only object of the agreement of the 7-9- 1946, was to get the purchasers of these shares appointed the managing agents of the company. The Tribunal also pointed out in its order that this was not an ordinary agreement of purchase and sale of shares of the company entered into in the ordinary course of business, and the only reason why it had rejected the assessee's contention was that the parties did not apportion the price of Rs. 65 to the shares and to the managing agency. Under section 12B(2) for the purpose of computing capital gain the full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange or transfer of the capital asset is made has to be taken into account. It was erroneous to suggest that the full value is necessarily the value which the parties place upon a capital asset. The full value must be the true value, not any artificial value, which parties for any purpose may assign to a particular capital asset. Here there was evidence that these shares were marketable and they had a market price which was Rs. 46 per share. The agreement also made it clear that it was a composite agreement by which not merely the shares were being sold but the shares and the managing agency rights. Therefore, the consideration paid by the purchasers, viz., Rs. 65 per share, was not the consideration paid for the shares alone but it was a consideration that was paid for the shares and also for the relinquishment of the managing agency by the vendors. It was therefore not possible to accept the contention that the full value of shares within the meaning of section 12B(2) of the Act was Rs. 65 per share. The full value was the market value of Rs. 46 per share and an additional amount was paid by the purchasers because they obtained not only the shares but also the important right to manage the company. It was difficult to understand how the mere fact that the parties had not apportioned the consideration between the two assets which were being dealt with by this agreement could make any difference to the rights of the parties. The position might have been different if the market value of the shares could not be ascertained. Then it might be said that it was difficult to put a proper value upon the shares and to put a proper value for the consideration of the assignment or relinquishment of the managing agency. But when the market value was available and when it was known for what price these shares could be purchased or sold, there was no difficulty whatsoever in the apportionment.

HEADNOTE: Section 2(13)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Adventure in nature of trade - Assessment years 1979-80 and 1981-82 - Assessee-company was an investment company - Assessee had received 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds on dissolution of a partnership firm as capital - After a retention for 13 months, 20 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold and surplus taken to capital reserve account - Then 5 Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased and 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold - Surplus realisation was again transferred to capital reserve account - Again 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased on 13-4-1979 and no sales were effected - It was on 11-7-1980 that entire balance holding of 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds was sold and surplus realisation transferred to capital reserve account - Whether, it could be said that sale of aforesaid bonds by assessee was an adventure in nature of trade and, therefore, excess realisation on sale of such bonds was assessable as assessee’s Income - Held, on facts, no

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1979-80 - Assessee-company made contributions to provident fund, which was a new account applied for - On asking Code No. Provident Fund Commissioner informed that it was not covered within definition of establishment - Aforesaid contributions made were returned and paid to employees as additional salary - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of such contributions to provident fund - Held, yes

FACT: During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee- company had made contributions to the provident fund, which was a new account. The assessee had asked for its Code No. The Provident Fund Commissioner, however, held that the assessee was not covered by the definition of ‘establishment’ so as to have a Code No. and contribute to a provident fund. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the disallowance.

On second appeal:

HELD: The circumstances under which the claim for deduction of contribution to provident fund as business expenditure was advanced by the assessee justified its allowability under section 37(1) . Therefore, the Commissioner ( Appeals) was not justified in disallowing the assessee’s claim.

assets under a deed of gift, bequest, will or transfer on irrevocable trust. In the instant case the question concerned was whether there had been a distribution of capital assets by the appellant under a will so as to bring him within the ambit of the third proviso. If the appellant comes within that ambit, then the sales which he made of the shares and securities would not be treated as transfer within the meaning of section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act. The appellant's argument that the expression "distribution of capital assets" in third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act must be give a meaning which will fulfill a purpose and correlate the proviso to the substantive provision in section 12B(1), could not be accepted as correct. Firstly, having regard to the definition of the expression "capital assets", it would be wrong to read "distribution of capital assets" as meaning "distribution of sale proceeds of capital assets". Obviously, there is a clear and vital distinction between "capital assets" and their "sale proceeds". If capital assets are sold first and a distribution of the sale proceeds is made afterwards, then the sale precedes distribution and, what is distributed is not capital assets but the sale proceeds thereof. Secondly, it could not be agreed with that the third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act serves no purpose if the expression "distribution of capital assets" is given its natural and plain meaning, viz., distribution in specie. The High Court expressed the view that by the proviso the Legislature might have intended to protect an assessee from a possible argument by the revenue that when an executor or administrator transferred the estate or part of the estate to the person entitled to it, there was a transfer within the meaning of sub-section (1) of section 12B of the 1922 Act. It seemed that the purpose of the proviso is abundantly clear if the scheme of sub-sections (1), (2) and (3) of section 12B of the 1922 Act is kept in mind. Assume that there is a distribution of capital assets in specie amongst the legatees, and one of the legatees sells the capital assets which he got in one of the ways mentioned in the third proviso; he at once becomes liable to tax on the profits made on the sale. Section 12B(3) of the 1922 Act makes that position clear and if the proviso is read in the context of the substantive provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act its purpose is quite clear. The purpose is this: as long as there is distribution of the capital assets in specie and no sale, there is no transfer for the purposes of the section ; but as soon as there is a sale of the capital assets and profits or gains arise therefrom, the liability to tax arises, whether the sale be by the administrator or the legatee. It is significant that the proviso uses the words "for the purposes of this section" and not merely section 12B(1). Indeed, the appellant was forced to concede that in view of the provisions of section (3) of section 12B of the 1922 Act, the expression "distribution of capital assets" must also mean distribution in specie because under section 12B(3) of the 1922 Act it is the capital asset which becomes the property of the assessee under any of the circumstances mentioned in the third proviso. He then contended that the expression meant both distribution in specie and distribution of sale proceeds. One did not see why an unnatural or forced meaning should be given to the expression, when by giving the expression its plain and natural meaning the third proviso fits in with the scheme of sub-sections (1), (2) and (3) of section 12B of the 1922 Act. On the interpretation sought to be placed on the third proviso on behalf of the appellant, the administrator will escape paying tax if he sells the capital assets; but the legatee will not escape if he sells the capital assets after having received them in specie from the administrator. This is an anomaly which is against the scheme of section 12B of the 1922 Act. Accordingly the High Court rightly held that the expression "distribution of capital assets" in the third proviso of section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act means distribution in specie and not distribution of sale proceeds.

In the High Court an alternative argument was also presented on behalf of the assessee to the effect that the third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act contemplated involuntary transfers.

The argument was that inasmuch as the administrator sold the shares and securities for the purpose of distributing the sale proceeds to the legatees, the sale was involuntary and was necessitated "by reason of" the terms of the will; therefore, he was protected under the third proviso. The High Court repelled this argument and for good reasons. Firstly, the question whether the sale was voluntary or involuntary is not germane to the scheme of section 12B of the 1922 Act. Secondly, on a proper reading of the proviso, the expression "by reason of" goes with the clause relating to compulsory acquisition of property and not with the distribution of capital assets.

HEADNOTE: Section 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - Assessment year 1982-83 - Assessee trust sold certain quantity of gold and claimed that net consideration of sale being kept in fixed deposit and utilized for acquiring new capital asset, capital gain on sale of gold would be exempt under section 11(1A) - Assessee's claim was rejected on ground that it had lent sale proceeds on interest - Whether since it was not clear whether assessee advanced loans out of income from fixed deposits or invested net consideration in fixed deposits, matter should be remanded back to Tribunal for fresh consideration - Held, yes

Note: Case remanded back.

the assessee in favour of 'K' was a transfer of a capital asset within the meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act and the gains arising to the assessee on account of this transfer of the capital asset was rightly taxed by the income-tax authorities. As regards the constitutional validity of section 12B, the Central Legislature has validly enacted section 12B in exercise of the authority conferred upon it by item 55 of List I of the 7th Schedule. The legislation enacted in section 12B is in pith and substance legislation relating to tax on the capital value of the assets. What is the standard by which the 'pith and substance' of a law may be determined? The answer is furnished by Latham C.J., in the Uniform Tax case 65 Com. L.R. 424. The true nature of a law is to be ascertained by examining its terms and speaking generally, ascertaining what it does in relation to duties, rights or powers which it creates, abolishes or regulates. The question may be put in these terms: 'What does the law do in the way of charging or creating or destroying duties or rights or powers'. It is true that section 12B has imposed certain conditions before tax can be assessed. The first condition is that there must be a transfer, sale or exchange of the capital asset and the Legislature states that the assessee shall pay the tax in respect of the gains or profits arising out of this transaction. In the second place, section 12B enunciates in what manner the capital value of the assets should be calculated for the purpose of imposing tax. The provisos to section 12B indicate that the Department must give deduction for the actual cost of the asset to the assessee and also the expenditure on the transaction incurred by the assessee. In other words, the Legislature did not intend to tax the full value of the capital asset as represented by the sale proceeds or the consideration for the transfer or exchange; but the Central Legislature permitted the assessee to deduct from the sale proceeds or consideration the actual cost of the capital asset and also the expenditure incurred by the assessee upon the transaction. If the transaction was a lease and not an outright sale, the amount of consideration would be less and the Income-tax Department would impose tax on the smaller amount realised by the transfer for the capital asset. But that does not mean that the tax was not a tax on value of the capital asset. The quality of the tax was the same though there might be quantitative difference. If the transaction was by way of lease, only the computation of profit would be affected. The difference was only a difference in computation. The quality of the tax was not affected and, the tax contemplated by section 12B falls within the ambit of item 55 of List I of the 7th Schedule. It followed that section 12B is constitutionally a valid piece of legislation.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

involved in Walji Damji case (supra) was a case of a sale of partnership assets by a receiver appointed by Court in a suit for dissolution and accounts. But apart from this aspect, section 12B(1) includes cases not merely of sales but also of transfers of capital assets. Undoubtedly there has been in this case a transfer of the assets and therefore it was certainly a transaction to which section 12B(1) was attracted. This argument was therefore repelled. The second ground urged was that even if section 12B(1) applied and the transaction was not covered by the third proviso, still the only sum which could be brought to charge as a capital gain would be the difference between the original cost and the sale price that was Rs. 61,140 and that the sum of Rs. 20,723 which was the total of the depreciation which had been allowed to the assessee could not be brought into account as part of the 'gain' by reason of the second proviso to section 12B(2).

If definition of "written down value" were read into the second proviso to section 12B(2) and the proviso stopped with the words "the actual cost to the assessee shall be its written down value as defined in section 10", the entirety of the difference between the written down value and the full value of the consideration for the sale, transfer or exchange would be brought to charge as a capital gain. The Department rightly urged that the expression "by any adjustment made" in the concluding words of the proviso, referred to a factual adjustment effected for the purpose of bringing to charge or allowing an exemption in regard to the computation of income under section 10 and not to a theoretical adjustment without reference to an actual assessment.

In the instant case, the Tribunal had held that the 'agreement for sale' entered into between the assessee-firm and the 'company' was a genuine transaction as the same evidenced a sale. This was essentially a finding of fact. The High Court had affirmed that finding. In that view, it could not be accepted that the transaction in question was exchange and not a sale, or it was merely a readjustment. Clause (1) of the agreement in specific terms said that 'the existing partner shall sell and the company shall purchase the shares and securities for a sum of rupees seventy-five lakhs'. Clause (3) of that agreement merely provided a mode of satisfaction of the sale price. The sale price fixed by the parties for the shares and the securities sold was Rs. 75 lakhs and nothing more. It could be that because of the allotment of the shares of the company in satisfaction of the sale price, the assessee-firm got certain benefits but that does not convert the sale into an exchange.

Under section 12B(2), the amount of capital gains has to be computed after making certain deductions from the full value of the consideration for which the sale is made. What exactly is the meaning of the expression 'full value of the consideration for which sale is made'? Is it the consideration agreed to be paid or is it the market value of the consideration? In the case of sale for a price, there is no question of any market value unlike in the case of an exchange. Therefore, in cases of sales to which the first proviso to sub-section (2) of section 12B is not attracted, all that we have to see is what is the consideration bargained for. To the facts of the instant case, the first proviso was not attracted. The price bargained for the sale of the shares and securities was only rupees twenty-five lakhs.

The full value of the sale price received by the assessee was only rupees seventy-five lakhs. That being so, the capital gains made by the company were Rs. 27,04,772 as held by the High Court.

The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee.
