In the instant case, the Tribunal had held that the 'agreement for sale' entered into between the assessee-firm and the 'company' was a genuine transaction as the same evidenced a sale. This was essentially a finding of fact. The High Court had affirmed that finding. In that view, it could not be accepted that the transaction in question was exchange and not a sale, or it was merely a readjustment. Clause (1) of the agreement in specific terms said that 'the existing partner shall sell and the company shall purchase the shares and securities for a sum of rupees seventy-five lakhs'. Clause (3) of that agreement merely provided a mode of satisfaction of the sale price. The sale price fixed by the parties for the shares and the securities sold was Rs. 75 lakhs and nothing more. It could be that because of the allotment of the shares of the company in satisfaction of the sale price, the assessee-firm got certain benefits but that does not convert the sale into an exchange.

Under section 12B(2), the amount of capital gains has to be computed after making certain deductions from the full value of the consideration for which the sale is made. What exactly is the meaning of the expression 'full value of the consideration for which sale is made'? Is it the consideration agreed to be paid or is it the market value of the consideration? In the case of sale for a price, there is no question of any market value unlike in the case of an exchange. Therefore, in cases of sales to which the first proviso to sub-section (2) of section 12B is not attracted, all that we have to see is what is the consideration bargained for. To the facts of the instant case, the first proviso was not attracted. The price bargained for the sale of the shares and securities was only rupees twenty-five lakhs.

The full value of the sale price received by the assessee was only rupees seventy-five lakhs. That being so, the capital gains made by the company were Rs. 27,04,772 as held by the High Court.

The case was decided partly in favour of the assessee.

■ The issue that arises for consideration is whether the assessee is eligible for exemption under section 11. This issue was already considered by the Co-ordinate Bench of this Tribunal in assessee’s own case in Bangalore Development Authority v. Dy. CIT [IT Appeal Nos. 1968 to 1971/Bang/2018, dated 04-6-2019] for the assessment years 2013-14 and 2014-15 in which the assessee's own case for the assessment year 2012-13 in Bangalore Development Authority v. Additional Commissioner of Income-tax [2019] 104 taxmann.com 266/176 ITD 833 (Bangalore - Trib.) was considered in which the Tribunal held that allotment of sites and flats to the economically weaker sections of society constitutes relief for the poor and that relief to the poor does not necessarily mean giving something free of cost to the poor. It also includes providing them things at a concessional rate. The Tribunal also embarked upon an enquiry as to whether the word 'poor' can mean only those who are below the official poverty line or does it include all those who are economically weaker, but not necessarily below the poverty line. The Tribunal concluded that it is not necessary that educational/medical assistance is to be given free only to those below the poverty line. It will suffice if education/medical assistance is provided at concessional rates. The Tribunal also held that the rules that govern the allotment of sites are so formed in order to facilitate the economically weaker sections of society to purchase these sites. In the case of construction of flats, it was clear from the very scheme and the name thereof, that these flats are meant only for the Economically Weaker Sections of society. The Tribunal held that the complaint of the revenue authorities that the assessee was not applying huge amount of profit generated from the activities towards any charitable activities such as relief of poor, education, medical relief and other objects of advancement of general public utility and such surplus is being invested in fixed deposits in order to earn interest income was also not correct inasmuch as the assessee was constructing grade separators, PRR Bridges on Flyovers, carrying out renovation and remodelling works, Maintenance of BBMP facilities, Development of Lakes, etc. The Tribunal also held that object of the assessee was planned urban development of Bangalore City and not with the purpose of profit making; i.e., the activity of formation of layouts and allotment of sites is only carried out with the primary and main object to ensure planned development of Bangalore City and not with the intention to make profits. It is clear that it is the basic motive behind the activity, which is important to be considered; whether it is one with profit motive or not. Merely because surplus is generated from a particular activity, it cannot be said that such activity is in the nature of trade, commerce or business. What needs to be seen is, what the intent and purpose of starting such activity is. The tribunal found that BDA's embarkation of the activity of setting up of residential layouts, including the activity of sale of sites and flats, is definitely not with a view to earn profit, but to ensure planned urban development and also to accomplish a social objective of providing an opportunity to economically weaker sections of society to be able to own a residence on their own. The tribunal also held that the process of auctioning of corner sites by the BDA was only to ensure that officials do not use their discretion to allot corner sites and was therefore an activity which will ensure no loss to the public exchequer. The Tribunal took note of the fact that the concerned Income Tax authorities have recognized the assessee as a public charitable organization by grant of registration under section 12A since 26-3-2003 and that the assessee's objects clause, i.e., section 14 of the BDA Act has not undergone any change or modification since its enactment; which is what must have prompted the Income Tax Department to take the view that it was charitable in nature. The Tribunal took note of the fact that after the introduction of the proviso to section 2(15), the Income Tax Department took a view that the activity of 'BDA' was in the nature of trade, commerce or business and cancelled the registration, granted under section 12A, vide order dated 8-11-2011. The assessee's registration under section 12A however stood restored by a decision of the Co-ordinate Bench of this Tribunal vide order in ITA No.12/Bang/2012 dated 10-4-2015. In this prevailing factual matrix, there is no change in the objects and the only issue which apparently prompts revenue to take the view it has taken, i.e., that the activity of the assessee is hit by the proviso to section 2(15); is the fact that the activity of the assessee has resulted in huge surplus or profits

FACT: The deceased left a will by which a bank was appointed executor of his estate. The bank gave the power of attorney to the appellant. The appellant made an application to the High Court under section 24I (sic) of the Indian Succession Act and on that application obtained letters of administration with a copy of the will annexed. In the course of administration of the estate of the deceased, the appellant sold certain shares and securities belonging to the deceased for the purpose of distributing the assets amongst the legatees. The sale of these shares and securities realised more than their cost price. The excess of the sale price over the cost price was treated by the ITO as capital gain under section 12B of the 1922 Act. These amounts of capital gain were brought to tax for the relevant assessment years along with certain dividend and interest income which had accrued or had been received in the relevant years of account. Not satisfied with these assessments, the appellant preferred appeal to the Tribunal and urged three points in support of his contention that the assessments were invalid: firstly, that section 12B of the 1922 Act imposing a tax on capital gains is ultra vires the Government of India Act, 1935; secondly, that under section 24B of the 1922 Act, the appellant was only liable to pay tax which the testator would have been liable to pay and as these capital assets were not sold by the testator, there was no liability upon the appellant; and thirdly, that the sale of the shares and securities by the appellant under the will of the deceased came within the purview of the third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act and, therefore, was not to be treated as a sale of capital assets under section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act. The Tribunal repelled the first two contentions, but accepted the third as correct and in that view allowed the two appeals in part. It directed the ITO to delete from the assessed income the capital gains made by the sale of shares and securities. On reference, the High Court decided against the appellant.

On appeal to the Supreme Court:

HELD: The question whether the levy of tax on capital gains under section 12B of the 1922 Act is ultra vires no longer survives by reason of the decision of the Supreme Court in Navinchandra Mafatlal v. CIT [1955] S.C.R 829; [1954] 26 ITR 758. This question was not, therefore, pressed. The question under section 24B was also not seriously pressed. The view of the High Court that section 24B of the 1922 Act does not limit the liability of the administrator or executor to the cases referred to under that section was correct; because the appellant was as much an assessee under the Act as any other individual and if he made capital gains, he was as much liable to pay tax as any other individual.

In view of the decision of the Supreme Court in Navin Chandra Mafatlat v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 758 it was to be held that the provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act levying a tax on capital gains are within the competence of the Central Legislature under the Government of the India Act, 1935. Under section 12B of the 1922 Act an assessee is liable to pay tax under the head "capital gains" in respect of any profits or gains, arising form the sale, exchange of a capital asset effected after 31-3-1946.

The vehicles and the route rights in the case of the buses admittedly belonged to the assessees. All these had been transferred to ‘S’ which was an entirely different legal entity.

The transfer was not gratuitous but for a price agreed on. In 1947 the assessees agreed to accept in lieu of cash fully paid up shares in ‘S’ for amounts very much smaller than the price at which the assets had been sold.

In order that section 12B of the 1922 act may apply, it is sufficient if in the relevant accounting year profits arise out of the sale of capital assets. What the parties did subsequent to the year will not have any bearing on their liability to tax in respect of that year.

Section 12B of the 1922 Act does not require that profits should have been actually received. It is sufficient if they have arisen.

Throughout the 1922 Act, the words "accrue" and "arise" are used in contradistinction to the words "receive" and indicate a right to receive.

Section 12B of the 1922 Act renders liable to tax the profits that have arisen to an assessee by the sale of this capital assets.

There was no controversy that the assets transferred by the assessees to ‘S’ constituted capital assets of the assessees. It was also not controverted that depreciation was allowed in respect of the vehicles in computing tax in the earlier years. One of the provisos to section 12B of the 1922 Act indicates that where in respect of a capital asset the assessee has obtained depreciation allowance in any year, the actual cost of the asset to the assessee shall be its written down value subject to certain adjustments.

There was no allegation that the sale of the assets to ‘S’ was effected with the object of avoiding or reducing the liability of the assessees to tax under section 12B of the 1922 Act. Therefore, the proviso which directed that in such cases the profits arising to the assessees shall be determined with reference to the fair market value of the assets sold did not apply.

The profits that arose had, therefore, to be ascertained by deducting the book value from the price at which the assets were sold. That price was first fixed at certain price but, in the same year it was reduced.

There was no allegation that the price was to be paid at any future time, which meant that the price became payable forthwith, that is to say, in the relevant accounting year.

The assessees therefore, obtained the right to receive the price in that year. Their profits, therefore, arose in that year. The assessees maintained their books on a mercantile basis and showed the sale price of their assets as receipts. If it subsequently happened that the money was not actually received, that would be a capital loss arising in the year when the money became irrecoverable. Even if it was supposed that the assessees found it difficult to receive in full the price for which they transferred their assets to ‘S’, and that in consequence they decided to accept paid up shares in the transferee company, that would be a capital loss which arose outside the accounting year, and, therefore, could not be taken notice of far the relevant accounting year. To attract liability to tax under section 12B of the 1922 Act it is sufficient if profits have arisen, that is to say, if the assessee has a right to receive the profits. It is not necessary that the assessee should have actually received them. And undoubtedly the assessees had the right to receive the price and, the profits during the relevant accounting year. Therefore, on the facts and circumstances of the case, there was material to support the assessment made on the assessees as capital gains and such assessment was valid.

The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

HEADNOTE: Section 45, read with section 2(14) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [corresponding to section 12B, read with section 2(4A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Assessment year 1947-48 - Whether share of a partner in partnership concern is property and, thus, a capital assest within meaning of section 2(4A) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Assessee and ‘G’ were partners in three partnership firms which were managing agents of three mills - Assessee’s share in one concern was transferred to ‘G’ in exchange for G’s share in other concerns and additional sum of Rs. 1,00,000 - Whether transaction in question involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets and had all elements of sale and, thus, sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was assessable to tax as capital gains - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee and one ‘G’ were partners in three partnership concerns and those concerns were managing agent of there different mills. As per partnership deeds they were free to sell or mortgage their shares in the partnership. The assessee transferred his shares in one company to ‘G’ and as a condition of transfer ‘G’ paid Rs. 1,00,000 in cash in addition to the shares held by him in other two firms to assessee. The department treated this sum as capital gains liable to tax under section 12B. The assessee appealed without success. The assessee contended that the right of a partner in a partnership which had a managing agency was not a capital asset as defined by section 2(4A) and even if it was a capital asset, the requirements of section 12B were not satisfied, because there was no sale, exchange or transfer.

On reference:

HELD: Except for what has been excluded by section 2(4A) itself the term property, has to be given its ordinary meaning in the English language. It would be impossible to hold that a share in a partnership is not property. A share in a partnership is a profit-yielding asset. That would certainly make it property within the meaning of section 2(4A). The congeries of rights which the appellants enjoyed under the agreements and which for a price he conveyed to ‘G’ constituted a capital asset. The assessee contended that what was payable under the managing agency agreement was really remuneration for services rendered by each of the partners, and that therefore the right to receive such remuneration would not be property within the meaning of section 2(4A). Clauses 16 and 19 of the managing agency agreement, which were already set out, should suffice to repel this contention. It was a transferable right that the company obtained under the managing agency agreement. Clause 19 specifically recognised the right of each partner of the partnership concern to transfer or assign his rights without in any way impairing the continuance of the managing agency agreement. Where a partnership acquires a right of managing agency, it carries on business, and the right of managing agency itself is one of the assets of that business. Therefore, the share which the assessee had in each of the three partnership concerns was a capital asset within the meaning of section 2(4A) of the Act.

As regards question of sale, it was a condition of the transfer of the share of the assessee in one concern to ‘G’, that ‘G’ transferred to the assessee the share held by ‘G; in the other two partnership concerns to the assessee and paid in addition a sum of Rs. 1,00,000. There were all the elements of a sale in the transaction, which involved both exchange and transfer of capital assets.

The second of the questions referred to this High Court was whether this sum of Rs. 1,00,000 represented the consideration for the transfer of ‘capital asset’ or was compensation for loss of future profits. The managing agency agreement between the concerned parties was left unimpaired by the transfer effected by the assessee in favour of ‘G’ of the transferee's share in the partnership concern. No doubt, thereafter the assessee was not entitled to claim any share in the profits earned by that firm, but it could hardly be said that the transaction between the assessee and ‘G’ should be viewed as compensation for loss of future profits which that firm could hope to earn.

The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was paid by ‘G’ as consideration in part for the transfer of a capital asset. The sum of Rs. 1,00,000 was, therefore, assessable to tax under section 12B.

Note : The case was decided in favour of revenue.

In the case of a bank, the business normally consists of dealing with money and credit. Depositors place their money with the bank and receive a small rate of interest. The bank advances loans to the borrowers from a large part of the deposits at somewhat higher rates of interest. The banker has always to keep enough cash or easily realizable securities to meet any probable demand by the depositors. In the instant case, the provident fund amount belonged to the employees and it could not be said to be stock-in-trade or circulating capital of the assessee and, hence, could not be said that the interest earned was derived from the banking business or was attributable to the same. Only that interest, which is earned on deposits necessary for the purpose of carrying on the banking business, is to be treated as income attributable to the banking business. In that circumstance, it should also not make any difference whether the deposit is made from the stock-in-trade or circulating capital. However, the money, if it did not belong to the assessee at all, would make the difference and in such a situation interest earned on such investment could not be said to be attributable or derived from the banking business. [Para 19]

Similarly, the rental income was neither attributable to nor derived from the business of banking. [Para 27]

Accordingly, the interest derived from investment of the provident fund amount and the rental income did not qualify for deduction under section 80P(2)(a)(i ). [Para 28]

From the reading of section 112(1), it may be noticed that sub-clause (a) ends with a proviso, sub-clause (b) had a proviso which was omitted with effect from 1-4-1996, sub-clause (c) does not have a proviso. At the end of each of sub-clauses (a), (b) and (c ), semi-colon, i.e., (;) is placed to connect independent clauses (a), (b), (c ) and (d) to indicate a closer relationship between them. But, at the end of clause (d ), a full-stop, i.e., (.) is placed to mark the end of declarative sub-clauses (a ), (b), (c ) and (d). Thereafter, a proviso is placed below sub-clause (d). Secondly, the first limb of the said proviso beginning with: 'Provided that where the tax payable in respect of any income arising from the transfer of a long-term capital asset being listed securities or unit or zero coupon bond,… ', applies to a particular kind of long-term capital asset and not to a person under the Act. These two circumstances would suffice to hold the view that the ambit of the said proviso extends not only to sub-clause (d ) to section 112(1) but to all the sub-clauses to section112(1). In other words, the proviso below sub-clause (d ) is a proviso to section112(1). [Para 18]

It is important to have a look at the definition of 'zero coupon bond' as it appears in the Act. A 'zero coupon bond' is defined under section 2(48). As per the definition introduced in the Finance Act, 2005, a zero coupon bond would mean a bond in which no benefit is received or receivable before the maturity or redemption and which are issued on or after 1-6-2005, by an infrastructure capital company or infrastructure capital fund or public sector company and specified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. The definition came into effect from 1-4-2006. The Finance Ministry has also come up with the guidelines to be followed for recognition of the zero coupon bonds issued by an infrastructure capital company or an infrastructure capital fund or a public sector company. The tax treatment of zero coupon bonds has also been rationalized. It had specified that income on transfer of a zero coupon bond would be treated as capital gains, except the income arising from business of dealing in zero coupon bonds. In the notification, the CBDT has issued guidelines stipulating that the application should be made at least three months before the date of issue of such bonds and cannot be filed for bonds to be issued beyond two financial years from the year of application. The applicants have also to fulfil certain conditions relating to tenure of the bond, credit rating and listing on stock exchanges and more importantly that the life of the bond should not be less than 10 years and more than 20 years. The zero coupon bonds are also to be listed at a recognised stock exchange in India. The money raised is to be invested in a manner specified in the guidelines. The manner in which pro rata amount of discount on a zero coupon bond is to be computed and allowed a deduction in the hands of the company or fund or public sector company that issues a zero coupon bond, has been provided.

Bonds and debentures are debt instruments with different types of exposure. They are fixed income instruments and are taken by investors looking for regular, fixed income through payment of interest on the principal purchase. A zero coupon bond pays no coupons and is a distinct financial instrument different from bond in the common parlance.

The 3rd proviso to section 48 brings out distinction in the species of bonds when it excludes 'bonds' which are 'capital indexed bonds issued by the Government'. Just as there are 'capital indexed bonds issued by the Government', there is another specie of bonds called 'zero coupon bonds' of separate and distinct nature to which reference is made by the proviso to section 112(1). The Legislature is conscious of this fact. [Para 19]

First ground of appeal relates to the exemption of capital gain of Rs. 75 lakhs. The Assessing Officer made addition of Rs. 1.54 crores by taking view that the assessee has such receipt during the year. The assessee before the Commissioner (Appeals) strongly objected to the addition by filing detailed written submissions. The Commissioner (Appeals) held that the assessee is a trust and is governed by sections 11, 12 and 13. The Commissioner (Appeals) prepared his summary of computation of total income of assessee. The assessee vehemently argued that its case is covered by the CBDT Instruction No. 883, dated 24-9-1975. The assessee deposited the entire sale consideration as per section 11(5) and ultimately purchased another immovable property for charitable purpose in the financial years 2022-23 and 2023-24. [Para 13]

The assessee has filed sufficient evidence to prove deposit of sale consideration in Nationalized bank. The assessee made investment in bank in fixed deposits of Rs. 50 lakhs on 29-4-2015 and Rs. 25 lakhs on 9-6-2016. The entire sale consideration received was kept in savings bank account with a bank and was converted into fixed deposit as expenditure. The fixed deposits were matured on 29-4-2008, which were further renewed up to 29-4-2021, which were later on converted into capital gain account scheme. Both the fixed deposits were converted into capital gain account with a bank. The assessee claimed that the investment in fixed deposits was held by the trust for the use of benefit of trust as well as in order to keep its corpus intact. [Para 14]

The CBDT in Instruction No. 883, dated 24-9-1975 directed that section 11(1A) provides that where a capital asset, being property held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes is transferred and the whole or any part of the net consideration is utilized for acquiring another capital asset to be so held, then the capital gain arising from the transfer shall be deemed to have been applied to charitable and religious purposes to the extent specified therein. It is referred in the instruction that the Board considered whether investments of the net consideration in fixed deposits with a bank would be regarded as utilization of the amount of the net consideration for acquiring another capital asset within the meaning of section 11(1A). The emerged view was that investments of the net consideration in fixed deposits with a bank for a period of six months or above would be regarded as utilization of the net consideration for acquiring another capital asset within the meaning of section 11(1A). [Para 15]

In view of the above factual and legal position the assessee qualifies of exemption under section 11(1A).

However, the assessee for the first time before Tribunal disclosed that entire amount of capital again was utilized for purchasing other immovable property in the financial years 2022-23 and 2023-24. Therefore, the jurisdictional Assessing Officer is directed to verify said facts and allow relief to the assessee. [Para 18]

There was no evidence to come to conclusion, that one of the lines of the business of the assessee-company was to promote companies and to sell out after the companies had been formed. Nor was it one of the regular lines of business of the assessee-company to acquire licences or permits and sell them. Nor even was it a regular line of business of the assessee-company to acquire managing agencies and sell them.

The licence obtained by the partnership, of which the assessee-company was a member, was a valuable asset and a capital asset in its hands. That capital asset was sold for a sum out of which the assessee received, its share of the receipt. It was capital receipt in its hands, and, therefore, the Assistant Commissioner was right in taking in view that being a capital receipt it fell within the scope of section 12B of 1922 Act. It was not assessable to tax as a trading receipt. Therefore, the claim of the assessee, that it was entitled to the benefit of section 4(3)(vii) of 1922 Act, was erroneous. It was in connection with the business activities of the assessee that the assessee received the sum. That it was a capital receipt in its hand did not make it any the less income from business, and it certainly could not be treated as something of a casual receipt or windfall.

Therefore, the amount in question was assessable to tax as capital gains under section 12B of 1922 Act.

The case of revenue was that if an asset held by a trust was not used for charitable purpose, then capital gains arising on its transfer would not be entitled to exemption under section 11(1A). [Para 10]

It was not disputed that assessee was a trust of long standing, registered in 1896 and was granted registration under section 12A. Its objects were undisputedly charitable. Once a trust is existing for charitable purposes and it is registered under section 12A, then its income has to be computed in accordance with sections 11, 12 and 13 and other provisions of the Act would not be applicable. [Para 11]

Once it was undisputed that trust was existing for charitable purposes and was registered under section 12A then benefit of exemption under sections 11 and 12 could not be denied to the assessee-trust subject to conditions laid down under section 13. The assessing authority and Commissioner (Appeals) had not pointed out any violation of any provisions of section 13, therefore, question of rejecting the exemption on account of provisions of section 13 would not arise. [Para 12]

Now, it had to be seen whether the assessee-trust after holding certificate of registration under section 12A could be denied exemption available to it under section 11(1A).

The provisions of section 11(1A) provide exemption from capital gains on transfer of the capital asset by the trust. In addition to sub-section (1A) which deals with capital asset, sub-section (1) deals with income derived from property held under the trust.

A joint reading of sub-sections (1) and (1A) clearly reveals that sub-section (1) is applicable for providing exemption to income derived from property held for charitable or religious purposes subject to sections 60 to 63. Whereas section 11(1A) deals with gain arising from transfer of capital asset held by a charitable trust, it also provides exemption from capital gains if new capital asset is acquired and held for charitable purposes. Sub-section (5) of section 11 gives the list of capital assets which can be acquired out of net consideration received by the assessee on transfer of property held under the trust. Sub-section (1A) was inserted in section 11 by the Finance (No. 2) Act of 1971 with retrospective effect from 1-4-1962, the object and provision of this insertion was explained in the Departmental Circular No. 72, dated 6-1-1972.

Further Instructions were issued by the Government in Instruction No. 883, dated 24-9-1975.

From the above Circular and Instruction issued by the Government, following propositions emerged :—

(1)

Only the income derived from property held under trust for charitable or religious purposes is exempt under sub-section (1).

(2)

Because of certain amendments by the Finance Act, 1970, a charitable trust would forfeit exemption if trust funds/property in corpus are invested in prohibited categories.

(3)

In order to suitably modify the investment portfolio and to avail the benefit of exemption, it was provided that if trust acquires another capital asset for the use and benefit of the trust by utilizing capital gain from the transfer of property in the corpus then capital gains so utilized would be regarded as applied to charitable or religious purposes of the trust.

(4)

In order to give effect to this intention, sub-section (5) was inserted in section 11 thereby if net consideration is invested in specified categories as enumerated in sub-section (5) then to that extent, trust would continue to avail exemption from the capital gains.

(5)

Where if net consideration on transfer of property in the corpus of the trust is invested in F.D. in a bank for a period of six months or above then it would be regarded as utilization of consideration for acquiring another capital asset within the meaning of section 11(1). The department had not disputed the investment of net consideration on transfer of land to SMC.

(6)

Investment of sale proceeds of the asset held by the trust in F.D. is permissible.

The assessee-trust had invested a sum of Rs. 16.63 crores in IDBI Bank on 31-5-2006 and reinvested in F.D. with State Bank of India on 30-8-2006. Therefore, the conditions laid down in section 11(5) were satisfied. [Para 13]

HEADNOTE: Section 45 read with section 2(14) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B, read with section 2(4A) of Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Whether provisions of section 12B of 1922 Act are not ultra vires - Held, yes - Assessee purchased agricultural land, constructed building, sold both land and building and made profit - There was no evidence that assessee held land for agricultural purposes or derived any agricultural income therefrom - Further more than two years before assessee sold land, and even before he purchased last of plots assessee had decided to put land to use for school house - Whether fact that at one time before assessee purchased said lands, they were agricultural lands, was not enough to sustain claim of assessee that he came within scope of exemption on section 2(4A)(iii) of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether, therefore, assessee was rightly assessed to capital gains tax on profits arising from sale in question - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee purchased some plots of cultivable land. Subsequently, assessee entered into an agreement with a school committee to construct a building for use as a school. The committee occupied the building and paid rent. Later on, the committee decided to buy the property and after some negotiations the assessee sold the land and building for profit. The assessee claimed that all the land, except that actually occupied by the building in use as a school house, was held by him as agricultural land, and that any profit made by the sale of such agricultural land was excluded from the operation of section 12B as agricultural land was not a capital asset as defined by section 2(4A). However, the department assessed the profits to capital gains tax which was upheld by the Tribunal .

On reference :

HELD: The provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act imposing a tax on capital gains are intra vires the Indian Legislature. The assessee admittedly received rent from the school committee. It was ‘income’ but obviously it was not ‘agricultural income’. The assessee failed to establish that he got any other income from the land in the years that preceded the sale. There was, thus, no evidence that the assessee derived ‘agricultural income’ from the lands in question. That the previous owners of the lands cultivated them and derived agricultural income therefrom could not be relevant. Therefore the nature of the lands before the assessee purchased them could not help in deciding the question at issue.

It was clear that more than two years before the assessee sold the land, and even before he purchased the last of the plots to complete the holding, the assessee had decided to put the land to use for a school house, on the construction of which he embarked after his agreement with the Committee in April 1944. Building operations commenced soon thereafter. It was difficult to conceive of any cultivation operations being carried on by the assessee in any extent of the land after the construction had commenced, or after the school authorities moved in. The need for a good bit of the land around the building for use as a playground should be obvious. In the experimental farm, agricultural or horticultural operations were obviously carried on by the school authorities and not by the assessee. The total extent of 2.54 acres could be hardly enough for the school. It was thus a case of a sale of building with a reasonable extent of land appurtenant thereto.

At one time before the assessee purchased the lands, they were agricultural lands, was not enough to sustain the claim of the assessee that he came within the scope of the exemption in sub-clause (iii) of section 2(4A). He did not hold the land for agricultural purposes. He did not derive any agricultural income therefrom.

The assessment of the capital gains was therefore valid.

Note: The case was decided in favour of revenue.

The proviso, to section 12B of 1922 Act contemplates that in case a capital asset is acquired prior to 1-1-1954, the owner has an option for computation of the capital gains to take into account the actual cost or the market value of such property on 1-1-1954.

In the instant case, the indenture clearly provided that the lease was for a period of 999 years commencing from 9-4-1943. The incorporation of such a provision in the indenture of lease showed that once the lease was executed in the manner required by law, the assessees acquired the leasehold interest in the property not from the date of execution of the lease but from 9-4-1943. It was not disputed that in fact from December, 1946, the assessees were in actual possession of the property.

After a registered lease of the type in the present case was executed the Governor of Bombay had merely a lessor's interest in plot from and after 9-4-1943. So, on the relevant date, namely, 1-1-1954, the assessees were the lessees of the leasehold interest under the indenture of lease which was later on executed on 12-5-1954, and got registered on 24-1-1955. In view of this indenture of lease, having regard to the retrospective operation being given to the commencement of the lease, the assessees became the owners of the leasehold interest much prior to 1-1-1954, and they would be entitled to exercise the option in computing the capital gains having regard to the market value of the leasehold interest on -1-1954, subject to such adjustment as may be permissible in law. Thus, the Tribunal was justified in holding that the assessees were entitled to the substitution of the market value of the leasehold interest as on 1-1-1954, for the purpose of computation of capital gains.

Note : The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: First proviso to section 136(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 [corresponding section 52 of the Income-tax Act, 1961] - Capital gains - Transfer in case of understatement of consideration - With a view to sequestering the shares held by assesses in a company from clutches of Government, it sold them at a price much lower than their market value and in fact incurred a loss - Revenue could not prove that consideration was understated - Whether first proviso to section 12B(2) was applicable to assessee's case - Held, no

FACT: The assessee-company was holding certain shares in a company. With a motive of sequestering the said shares from being taken over by the revenue department in settlement of tax dues, it sold said shares at a value much lower than its market value. In fact, the said sale transaction resulted in a loss to the assessee. Applying first proviso to section 12B(2), the ITO computed capital gains on the sale of shares and taxed the same. The Tribunal upheld the ITO's order. The High Court quashed the Tribunal's order observing, inter alia, that though it had been found in this case that the sale was true, the consideration was not understated, and the explanation given by the assessee for effecting the sale was not acceptable ; but it could not be said from the said facts that the sales were effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of liability of the assessee for capital gains.

On appeal:

HELD: The first proviso to section 12B(2) provides 'full value of the consideration for which the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer is made' to be taken as the basis for the computation of the capital gains. Therefore, unless there is evidence that more than what was stated was received, no higher price can be taken to be the basis for computation of capital gains. The onus is on the revenue the inference might be drawn in certain cases but to come to a conclusion that a particular higher amount was in fact received must be based on such material from which such an irresistible conclusion follows. The proviso helps or enables the department by providing a way to determine the market value. But the proviso is applicable only where the full value for the consideration has not been stated. In K.P. Varghese v. ITO [1981] 131 ITR 597, the Supreme Court has held that the second ingredient that is to say that the word 'declared' in sub-section (2) of section 52 is very eloquent and revealing. It clearly indicates that the focus of sub-section (2) is on the consideration declared or disclosed by the assessee as distinguished from the consideration actually received by him and it contemplates a case where the consideration received by the assessee in respect of transaction is not truly declared or disclosed by him but is shown at a different figure. Capital gains is intended to tax the gains of an assessee, not what an assessee might have gained.

In the instant case, the relationship between the parties had been established. The desire to defeat the claims of the revenue had also been established but the fact that for this the assessee had stated a false fact in the document was not established. There was no evidence, direct or inferential, that the consideration actually received by the assessee was more than what was disclosed or declared by him.

Accordingly, the High Court was justified in holding that first proviso to section 12B(2) was not applicable to the instant case.

FACT: The assessee-firm consisted of two partners. After the death of one of the partner on 3-4-1946 there was litigation. The business was stopped on 20-4-1947. The assets of the firm were disposed of by the commissioner appointed by the court on 24-4-1947. The sale amount realized in excess of the written down value was Rs. 81,863. The sale amount in excess of the original cost was Rs. 61,140. The assessee had claimed depreciation of Rs. 20,723. This was the difference between the original cost and the written down value. The ITO held that Rs. 20,723 should be included in assessable income under section 10(2)(vii) while Rs. 61,140 should be treated as capital gain under section 12B. On appeal, the AAC enhanced the capital gain was from 61,140 to Rs. 81,863 rejecting assessee's claim that the capital gain was exempt from charge on the ground of its falling within the third proviso to section 12B (1). The Tribunal upheld the order of the AAC.

On reference:

HELD: In Sri Kannan Rice Mills Ltd. v. CIT [1954] 26 ITR 351, it was held that the third proviso section 12B(1) applied only to cases of distribution of capital assets in specie and not to cases where the distribution was of the sale proceeds of the assets. A similar construction of the third proviso has been adopted by the Bombay High Court in CIT v. James Anderson [1955] 28 ITR 914. In view of these authorities the capital gains or Rs. 81,863 was not exempt under the third proviso of section 12B(1).

The assessee put forward two contentions which had not been urged before the Tribunal. The first was that the instant case was not within the operative words of the first paragraph of section 12B(1) on the ground that the sale which undoubtedly took place was not by the assessee and was therefore not one on the occurrence of which the charge was attracted. It was urged that the sale contemplated by section 12B(1) was a consensual one in which there was mutual assent of the assessee and the purchaser, and that as in the instant case the sale was effected by a commissioner appointed by the Court, it was so to speak in invitum and therefore not within the category of sales under section 12B(1). This contention had no merit and had to be rejected on more than one ground. In the first place, when a Court appoints a commissioner or a receiver to effect a sale, the commissioner so appointed represents the parties to the litigation and is clothed with all the powers which the parties would have. If, therefore, he effects a sale, such sale has for all legal purposes, the same effect as a sale by the parties themselves. In this connection it may be noted that the sale involved in Walji Damji case (supra) was a case of a sale of partnership assets by a receiver appointed by Court in a suit for dissolution and accounts. But apart from this aspect, section 12B(1) includes cases not merely of sales but also of transfers of capital assets. Undoubtedly there has been in this case a transfer of the assets and therefore it was certainly a transaction to which section 12B(1) was attracted. This argument was therefore repelled.

The assessee-company purchased vacant land with an object to grow herbs and plants for medicinal purposes and to construct a warehouse for stocking its goods. The land was, however, compulsorily acquired by the State Government and the assessee obtained a sum as compensation and, made a profit out of the purchase of said land.

The assessee claimed exemption from tax on this amount on the ground that section 12B(1) of 1922 Act was not applicable. The ITO held that the land was a 'capital asset' within the meaning of section 2(4A) of 1922 Act, and therefore, section 12B of 1922 Act was attracted. On appeal, the AAC upheld the order of the ITO. On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the order of AAC.

that as it may, if one were to peruse the object for which the assessee, viz., BDA was constituted, it is clear that the intent and purpose is for planned urban development of Bangalore City and not with the purpose of profit making; i.e., the activity of formation of layouts and allotment of sites is only carried out with the primary and main object to ensure planned development of Bangalore City and not with the intention to make profits. [Para 5.9.3] Carrying on business connotes some substantial, systematic and organized activity with the object of making gain and profit thereon, with the inevitable control and direction vis-à-vis such activity of business. Profit motive is surely the essence of trade, commerce or business and therefore in situations and circumstances in which services are rendered without a profit motive, such rendering of service will not have anything in common with trade or commerce or business. If one were to test the proviso to section 2(15) against the background of a recognized charitable organization, then one has to see whether the predominant object of the activity is to make profit or whether the predominant object of the activity is to carry out charitable purposes and not profit making. [Para 5.9.4]

It is the basic motive behind the activity, which is important to be considered; whether it is one with profit motive or not. Merely because surplus is generated from a particular activity of a assessee society; it cannot be said that such activity is in the nature of trade, commerce or business and what needs to be seen is, what the intent and purpose of starting such activity is. In the case on hand, the BDA's embarkation of the activity of setting up of residential layouts, including the activity of sale of sites and flats, is definitely not with a view to earn profit, but to ensure planned urban development and also to accomplish a social objective of providing an opportunity to economically weaker sections of society to be able to own a residence on their own. [Para 5.9.5]

The view of the Assessing Officer which is impliedly endorsed by the Commissioner (Appeals) in the impugned order; i.e., that (iv) "The activities of the assessee and the generation of profits on account of the same are akin to the activities carried on by real estate companies, property developers, infrastructure firms, etc., and therefore, the activities of the assessee squarely fall under the ambit of activities which are in the nature of trade, commerce and business,accordingly the activities of the assessee are hit by the first proviso to section 2(15)"; is rather superfluous in nature. No doubt, it is a fact that one will see a lot of similarities in the activity of the assessee vis-à-vis that of a real estate developer. However, the issue to be considered is, not whether the activity of the assessee is similar to that of the private real estate developer or not, but whether the underlying purpose of the activity is the same as that of the private real estate developer, i.e., making and maximization of profit. In the case of this assessee; viz., BDA, the underlying motive / objective is not making and maximizing of profits, but planned development of Bangalore City. It is important in this context to note the fact that concerned Income tax authorities have recognized the assessee as a public charitable organization by grant of registration under section 12A since 26-3-2003 and that the assessee's objects clause, i.e., section 14 of the BDA Act has not undergone any change or modification since its enactment; which is what must have prompted the Income Tax Department to take the view that it was charitable in nature. In other words, the Income Tax Department considered the assessee, 'BDA' to be covered by the provisions of section 2(15). [Para 5.10.1]

It is after the introduction of the proviso to section 2(15) that the Income Tax Department took a view that the activity of 'BDA' was in the nature of trade, commerce or business and cancelled the registration, granted under section 12A, vide order dated 8-11-2011. The assessee's registration under section 12A however stood restored by a decision of the co-ordinate Bench of this Tribunal. In this prevailing factual matrix, there is no change in the objects and the only issue which apparently prompts revenue to take the view it has taken, i.e., that the activity of the assessee is hit by the proviso to section 2(15); is the fact that the activity of the assessee has resulted in huge surplus or profits. The fact of surplus or shortfall is not to be reckoned as the test for applicability of the proviso to section 2(15); but rather, whether the activity is embarked upon solely with the view to earn profit or not; which the Assessing Officer and Commissioner (Appeals) have not done. [Para 5.10.2]

In view of the factual and legal matrix of the case, as discussed above, the activities of the assessee, development authority are not hit by the proviso to section 2(15). Having held so, the Assessing Officer is directed to allow the assessee the benefits of section 11 while giving effect to this order. [Para 5.10.5]

The assessee purchased some plots of cultivable land. Subsequently, assessee entered into an agreement with a school committee to construct a building for use as a school. The committee occupied the building and paid rent. Later on, the committee decided to buy the property and after some negotiations the assessee sold the land and building for profit. The assessee claimed that all the land, except that actually occupied by the building in use as a school house, was held by him as agricultural land, and that any profit made by the sale of such agricultural land was excluded from the operation of section 12B as agricultural land was not a capital asset as defined by section 2(4A). However, the department assessed the profits to capital gains tax which was upheld by the Tribunal .

On reference :

Levy of capital gains was in force only for a short period and it was discontinued with effect from 1-4-1949. The levy was revived by the Finance (No. 3) Act of 1956 with effect from 1-4-1957. By the said Finance Act of 1956, certain modifications were made to the provision as it existed, one of the modifications being to bring within the scope of this provision any gain resulting from the relinquishment of a capital asset. The third proviso to section 12B(1) was re-enacted, but there was no reference to the compulsory acquisition not being treated as sale, exchange or transfer of capital assets. When the Income-tax Act of 1961 was enacted the provisions of section 12B were substantially adopted, but with some modifications. In order to avoid the repetition of the words "sale, exchange, etc." in the provision it was thought desirable to use the word "transfer" and Parliament defined it in section 2(47).

It is now well settled that the provision has to be interpreted on its own terms. The word "transfer" would comprehend a transfer by Act of parties as well as by operation of law. A compulsory acquisition is a transfer by preparation of law. Therefore, the provision, even before 1956, was wide enough to rope in gains an compulsory acquisitions. Thus, even proceeding on the basis that the legislature should be taken to have assumed that the transfer did not include compulsory acquisition until the Act of 1961, still it would not be a proper assumption. The very fact that the exemption originally granted in the third proviso was taken away in 1956 clearly goes to show that Parliament intended to tax gains on compulsory acquisition.

The beliefs or assumptions of those who frame Acts of Parliament cannot make the law. The modification made to the third proviso to section 12B of the 1922 Act when the provision was being re-cast in 1956, goes to show that the compulsory acquisition was not intended to enjoy exemption under the Finance Act, 1956. If the draftsman in 1961 assumed that it did enjoy the exemption even after 1956, it would be contrary to the provisions and the consequence following the amendment in 1956. There was no substance in the submission that compulsory acquisition was brought within the ambit of "capital gains" only 1961.

Taking the language of section 12B of the 1922 Act, it would be found that it provides for tax on capital gains. Such tax has to be levied on the profits or gains arising from certain stated transactions after a particular date. Such profits and gains are to be deemed to be the income of the previous year in which the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer took place. There is, thus, a statutory fiction introduced in section 12B of the 922 Act. The fiction overrides all other considerations. Under the provision, as it is one, has to find out what are profits and gains in the transaction. Such profits and gains would then have to be deemed to be the income of the previous year in which the relevant transaction took place. There is no warrant for splitting up the profits and gains. In order to arrive at the profits and gains, on has to take the totality of the receipts of one or more years, and then substract therefrom the deductions authorised by section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act. Considered in this light, whatever be the year in which the further compensations was awarded, the amount would have to be brought to tax in the year in which the acquisition took place. What gives rise to the compensation is the taking over of the property. It was not disputed that this taking over happened in relevant year. The further amounts given by the City Civil Court and by the High Court have all their origin or root in the acquisition which took place in the material year. Importing the statutory fiction the amounts subsequently awarded would have to be retrospectively attributed to the year in which the transaction took place.

Section 12B has, by importing a fiction rendered the sum liable to tax in the year in which the transaction took place. The circumstance that the subsequent amounts were awarded only in later years did not affect the assessability of the amount in the year under consideration

ITAT’s decision 14. Now we shall turn our attention to the order of the ITAT, "H" Bench, Mumbai in ITA No. 2552 of 2005 on which strong reliance has been placed by Revenue. The learned Members of the Tribunal held that the Legis- lature never intended to give the benefit of proviso to section 112(1) to those cases where long-term capital gain is required to be computed under the first proviso to section 48. The Tribunal purported to reach the con- clusion on a literal construction of the proviso, the language of which, the Tribunal acknowledges, is unambiguous. With due respect to the lear- ned Members of Tribunal, we find it difficult to appreciate the observation that the literal construction of proviso leads to the meaning it has attributed to the provision. The Tribunal failed to note that there are no words of exclusion of the assessees like the applicant governed by the first proviso to section 48. Nor can they be inferred by necessary implication. It appears that the Tribunal’s views is based on the premise that the legislature did not intend to provide two reliefs to a non-resident assessee - one under the proviso to section 48 and another under the proviso to section 112(1). As already discussed in the preceding para, no such legislative intention can be imputed to the legislature except by way of some guess work or a priori reasoning. The assumption of the Tribunal that it was giving effect to literal construction as well as legislative intent is incorrect. The further observation of the Tribunal that if the legislature intended to cover the cases falling under the first proviso to section 48, it would not have used the words ‘second proviso to section 48’ [in the proviso to section 112(1)] is based on a wrong premise. One does not follow from the other. The second proviso to section 48 should necessarily be mentioned in the proviso to section 112(1) as the tax rate of 10 per cent should be calculated without reference to the indexation formula that is applicable to the resident assessees. Hence, the reference to 2nd proviso to section 48 cannot be avoided. The only question is about the connotation of the expression "before giving effect to the second proviso to section 48" - whether those words have the effect of excluding those who cannot avail of the indexation benefit under the 2nd proviso, that is to say, the non-residents including foreign companies. We are of the considered opinion, for the reasons already set out, that the crucial phrase in the proviso to section 112(1) does not have such effect.

14.1 The learned Members of the Tribunal placed much reliance on sub-section (3) to section 115AD by way of contrast with the language of the proviso to section 112(1). Section 115 AD, inter alia, provides that where the total income of a foreign institutional investor includes income by way of capital gain arising from the transfer of securities, the amount of income-tax calculated on the said income shall be at the rate of 10 per cent. Sub-section (3) says nothing contained in the first and second provisos to section 48 shall apply for the computation of capital gains arising out of the transfer of securities...’. After referring to sub-section (3), the Tribunal makes an observation that "if the legislature had intended to give benefit of marginal relief of tax to all non-residents, it could have easily used the words ‘first and second provisos of section 48’. The Tribunal missed to note that by adding the words ‘first proviso’, the intended result will not be achieved. On the other hand, the position of non-resident will be worse. For these reasons, we have no hesitation in differing with the view taken by the Tribunal.

Section 12B was inserted in the 1922 Act by the Indian Income-tax and Excess Profits Tax (Amendment) Act, 1947 which was a Central Act. Under section 100 of the Government of India Act, 1935, the Central Legislature was empowered to make laws with respect to matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule to that Act. Entry 54 in list I caused taxes on income other than agricultural income while entry 55 caused taxes on the capital value of the assets, exclusive of agricultural land, of individuals and companies, and taxes on the capital of companies.

In construing an entry in a List conferring legislative powers the widest possible construction according to their ordinary meaning must be put upon the words used therein. The cardinal rule of interpretation, is that words should be read in their ordinary, natural and grammatical meaning subject to this rider that in construing words in a constitutional enactment conferring legislative power the most liberal construction should be put upon the words so that the same may have effect in their widest amplitude. Thus the word 'income' occurring in said entry 54 should be given its widest connotation in view of the fact that it occurs in a legislative head conferring legislative power. The argument that the word should be interpreted on basis of assumed legislative practice in England was not acceptable. It was, therefore, to be held in the instant case that Act of 1947 which amended the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 by enlarging the definition of the term income in section 2(6C) of the 1922 Act and introducing a new head of income in section 6 and inserting the new section 12B of the 1922 Act was intra vires the powers of the Central Legislature acting under Entry 54 in List I of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act, 1935.

Now, it had to be seen whether the assessee-trust after holding certificate of registration under section 12A could be denied exemption available to it under section 11(1A).

The provisions of section 11(1A) provide exemption from capital gains on transfer of the capital asset by the trust. In addition to sub-section (1A) which deals with capital asset, sub-section (1) deals with income derived from property held under the trust. A joint reading of sub-sections (1) and (1A) clearly reveals that sub-section (1) is applicable for providing exemption to income derived from property held for charitable or religious purposes subject to sections 60 to 63. Whereas section 11(1A) deals with gain arising from transfer of capital asset held by a charitable trust, it also provides exemption from capital gains if new capital asset is acquired and held for charitable purposes. Sub-section (5) of section 11 gives the list of capital assets which can be acquired out of net consideration received by the assessee on transfer of property held under the trust. Sub-section (1A) was inserted in section 11 by the Finance (No. 2) Act of 1971 with retrospective effect from 1-4-1962, the object and provision of this insertion was explained in the Departmental Circular No. 72, dated 6-1-1972.

Further Instructions were issued by the Government in Instruction No. 883, dated 24-9-1975.

From the above Circular and Instruction issued by the Government, following propositions emerged :—

(1)

Only the income derived from property held under trust for charitable or religious purposes is exempt under sub-section (1).

(2)

Because of certain amendments by the Finance Act, 1970, a charitable trust would forfeit exemption if trust funds/property in corpus are invested in prohibited categories.

(3)

In order to suitably modify the investment portfolio and to avail the benefit of exemption, it was provided that if trust acquires another capital asset for the use and benefit of the trust by utilizing capital gain from the transfer of property in the corpus then capital gains so utilized would be regarded as applied to charitable or religious purposes of the trust.

(4)

In order to give effect to this intention, sub-section (5) was inserted in section 11 thereby if net consideration is invested in specified categories as enumerated in sub-section (5) then to that extent, trust would continue to avail exemption from the capital gains.

(5)

Where if net consideration on transfer of property in the corpus of the trust is invested in F.D. in a bank for a period of six months or above then it would be regarded as utilization of consideration for acquiring another capital asset within the meaning of section 11(1). The department had not disputed the investment of net consideration on transfer of land to SMC.

(6)

Investment of sale proceeds of the asset held by the trust in F.D. is permissible.

The assessee-trust had invested a sum of Rs. 16.63 crores in IDBI Bank on 31-5-2006 and reinvested in F.D. with State Bank of India on 30-8-2006. Therefore, the conditions laid down in section 11(5) were satisfied. [Para 13]

Instruction No. 883, dated 24-9-1975 clarifies that deposit with the bank would qualify for exemption as per section 11(1A). Now, the only controversy survived for adjudication was whether in case of non-use of land, assessee would lose exemption under section 11(1A). The phrase used in section 11(1A) is 'Where, capital asset being property under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes'. So far as land acquired by SMC was concerned, it was undisputedly owned by the trust. Property is a term of wide import and subject to any limitation or qualification which the context require it, signifies every possible interest which a person can acquire wholly and enjoy. The capital asset is defined under section 2(14) and it will include land owned by the assessee. Thus, there was no dispute on the proposition that land acquired by SMC was a capital asset and was a property owned by the trust. Thus, the controversy was further reduced to the interpretation of the term 'held under trust wholly for charitable or religious purposes'.

Meaning and explanation of word 'held'

The term 'held' embraces two items. One is actual possession of some subject or property in which legal title is invested, or right to hold or claim such possession. Such possession could be actual or constructive. The term 'held' also connotes ownership as well as possession. The word 'held' cannot be interpreted only to mean in the sense of possession but would also mean an owner who is not in actual possession. In some cases, it has been held that word "held" connotes the existence of a right or a title in the holder. In the instant case, the land acquired by SMC was under legal ownership of the trust and was possessed by the trustees on behalf of the trust in their fiduciary capacity.

The second part of the third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act relates to distribution of assets either at the time of partition or on the dissolution of partnership, or on a liquidation of a company and for that purpose, the assets are valued for distribution. The expression, "any distribution of capital assets" occurring in this proviso, thus, governs not only partition of a HUF but also the dissolution of a firm and the other association of persons or the liquidation of a company. In the instant case, as there was no distribution of the capital assets as such but only for the sale proceeds of the assets after sale was effected by the liquidator, the contention of the assessee that any transfer of a capital asset on the occasion of either dissolution of a firm or liquidation of the company would also be covered by the language of the section was not acceptable. Whatever may be the functions of a liquidator in liquidation proceeding and even if he is to sell the assets for discharging the liabilities and distributing the surplus, that does not mean that the operation by sale for that end would be a distribution of capital assets within the meaning of the proviso. Therefore, profit realized by sale of the plant, machinery and buildings by the assessee was not exempt from capital gains tax under the third proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act.

As regards applicability of the second proviso, it applies only to property, the income of which is chargeable under section 9 of the 1922 Act. For purposes of computation of income of the property under section 9 of the 1922 Act, the property taken into consideration is only such portion of the property, which is not in the occupation of the assessee for the purposes of any business or vocation carried on by him. Since the property in question was in the occupation of the assessee for the purpose of his business, which is never made chargeable under section 9 of 1922 Act, the second proviso also did not apply to the instant case. Hence, the profit realized by sale of that portion of the buildings which was used for the assessee’s business was not exempt from capital gains tax under the second proviso to section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

was not made with the object of avoidance or reduction of tax liability but made for the purpose of benefiting the ladies and as a matter of fact, the motive for the sale might have been the natural love and affection for and desire to provide the ladies. The Tribunal, therefore, held that the second condition for application of the proviso to section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act had not been satisfied and that, therefore, the proviso could not be invoked.

On reference: HELD: The main requisites for application of the proviso are: (1) acquisition by a person from the assessee of a capital asset by one of the modes mentioned in section 12B(1)of the 1922 Act; (2) connection directly or indirectly of the purchaser with the assessee who is the vendor; (3) consideration for such a transaction as expressed or found being less than the fair market value; and (4) the motive for the transaction, namely, avoidance or reduction of liability to tax, impliedly with reference to the difference in price not reflected in the transaction. It is obvious that the transaction should be a real one and has been acted upon. But the connection directly or indirectly between the vendor and purchaser may serve as the starting point for a probe as to the motive for the transaction. If in the search for the motive in the light of tangible material the ITO is of opinion that the consideration recited for the transaction, which is lower than the fair market value, was a means to avoid or reduce the tax liability, all the requisites required for invoking and applying the proviso would have been satisfied. But where it is found or there is nothing to show that the consideration for the transaction, though lower than the fair market value is not a means or device or a cloak to avoid or reduce the tax liability, the proviso will have no application. It reduces itself to this that if the consideration for the transaction has been honestly agreed upon, with a view to benefit the purchaser and out of love and affection on account of the relationship, or with reference to particular circumstances, there will then be little room and there will, be no justification for imputing a motive to the vendor to avoid or reduce the tax liability. The consideration cannot be said to be the result of an honest dealing and at the same time it be dubbed as a device for avoidance or reduction of tax liability. What the proviso gets at for charge is the actual capital gain which the vendor should, in the circumstances, have made but is made to appear that the gain as shown by the consideration for the transaction to be much less or nil. It would not be said that the proviso discourages or avoids honest transactions made out of love and affection or for other conceivable reasons on pain of being on an assumption, hauled up, if one may use the expression, for having attempted to avoid or reduce the tax liability and on that basis made liable to tax on the difference between the consideration for the transaction and the fair market value. That simply, as one read the proviso, is not its purpose. It does not treat what is not an actual capital gain as a deemed capital gain. In fact, occurring as it does as the first proviso to sub-section (2) dealing with the procedural aspect of computation, it should be interpreted as limited to escaped capital gain, which is so in truth and in fact, and not intended to bring about fictional gain on an assumption and charge the same.

The Tribunal was, therefore, right in holding that the proviso to section 12B of the 1922 Act had no application.

HEADNOTE: Section 48 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B(2) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Computation of - Assessment year 1960-61 - Whether for purpose of taking fair market value, to be value on basis of which capital gains are to be computed, two conditions as required by first proviso to section 12B(2) of 1922 Act should be fulfilled and these conditions are cumulative - Held, yes - Whether if on computation made these is capital loss then there cannot be any liability for capital gains under section 12B of 1922 Act - Held yes

FACT: During the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1960-61, the assessee sold certain shares and shown profit. When the ITO went into the question of levying capital gains on those transactions, the assessee requested substitution of the fair market value of the shares as on 1-1-1954, under the second proviso to sub-section (2) of section 12B of 1922 Act in place of cost price. The ITO worked out the fair market value of the shares on the basis of the break-up value as on the 1-1-1954, at Rs. 14.62 per share. With regard to the sale price the ITO found that the sales were effected by the assessee at Rs. 2.25 per share. On the facts of the case, the ITO held that the sales were to persons with whom the assessee was directly or indirectly connected as the assessee was a Birla group of concerns and the sales were to the members of the Birla family. In those circumstances, the ITO came to the conclusion that, even though the shares were of very high value, the sales were effected with the object of reducing the assessee's liability under section 12B of 1922 Act and determined the fair market value of the shares on the break-up method at Rs. 14.45 per share. On second appeal, it was contended before the Tribunal that the first proviso to section 12B(2) of 1922 Act had no application and, alternatively, in arriving at the sale price, deduction should be given for the brokerage on the sale of the shares. The Tribunal held that proviso to section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act was applicable only if: (i) the person acquiring the share, that is, the purchaser, is one with whom the assessee is directly or indirectly connected; and (ii) the ITO has reason to believe that the sale, was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of liability under this section. The Tribunal, however, was of the view that the two conditions were cumulative and had to be simultaneously satisfied. Finding that there was no liability to capital gains according to the ITO’s own computation, he having arrived at a capital loss, the Tribunal held that there was no proved attempt at avoidance or reduction of liability to tax. It was held that the second condition was not satisfied and the proviso did not, therefore, apply. The ITO was directed to modify the assessment in the light of the finding of the Tribunal.

On reference :

HELD: For the purpose of taking the fair market value, to be the value on the basis of which capital gains are to be computed, two conditions are required by the first proviso to the section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act, to be fulfilled, namely, the sale must be to a person with whom the assessee is directly or indirectly connected and, secondly, that the transaction must be entered into with the object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee under the section. It is apparent that the two conditions are cumulative and the Tribunal had so held. If on the computation made there is capital loss then there cannot be any liability for capital gains under section 12B of the 1922 Act. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in view of the calculations made that there was no liability on the assessee under section 12B. If there was no liability then no question arose of attempt being made at the reduction of liability to tax and of entering into transaction with that view in the end. The second condition of the first proviso to the sub-section requires that the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer must be with the object of avoidance or reduction of "liability of the assessee under the section". But if there is no liability or if the transaction is of such a nature that no liability could arise, then there cannot be any attempt to reduce the liability by selling at a value less than the fair market value. Such a finding by the Tribunal could not be described as perverse in the sense that no reasonable person could come to such a finding.

INTRODUCTION

Capital gains, being the fourth specie of total income of an assessee, are covered in sections 45 to 55AA of the Income-tax Act (the Act) and are contained in Chapter IV-E of the Act. Though these sections numbering about 25 form approximately 7 to 8% of the entire Income-tax Act, capital gain issues occupy nearly 15 to 20% of the cases reported in various tax journals and websites. One of the main issues which should engage the attention of the Legislature is prohibiting an assessee from making a claim in respect of investments in an altogether different name or in the name of distant relative as, in the considered opinion of the author, it is not the intention of the Legislature. The proviso to section 54F of the Act imposes certain restrictions with regard to holding and acquiring properties and so if the investments in different names are permitted to be made, the provisions of section 54F of the Act may get defeated/ diluted and the issue may go out of the purview of the Revenue as the assessee, if given an option, may invest in the name of another person thereby making way for probable escapement of income. In this article case laws pertaining to investment made in the names different relatives have been analyzed. The various decisions rendered by the judicial authorities have not been grouped in one or two paragraphs but have been covered in different paragraphs in order to highlight the issues covered in those decisions by these judicial authorities.
