In the instant case, there was no material or an iota of evidence that the original agreement of sale had undergone any change or was modified or was altered. The only circum stances on which reliance was placed was that there was no sale deed executed by the assessee in favour of ‘T’, but, on the other hand, the assessee company had resigned itself the managing agency. In the absence of any evidence or any material that the resignation was the consequence of any agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ altering the terms of the original contract, that circumstance would make no difference, but it would only amount to the mode of performance of the contract of sale. In what form, by what mode, the contract is performed is not to be determined in accordance with the general provisions of law, but in construing section 12B of the 1922 Act one must not give to the expression 'sale or transfer' its technical meaning, nor must one attribute to 'sale or transfer' as used by the legislature in section 12B of the 1922 Act a transaction clothed with all its legal formalities. What is to be seen is what actually was the contract between the parties. The agreement between the parties was that the managing agency was to be sold or transferred by the assessee company to ‘T’. That objective had been achieved by the resignation of the assessee from the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents as part of the one and the same transaction.

It is clear that what is vital and what is determinative is the nature of the transaction as embodying in the documents in which the parties have chosen to embody, the terms of the transaction, and not the mode by which it is performed. In the instant case, the documents in which the parties had embodied the transaction between them was only the offer of purchase made by ‘T’ by their letter of 31-8-1946, and its acceptance by the assessee on 22-9-1946, and, on the construction of these two documents, there could not be any doubt that the transaction between the parties was one of sale or transfer of the share as well as the managing agency. Further, the steps taken by the assessee also left no doubt that this agreement between the parties had been performed by the assessee by tendering their resignations simultaneously with the appointment of T as managing agents. The consideration had been received by the assessee. It was thereafter that on 7-1-1947, the resignation had been tendered by the assessee of their managing agency. It had to be kept in view that all the shares of the managed company were held by the assessee. The managing agency firm consisted of only two persons as partners.

Within two days the assessee ceased to be managing agents, and ‘T’ became managing agents of the managed company simultaneously. This exactly was the result which the agreement between the assessee and ‘T’ contemplated. The resignation by the assessee of the managing agency and the appointment of ‘T’ as managing agents, therefore, was nothing but the mode of performance of the agreement to sell the managing agency arrived at between the assessee and ‘T’. That being the position, the income-tax authorities were justified in holding that the provisions of section 12B of the 1922 Act were attracted to the facts of the case.

It is important to have a look at the definition of 'zero coupon bond' as it appears in the Act. A 'zero coupon bond' is defined under section 2(48). As per the definition introduced in the Finance Act, 2005, a zero coupon bond would mean a bond in which no benefit is received or receivable before the maturity or redemption and which are issued on or after 1-6-2005, by an infrastructure capital company or infrastructure capital fund or public sector company and specified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. The definition came into effect from 1-4-2006. The Finance Ministry has also come up with the guidelines to be followed for recognition of the zero coupon bonds issued by an infrastructure capital company or an infrastructure capital fund or a public sector company. The tax treatment of zero coupon bonds has also been rationalized. It had specified that income on transfer of a zero coupon bond would be treated as capital gains, except the income arising from business of dealing in zero coupon bonds. In the notification, the CBDT has issued guidelines stipulating that the application should be made at least three months before the date of issue of such bonds and cannot be filed for bonds to be issued beyond two financial years from the year of application. The applicants have also to fulfil certain conditions relating to tenure of the bond, credit rating and listing on stock exchanges and more importantly that the life of the bond should not be less than 10 years and more than 20 years. The zero coupon bonds are also to be listed at a recognised stock exchange in India. The money raised is to be invested in a manner specified in the guidelines. The manner in which pro rata amount of discount on a zero coupon bond is to be computed and allowed a deduction in the hands of the company or fund or public sector company that issues a zero coupon bond, has been provided.

When the Income-tax Act of 1961 was enacted the provisions of section 12B were substantially adopted, but with some modifications. In order to avoid the repetition of the words "sale, exchange, etc." in the provision it was thought desirable to use the word "transfer" and Parliament defined it in section 2(47). It is now well settled that the provision has to be interpreted on its own terms. The word "transfer" would comprehend a transfer by Act of parties as well as by operation of law. A compulsory acquisition is a transfer by preparation of law. Therefore, the provision, even before 1956, was wide enough to rope in gains an compulsory acquisitions. Thus, even proceeding on the basis that the legislature should be taken to have assumed that the transfer did not include compulsory acquisition until the Act of 1961, still it would not be a proper assumption. The very fact that the exemption originally granted in the third proviso was taken away in 1956 clearly goes to show that Parliament intended to tax gains on compulsory acquisition.

The beliefs or assumptions of those who frame Acts of Parliament cannot make the law. The modification made to the third proviso to section 12B of the 1922 Act when the provision was being re-cast in 1956, goes to show that the compulsory acquisition was not intended to enjoy exemption under the Finance Act, 1956. If the draftsman in 1961 assumed that it did enjoy the exemption even after 1956, it would be contrary to the provisions and the consequence following the amendment in 1956. Taking the language of section 12B of the 1922 Act, it would be found that it provides for tax on capital gains. Such tax has to be levied on the profits or gains arising from certain stated transactions after a particular date. Such profits and gains are to be deemed to be the income of the previous year in which the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer took place. There is, thus, a statutory fiction introduced in section 12B of the 922 Act. The fiction overrides all other considerations. Under the provision, as it is one, has to find out what are profits and gains in the transaction. Such profits and gains would then have to be deemed to be the income of the previous year in which the relevant transaction took place. There is no warrant for splitting up the profits and gains. In order to arrive at the profits and gains, on has to take the totality of the receipts of one or more years, and then substract therefrom the deductions authorised by section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act. Considered in this light, whatever be the year in which the further compensations was awarded, the amount would have to be brought to tax in the year in which the acquisition took place. What gives rise to the compensation is the taking over of the property. It was not disputed that this taking over happened in relevant year. The further amounts given by the City Civil Court and by the High Court have all their origin or root in the acquisition which took place in the material year. Importing the statutory fiction the amounts subsequently awarded would have to be retrospectively attributed to the year in which the transaction took place.

Section 12B has, by importing a fiction rendered the sum liable to tax in the year in which the transaction took place. The circumstance that the subsequent amounts were awarded only in later years did not affect the assessability of the amount in the year under consideration

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Whether expression 'Transfer' in section 12B of 1922 Act includes not only a permanent transfer but also a temporary transfer of title to property and lease of mines for any period would fall within ambit of section 12B of 1922 Act - Held, yes - Whether a lease of land is transfer of interest in land and creates a right in rem and there is a transfer of title in favour of lessee though lessor has right of reversion after period of lease terminates - Held, yes - Whether legislation enacted in section 12B of 1922 Act is in pith and substance legislation relating to tax on capital value of assets and enactment of section 12B is constitutionally a valid piece of legislation - Held, yes

FACT: During the relevant accounting year, the assessee-company executed an indenture of lease in favour of 'K' for 99 years and received certain consideration. The lease related to surface right together with nine mica mines located in the area demised. The ITO determined the cost of the mineral right with respect to the nine mines transferred to the company on a proportionate basis. After deducting this amount from the salami which the assessee received from 'K', the ITO found that the assessee had made a capital gain and taxed this amount under section 12B.

On appeal, the AAC as also the Tribunal upheld the view taken by the ITO.

On reference :

HELD: The expression 'transfer' in section 12B includes not only a permanent transfer but also a temporary transfer of title to the property in question and lease of mines for any period would fall within the ambit of section 12B. A lease of land is transfer of interest in the land and creates a right in rem; and there is a transfer of title in favour of the lessee though the lessor has right of reversion after the period of the lease terminates. For these reasons, the transaction of the lease granted by the assessee in favour of 'K' was a transfer of a capital asset within the meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act and the gains arising to the assessee on account of this transfer of the capital asset was rightly taxed by the income-tax authorities. As regards the constitutional validity of section 12B, the Central Legislature has validly enacted section 12B in exercise of the authority conferred upon it by item 55 of List I of the 7th Schedule.

Proviso to section 112(1) 10. The proviso to section 112(1) was introduced by the Finance Act, 1999 with effect from 1-4-2000. The background for introducing the proviso will be adverted to later. Prior to the insertion of the proviso, section 112(1) provided for uniform rate of 20 per cent tax on all long-term capital gains accruing to the four categories of assessees out of which three are residents. However, certain categories of non-residents viz., foreign institutional investors were having the benefit of lesser rate of tax of 10 per cent (vide section 115AD) in respect of gains arising from the transfer of securities. The proviso in question was enacted with a view to provide maximum rate of 10 per cent on long term capital gains in respect of listed securities. Later, two more items i.e., units and zero coupon bonds were added. The proviso occurring at the end of the section cannot be viewed as the proviso to clause (d) only. In fact, it is not so contended either by the applicant or by the revenue. Without delving further on this point, suffice it to say that it would be irrational and even incongruous to allocate the proviso only to the preceding clause.

Area of Controversy

11. Whereas it is the contention of the revenue that having regard to the language employed in the proviso, it has no application to non-residents and foreign companies, specified in clause (c), according to the applicant, the proviso ought to be applied to clause (c) category assessee’s also. That is the area of controversy. Both sides sought to project the objective of the proviso in different light. If the Revenue’s contention is accepted, the non-residents who are afforded protection from the adverse effect of rupee volatility under the first proviso to section 48 cannot invoke the benefit of concessional tax under the proviso to section 12(1).

Interpretation of Proviso

12. What then is the real purport, scope and meaning of the proviso to section 112(1)? Let us address ourselves to that question.

12.1 We are of the view that the benefit of the proviso to section 112(1) cannot be denied to the non-residents/foreign companies who are also entitled to a different relief in terms of first proviso to section 48. At the outset, while interpreting the proviso to section 112(1), it should be borne in mind that the said proviso is a special provision in relation to the transfer of certain long-term capital assets viz., listed securities, units and zero-coupon bonds. In our view, there is no warrant to limit the 10 per cent effective rate provided therein as against the normal rate of 20 per cent only to the three categories of resident assessees specified in clauses (a), (b) and (d ). Clear words would have been deployed in the proviso if one particular category i.e., non-residents are to be excluded. It is difficult to hold that such a result was intended to be achieved by means of the phraseology - ‘before giving effect to the second proviso to section 48’. Nor can it be said that the said phrase by necessary implication excludes clause (c) category of assessees who are, of course, entitled to another benefit conferred by the first proviso to section 48.

12.2 In plain and peremptory words, the proviso limits the rate of tax on the gains from the transfer of listed securities to 10 per cent, but, with an important rider that the quantum of capital gains should be arrived at without taking into account the formula laid down in the second proviso to section 48 based on the indexed cost of acquisition. In other words, while computing the capital gains on the listed securities held for more than 12 months, do not give effect to the calculation spelt out in the second proviso to section 48 wherever it is applicable, or to put it in a different language, let not the indexation formula enter into the computation process - that is the mandate of controversial phrase in the proviso to section 112(1). It does not say - deny the concessional rate of tax to the category of assessees who are not eligible to have the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition under the second proviso. In other words, the eligibility to avail the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition (under the second proviso to section 48) is not a sine qua non for applying the reduced rate of 10 per cent prescribed by the proviso to section 112(1). The second proviso to section 48 is only a mode of computation of capital gains. The crucial words relied upon by the Revenue cannot be construed as the words of exclusion of a category of assessees i.e., non-residents who cannot avail of indexation benefit.

Proviso to section 112(1) 10. The proviso to section 112(1) was introduced by the Finance Act, 1999 with effect from 1-4-2000. The background for introducing the proviso will be adverted to later. Prior to the insertion of the proviso, section 112(1) provided for uniform rate of 20 per cent tax on all long-term capital gains accruing to the four categories of assessees out of which three are residents. However, certain categories of non-residents viz., foreign institutional investors were having the benefit of lesser rate of tax of 10 per cent (vide section 115AD) in respect of gains arising from the transfer of securities. The proviso in question was enacted with a view to provide maximum rate of 10 per cent on long term capital gains in respect of listed securities. Later, two more items i.e., units and zero coupon bonds were added. The proviso occurring at the end of the section cannot be viewed as the proviso to clause (d) only. In fact, it is not so contended either by the applicant or by the revenue. Without delving further on this point, suffice it to say that it would be irrational and even incongruous to allocate the proviso only to the preceding clause.

Area of Controversy

11. Whereas it is the contention of the revenue that having regard to the language employed in the proviso, it has no application to non-residents and foreign companies, specified in clause (c), according to the applicant, the proviso ought to be applied to clause (c) category assessee’s also. That is the area of controversy. Both sides sought to project the objective of the proviso in different light. If the Revenue’s contention is accepted, the non-residents who are afforded protection from the adverse effect of rupee volatility under the first proviso to section 48 cannot invoke the benefit of concessional tax under the proviso to section 12(1).

Interpretation of Proviso

12. What then is the real purport, scope and meaning of the proviso to section 112(1)? Let us address ourselves to that question.

12.1 We are of the view that the benefit of the proviso to section 112(1) cannot be denied to the non-residents/foreign companies who are also entitled to a different relief in terms of first proviso to section 48. At the outset, while interpreting the proviso to section 112(1), it should be borne in mind that the said proviso is a special provision in relation to the transfer of certain long-term capital assets viz., listed securities, units and zero-coupon bonds. In our view, there is no warrant to limit the 10 per cent effective rate provided therein as against the normal rate of 20 per cent only to the three categories of resident assessees specified in clauses (a), (b) and (d ). Clear words would have been deployed in the proviso if one particular category i.e., non-residents are to be excluded. It is difficult to hold that such a result was intended to be achieved by means of the phraseology - ‘before giving effect to the second proviso to section 48’. Nor can it be said that the said phrase by necessary implication excludes clause (c) category of assessees who are, of course, entitled to another benefit conferred by the first proviso to section 48.

12.2 In plain and peremptory words, the proviso limits the rate of tax on the gains from the transfer of listed securities to 10 per cent, but, with an important rider that the quantum of capital gains should be arrived at without taking into account the formula laid down in the second proviso to section 48 based on the indexed cost of acquisition. In other words, while computing the capital gains on the listed securities held for more than 12 months, do not give effect to the calculation spelt out in the second proviso to section 48 wherever it is applicable, or to put it in a different language, let not the indexation formula enter into the computation process - that is the mandate of controversial phrase in the proviso to section 112(1). It does not say - deny the concessional rate of tax to the category of assessees who are not eligible to have the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition under the second proviso. In other words, the eligibility to avail the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition (under the second proviso to section 48) is not a sine qua non for applying the reduced rate of 10 per cent prescribed by the proviso to section 112(1). The second proviso to section 48 is only a mode of computation of capital gains. The crucial words relied upon by the Revenue cannot be construed as the words of exclusion of a category of assessees i.e., non-residents who cannot avail of indexation benefit.

The Tribunal passed its second order because the issue of the inclusion of capital gains had been left open at the time of passing the original order. The CBDT Circular dated 19-6-1968 was given statutory force by the insertion of section 11(1)(a) in 1972 with retrospective effect from 1961. Further, the Commissioner had issued a clarification on 25-3-1976 stating that if the net consideration received on the sale of shares involving capital gains was invested in fixed deposits in a bank for a period of six months, the net consideration could be regarded as having been utilised for acquiring another capital asset within the meaning of section 11(1)(a). of the 1922 Act.

It would be necessary to examine the agreement which was a part of the statement of the case and the records of reference. It was called the memorandum of agreement. It was between the vendor which was expressly said to include collectively the partners of the firm described as "the sole co-owners and co-proprietors thereof’’, on the one hand and the company as the purchaser on the other hand. It recited inter alia, the objects of the company. There was no obvious profit or gain in money or material. The shares of the partners were converted into shares of the company. No money in cash or in kind passes according to ordinary or even remote acceptation of these terms. It was a kind of a conversion of partners 'share into a shareholders' share. It was at best a transformation of one kind of property into another. If for an equivalent amount of money paid, a cheque for the same amount of cash given is issued, or vice-versa, then there is no capital gain producing no profit or gain within the meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

The first two provisos, of the first sub-section of section 12B of the 1922 Act are significant. The first proviso, inter alia, exempts distribution of capital assets on the total or partial partition of a HUF or under deed of gift, bequest or will which is expressly said to be not sale or exchange or relinquishment or transfer of capital assets. The second proviso exempts in a sense the transfer of a capital asset by a company to a subsidiary, the whole of the share capital of which is held by the parent company or by the nominees thereof and that is expressly said to be not a sale, exchange or transfer within the meaning of this section. These two provisos under sub-section (1) of section 12B of the 1922 Act do not make it clear either expressly or by necessary implication that goodwill was at all a contemplated subject of taxable capital gain within the meaning of the section. On the contrary, if the first proviso is taken of section 12B(1) of the 1922 Act many undivided Hindu families may have joint family businesses of great goodwill and obviously the transfer of such a goodwill of a HUF under a partition would not be a capital gain. To include goodwill as taxable capital gain within the meaning of section 12B of the 1922 Act would then be to discriminate between the transfer of the goodwill of a Hindu family business in the case of a partition of a HUF which will not be taxable capital gain under section 12B of the 1922 Act and transfer of the goodwill of other kinds of businesses such as belonging to partnerships or companies. It is an inherent indication that goodwill as such was not intended to be a taxable capital gain within the meaning of a section 12B of the 1922 Act. Otherwise the incongruous and illogical distinction would arise that goodwill transferred in the case of a partnership or company will be taxable capital gain but not goodwill transferred in the case of a partnership (sic ). That could not have been the intention of Parliament.

Proceeding further with the interpretation of section 12B of the 1922 Act, a glance at sub-section (2) of section 12B of the 1922 Act indicates the principles of deduction. Sub-section (2) of section 12B provides how the amount of a capital gain shall be computed after making certain deductions from the value of the consideration for which the sale or exchange or relinquishment or transfer of the capital asset is made. Looking at the list of deductions, as for instance in section 12B(2)(i) of the 1922 Act, there is, ‘expenditure incurred solely in connection with such sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer’. It means that only that deduction is allowable which is in respect of an expenditure incurred solely for this purpose. There cannot be an expenditure in this connection for transfer of goodwill which can be separated from other expenditure to say that this is an expenditure incurred solely for the transfer of goodwill. Again in sub-clause (ii) of section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act there is the mention of the actual cost to the assessee of the capital asset including any expenditure of a capital nature incurred and borne by him in making additions or alterations thereto. It is difficult to imagine from the practical point of view or even in legal notion how there can be an expenditure which will separate the actual cost of a goodwill in the assessee's capital asset and particularly for making any addition or alteration to such goodwill. These are compelling considerations which appear to exclude goodwill from the concept and ambit of section 12B of the 1922 Act.

Finally, coming to the different provisos in sub-section (2) of section 12B of the 1922 Act dealing with the valuation of the capital assets with reference to the fair market value on the date of sale or exchange or relinquishment or transfer and providing even, as in the third proviso, for substitution for the actual cost, such fair market value, appear to militate against any interpretation which includes goodwill within its ambit. The ‘actual cost’ in the case of goodwill seems to be an incongruous expression to be applicable to the case of a goodwill.

For the purpose of taking the fair market value, to be the value on the basis of which capital gains are to be computed, two conditions are required by the first proviso to the section 12B(2) of the 1922 Act, to be fulfilled, namely, the sale must be to a person with whom the assessee is directly or indirectly connected and, secondly, that the transaction must be entered into with the object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee under the section. It is apparent that the two conditions are cumulative and the Tribunal had so held. If on the computation made there is capital loss then there cannot be any liability for capital gains under section 12B of the 1922 Act. Therefore, the Tribunal was right in view of the calculations made that there was no liability on the assessee under section 12B. If there was no liability then no question arose of attempt being made at the reduction of liability to tax and of entering into transaction with that view in the end. The second condition of the first proviso to the sub-section requires that the sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer must be with the object of avoidance or reduction of "liability of the assessee under the section". But if there is no liability or if the transaction is of such a nature that no liability could arise, then there cannot be any attempt to reduce the liability by selling at a value less than the fair market value. Such a finding by the Tribunal could not be described as perverse in the sense that no reasonable person could come to such a finding.

Note: The case has been decided in favour of the assessee.

In the case of sale for a price, there is no question of any market value unlike in the case of an exchange. Therefore, in cases of sales to which the first proviso to sub-section (2) of section 12B is not attracted, all that we have to see is what is the consideration bargained for. In CIT v. Hindustan Welfare Trusts [1993] 70 Taxman 93 (Cal.) the assessee sold shares in limited companies resulting in capital gain being Rs. 40.27 lakhs. The assessee trust made a fixed deposit with a scheduled bank for a period of 60 days. In the next financial year, the assessee trust encashed the fixed deposit and gave loans to various parties. The assessee received a portion of sale consideration in the next previous year and the trust exercised the option of applying the capital gains in the following previous year as provided in Explanation 2 to section 11(1).

The Assessing Officer taxed the entire amount of capital gain as income of the trust and held that the fixed deposit is not a capital asset and hence the benefit of section 11(1A) could not be claimed by the trust. The first appellate authority viz. CIT (Appeals) upheld the order of Assessing Officer saying that the fixed deposit is not equivalent to acquisition of capital asset. The Tribunal however held that the fixed deposit is an investment which amounted to acquisition of capital asset and hence the benefit of section 11(1A) must be given to the assessee.

The Court held that making deposit in a bank would amount to acquisition of capital asset and therefore eligible for the exemption under section 11(1A). The decision was given in favour of the assessee holding that fixed deposit in banks are capital assets. Also, the Court held that "no minimum duration of the deposit can be set forth as the determinative criterion to decide whether a bank deposit in a bank takes on the colour of an asset of a specie separate from cash fund from the sale of an asset". CBDT's Instruction No. 883 clarifying that only fixed deposits with bank for 6 months or mere would be capital asset for section 11(1A) was held to be without any legal basis.

FACT: In the accounting period 1-4-1980 to 31-3-1981 relevant to the assessment year,1981-82, the assessee-trust sold the shares of certain companies held by it. The proceeds so realised were invested in fixed deposits with different parties. The assessee claimed that the net consideration of capital gain arose out of the sale of shares deemed to have been applied for charitable purpose since it had acquired ‘another capital asset’ within the meaning of the aforesaid term occurring in section 11(1A). The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim and held that the capital gain arose on sale of shares was assessable as its income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal:

HELD: When money is placed in a fixed deposit, it is not the same as keeping the money idle at home because the money is given to the bank

for making a deposit for the benefit of the person who hands it over which benefit would not accrue to such person if the money is kept idle at home. The fixed deposits are considered by the public as investments and, therefore, from a commercial angle also fixed deposits are considered as property, i.e., income-yielding investments. It is so recognised by the statute in section 11 itself. Thus, the ‘fixed deposits’ are property and would, therefore, within the meaning of section 2(14) clearly constitute ‘capital asset’ and such capital asset is entirely different from the money deposited for getting the fixed deposit. The net consideration invested in the fixed deposit is, therefore, an investment for acquiring another capital asset.

Accordingly, no part of the capital gain as above could be brought to tax in the relevant assessment year.

deal in those shares but with a view to obtain the managing agency and control of the company, and therefore, excess realised on the sale of those shares was not income liable to tax. On reference the High Court held that there was no material for the finding that the shares in question were purchased by the assessee with a view to acquire the managing agency and control of the company. It was further held that the shares constituted the stock-in-trade of the assessee.

On appeal to the Supreme Court. HELD: The question with which the High Court was concerned was whether there was material before the Tribunal for arriving at the finding that the shares in question had been purchased by the assessee with a view to acquire the managing agency and control of the said company. Perusal of the judgment of the High Court showed that the High Court did not discuss this aspect of the matter. On the contrary, the High Court proceeded straightaway to deal with the matter as if it had itself to arrive at an independent finding on the point as to whether the shares in question had been purchased by the assessee with a view to acquire the managing agency and control of the company. This approach of the High Court was wholly erroneous and not warranted by law. It is for the Tribunal to decide questions of fact, and the High Court in a reference under section 66 of the 1922 Act cannot go behind the Tribunal's findings of fact. The High Court can only lay down the law applicable to the facts found by the Tribunal. The High Court and the Supreme Court, in an appeal against the judgment of the High Court given in a reference under section 66 of the 1922 Act, are not constituted courts of appeal against the order of the Tribunal. These courts only exercise advisory jurisdiction in such references. The High Court in a reference under section 66 of the 1922 Act can, however, go into the question as to whether the conclusion of the Tribunal on a question of fact is based upon relevant evidence. If the High Court finds that there is no such evidence to support the finding of fact of the Tribunal, this circumstance would give rise to a question of law and can be agitated in a reference. It is also well-established that when a Tribunal acts no material which is irrelevant to the enquiry or considers material which is party relevant and partly irrelevant or bases its decision partly on conjectures, surmise and suspicions and partly on evidence, then in such a situation an issue of law arises and the finding of the Tribunal can be interfered with. The finding may also be interfered with if it be found to be so unreasonable that no person acting judicially and properly instructed as to the relevant law could have arrived at it. None of the circumstances justifying interference with the finding of fact of the Tribunal has been shown to exist in the instant case. In the absence of any such circumstances, the High Court was not justified in interfering with the finding of fact of the Tribunal. The fact that the High Court on appreciation of evidence would have arrived at a conclusion of fact different from that of the Tribunal did not warrant interference with the finding of the Tribunal.

The Tribunal in arriving at the conclusion that the purchase of the shares in question by the assessee was a view to obtain the managing agency and control of the said company and that those shares were not purchased as stock-in-trade referred to a member of circumstances. It was found by the Tribunal that the shares in question were out of the lot by the Tribunal that the shares in question were out of the lot sold by the firm. It was also found that the shares had been transferred to the assessee at the original price at which these shares had been sold by the Sassoons and not at the price which was prevailing at the time of transfer. The Tribunal further found that 62,500 shares represented the portion of the assessee in the total number of shares originally purchased by the firm. In the light of those findings, the Tribunal recorded, its conclusion. The above conclusion of the Tribunal was based upon relevant material and could not be interfered with in a reference under section 66 of the 1922 Act.

The High Court in arriving at the conclusion that the shares in question had been purchased not with a view to obtain the managing agency but as a stock-in-trade had referred to the fact that the assessee took loan for the purchase of those shares and subsequently transferred 43,700 shares out of 62,500 shares. This circumstances, would not by itself go to show that the purchase of shares was not to facilitate the acquisition of the managing agency.

Therefore, the answer given by the High Court was not correct. There was material for the finding that the shares in question had been purchased by the assessee with a view to acquire the managing agency and control of the said company and that the shares did not constitute the stock-in-trade of the assessee.

It was the common case of the parties that if the shares in question were held to be not stock-in-trade of the assessee, in that case the profits made on the sale of those shares would constitute capital made on the sale of those shares would constitute capital gain chargeable to income-tax under section 12B of the 1922 Act. Looking to the facts, the profit made on the sale of those shares constituted capital gain chargeable to income-tax under section 12B of the 1922 Act.

The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 [Corresponding to section 12B of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922] - Capital gains - Chargeable as - Whether Indian Income-tax and Excess Profits Tax (Amendment) Act, 1947 which amended 1922 Act, by enlarging definition of term income in section 2(6C) of 1922 Act and introducing a new head of income in section 6 of 1922 Act and inserting new section 12B, was intra vires powers of Central Legislature acting under entry 54 in List I of Seventh Schedule of Government of India Act, 1935 - Held, yes

FACT: The appellant was assessed to income-tax, for the assessment year 1947-48 on a total income including a sum representing capital gains assessed in the hands of the appellant under section 12B which represented his half share in certain immovable properties which were sold by him during the relevant accounting year.

This was confirmed by the AAC and the Tribunal. On reference, the High Court held that the imposition of a tax under the head 'capital gains under section 12B by the Central Legislature was not ultra vires.

On appeal to the Supreme Court :

HELD: Section 12B was inserted in the 1922 Act by the Indian Income-tax and Excess Profits Tax (Amendment) Act, 1947 which was a Central Act. Under section 100 of the Government of India Act, 1935, the Central Legislature was empowered to make laws with respect to matters enumerated in List I in the Seventh Schedule to that Act. Entry 54 in list I caused taxes on income other than agricultural income while entry 55 caused taxes on the capital value of the assets, exclusive of agricultural land, of individuals and companies, and taxes on the capital of companies.

In construing an entry in a List conferring legislative powers the widest possible construction according to their ordinary meaning must be put upon the words used therein. The cardinal rule of interpretation, is that words should be read in their ordinary, natural and grammatical meaning subject to this rider that in construing words in a constitutional enactment conferring legislative power the most liberal construction should be put upon the words so that the same may have effect in their widest amplitude. Thus the word 'income' occurring in said entry 54 should be given its widest connotation in view of the fact that it occurs in a legislative head conferring legislative power. The argument that the word should be interpreted on basis of assumed legislative practice in England was not acceptable. It was, therefore, to be held in the instant case that Act of 1947 which amended the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922 by enlarging the definition of the term income in section 2(6C) of the 1922 Act and introducing a new head of income in section 6 and inserting the new section 12B of the 1922 Act was intra vires the powers of the Central Legislature acting under Entry 54 in List I of the Seventh Schedule of the Government of India Act, 1935.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the revenue.

First proviso to section 48(1) provides for computation of capital gain on sale of shares by an assessee who is a non-resident. The non-resident Indians who invest in shares and debentures of the Indian companies have been representing that due to the fall in value of the Indian rupee vis-a-vis the foreign currency in which the investment is made by them, they are adversely affected when they sell such shares or debentures. In order to overcome this situation, the first proviso was inserted. Thus, the non-resident Indian investor will be compensated for the lower earnings in foreign currency on account of the fall in the value of the Indian rupee. [Para 11]

Second proviso to section 48(1) gives the benefit of indexation while determining the cost of acquisition and improvements to the capital asset. The second proviso was inserted to offset the effect of inflation. A fair method of allowing such relief taking several factors was to link all factors to the period of holding. For this purpose, the cost of acquisition of and the cost of improvement to the asset are to be inflated to arrive at the indexed cost of acquisition and indexed cost of improvement and then deduct these amounts from the sale consideration to arrive at the long-term capital gains. [Para 12]

Section 112 prescribes the rate of tax on long-term capital gain. [Para 13]

It is by now settled that the benefit of the proviso to section 112(1) cannot be denied to the non-residents/foreign companies who are also entitled to a different relief in terms of first proviso to section 48. It has been held that while interpreting the proviso to section 112(1), it should be borne in mind that the said proviso is a special provision in relation to the transfer of certain long-term capital assets, viz., listed securities, units and zero-coupon bonds; that there is no warrant to limit the 10 per cent effective rate provided therein as against the normal rate of 20 per cent only to the three categories of the resident assessees specified in clauses (a ), (b) and (d ). Clear words would have been deployed in the proviso if one particular category, i.e., non-residents were to be excluded. It is difficult to hold that such a result was intended to be achieved by means of the phraseology - 'before giving effect to the second proviso to section 48', nor can it be said that the said phraseology by necessary implication excludes clause (c ) category of the assessees who are, of course, entitled to another benefit conferred by the first proviso to section 48. In plain and preemptory (sic ) words, the proviso limits the rate of tax on the gains from the transfer of listed securities to 10 per cent but with an important rider that the quantum of capital gains should be arrived at without taking into account the formula laid down in the second proviso to section 48 based on the indexed cost of acquisition. In other words, while computing the capital gains on the listed securities held for more than 12 months, the proviso (sic ) does not give effect to the calculation spelt out in the second proviso to section 48 wherever it is applicable, or to put it in a different language, let not the indexation formula enter into the computation process - that is the mandate of controversial phrase in the proviso to section 112(1). It does not say 'deny the concessional rate of tax to the category of assessees who are not eligible to have the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition under the second proviso'. In other words, the eligibility to avail of the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition (under the second proviso to section 48) is not a sine qua non for applying the reduced rate of 10 per cent prescribed by the proviso to section 112(1). The second proviso to section 48 is only a mode of computation of capital gains. The crucial words relied upon by the revenue could not be construed as the words of exclusion of a category of the assessees, i.e., non-residents who cannot avail of indexation benefit. [Para 14]

A new provision in the form of section 115AD was introduced from 1-4-1993 and it applies in relation to the assessment year 1993-94 and subsequent years. It provides tax incentive for the Foreign Institutional Investors investing in securities. [Para 15]

HEADNOTE: Section 45 of the income-tax Act, 1961-Capital gains-Chargeability of-Assessee, holder of two-third shares of a company and also managing agent of said company, sold its entire shareholding in one block to a third company gaining some profit and  surrendering said managing agency-No finding on record that assessee was a dealer in managing agency and transaction was a colourable one-Whether surplus realised out of sale of shares was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains-Held, on facts, yes

FACT: The assessee-company had held two-third shares of company A and was also its managing agent. During the accounting year relevant for the assessment year 1960-61, the assessee sold all these shares to company B at a profit of Rs. 3,14,519 and claimed that the surplus realised was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains. The ITO took the view that the assessee had acquired these shares to procure the managing agency and it had, in fact, carried on multifarious activities in various lines including banking, financing of various companies as well as managing agency. He, accordingly, held that the entire profit from the sale of these shares represented business profit. On appeal, the AAC held that a major portion of the sale proceeds was relatable to the assessee's right to the managing agency which passed along with the shares. He further held that in view of the numerous agencies which the assessee carried on, this transaction involving the giving up of the managing agency was of a revenue nature. Consequently, the AAC upheld the ITO's order. On second appeal, the Tribunal found that the assessee had parted with an asset of enduring nature and observed that nothing had been received by the assessee as price for its foregoing managing agency rights. What it had legally received was the value of the shares though it could not be denied that it received a higher value because the shares carried with it the managing agency rights. Further, the Tribunal was of the view that it was concerned with the true and legal realisation resulting from the transaction which appeared to be that of the sale of shares and that the shares were not the assessee's stock-in- trade It, accordingly, held that the impugned profit was liable to be taxed as capital gains and not as revenue gains.

On reference:

HELD: Having regard to the facts and findings recorded by the Tribunal and in view of the fact that there was no finding to the effect that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency or that the transaction in question was a colourable one in the sense that though the transaction was shown apparently to be a transaction for the sale of shares it was really something else or that the consideration for the transaction was for something else, it could not be said that the transaction in question was of a revenue nature.

Even if it was assumed that the impugued payment was for surrendering of the managing agency, unless there was a finding that the assessee was a dealer in managing agency, this aspect would not support the revenue's stand.

Accordingly, the surplus arising out of the transaction of sale of shares was capital gains as distinct from revenue gains.

The assessee-trust’s income had been held to be exempt under section 11 in the earlier years. In the assessment year 1981-82 the assessee acquired shares of company K through donation and purchase. Two persons J and S were substantial, contributors to the assessee within the meaning of section 13(3)(b). Those two persons had also purchased shares in company K. Prior to 24-3-1981 some of the funds of the assessee wore invested in company K. But during that period J and S taken together did not have a substantial interest in company K as their combined shareholdings in that company was less than, 20 per cent of the voting power of the said company and the condition in Explanation 3( i) to section 13(4) was not satisfied during that period. On 24-3-1981, the assessee gifted away its entire block of shares in the company K to S and other parties. As a result of that donation, the two persons together became the substantial investors in company K after 24-3-1981 by virtue of Explanation 3(i) to section 13(4). After 24-3-1981 no part of the funds of the assessee remained invested in that company. Further, the assessee realised certain capital gains in selling some of its assets. Soon, thereafter, the assessee invested the sale proceeds in a fixed deposit with Allahabad Bank for a period of seven months. The assessee claimed that the capital gain was exempt from tax in view of Instruction No. 883, dated 24-9-1975 of the CBDT which Stated that fixed deposits for a period of more than six months should be regarded as a capital asset for the purpose of section 11(1A). The ITO held that J and S had substantial interest in company K and so the investments of the assessee’s funds in the same concern, in which two of its substantial contributors had substantial interest, was hit by section 13(2)(h) and the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section 11 and as a consequence to that fact no exemption under section 11(1A) could also be allowed. Scope of Part B of ICDS-VIII (Revised) dealing with Securities held by a Scheduled Bank or Public Financial Institution

Para 1 of Part B of this ICDS clarifies that this part deals with securities held by the following entities:

a scheduled bank or

public financial institutions formed under a Central or a State Act or so declared under the Companies Act, 1956 or the Companies Act, 2013

Unlike Part A, this Part (Part B) deals with securities held by Scheduled banks or public financial institutions. Therefore, this Part will not apply to securities held by mutual funds, banks other than scheduled banks, insurance companies and financial institutions other than Public Financial Institutions.

Part A deals with securities held as stock-in-trade while this Part is silent on this aspect. A question, therefore, arises whether this Part will also apply to securities held as investments. Securities held as stock-in-trade are excluded from the definition of 'capital asset' in section 2(14) of the Act while securities held as investments are very much capital assets. Therefore, profits and gains from sale/transfer of securities held as investments will be taxed as capital gains. ICDSs do not apply to computation of income under the head "Capital Gains". Therefore, Part B also applies only to securities held as stock in trade.

The classification of securities by bank as stock-in-trade or as investment should be made according to RBI Guidelines and norms. CBDT's Circular No. 665, dated 5 October, 1993, clarifies as follows:

"The question whether a particular item of investment in securities constitutes stock-in-trade or a capital asset is a question of fact. In fact, the banks are generally governed by the instructions of the Reserve Bank of India from time to time with regard to the classification of assets and also the accounting standards for investments. The Board has, therefore, decided that the Assessing Officers should determine on the facts and circumstances of each case as to whether any particular security constitutes stock-in-trade or investment taking into account the guidelines issued by the Reserve Bank of India in this regard from time to time."

Part B of ICDS is also silent on provision regarding recognition of income on securities (interest/dividend etc.). Therefore, computation of income from such sources would be as per normal provisions of the Act read with ICDS IV(Revised)- Revenue Recognition.

On reference : HELD: As regards set off of loss incurred in the assessment year 1951-52 against capital gain for the assessment year in question, on account legislative charges the tax on capital gains was not in force from 1st April, 1948 to 31st March, 1956. Thus, any profit earned by the assessee from the activity of sale, exchange, relinquishment of transfer of capital asset after 31-3-1948 could not be considered to be profits falling under the head "capital gain". In the circumstances, no question of sustaining any loss of profit under that head could possibly arise, in respect of a transaction effected after March 31, 1948. The loss suffered by the assessee in the year 1951-52, therefore, could not be considered to be loss of profit falling under the head "capital gain." On the same basis capital loss for the assessment year 1951-52 could not he carried forward to future years and set off against capital gains of the year 1956 onwards when tax an capital gains was reintroduced. Further, in the question the amount in dispute has been described as "capital loss" and not as "loss" falling under the head "capital gain". The expression "Capital loss" cannot be equated with the loss falling under the head "capital gain". In the assessment year 1951-52 the assessee claimed the deduction of the amount as revenue loss. The claim was rejected on the ground that the loss suffered was of a capital nature as distinguished from revenue loss. In the circumstances, the finding that the loss in question was capital loss, merely meant loss of capital. By no stretch of imagination it could be said that the finding that loss of Rs. 1,05,067 was capital loss, implied a finding that it was a loss occasioned by sale, exchange, relinquishment or transfer of a capital asset. Thus, the assessee was not entitled to carried forward losses incurred in the year 1951-52 to the assessment year 1959-60 for being adjusted against capital gains in that year.

As regards the claim of the assessee for adopting higher value of 3,040 shares, as on 1-1-1954 under the Third proviso to section 12B(2), It was not possible for the Income-tax Officer to have given the benefit of the third proviso to section 12B(2) merely because there was a possibility of increase in the value of shares on account of increase in earning capacity of the company without there being sufficient material for determining their fair market value as on January 1, 1954. The Tribunal was, therefore, right in holding that, in the circumstances of the case, the capital gains of the assessee could not be calculated on the basis of the third proviso to section 12B(20).

. However, the dispute regarding rate of tax had arisen between the assessee and the revenue after insertion of the proviso to section 112(1). The contention of the assessee was that the proviso would also apply to non-residents falling under the scope of the first proviso to section 48; while the stand of the revenue was that the proviso was exclusively applicable to those cases which fell within the ambit of the second proviso to section 48. [Para 11] A perusal of the two provisos to section 48 shows that computation of capital gain is bifurcated into two parts. The first proviso covers those cases where the capital asset being the shares in or debentures of an Indian company are acquired by a non-resident by utilizing the foreign currency. In such cases, the cost of acquisition, expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with transfer of such shares as well as the sale consideration is required to be converted in the same foreign currency which was utilised for acquiring such shares/debentures so as to compute the capital gain in foreign currency. The capital gain so computed is then reconverted into Indian currency for the purpose of computing tax thereon. This method is applicable to short-term as well as long-term capital asset, asset being shares in or debentures of an Indian company. Other assets are not covered under this proviso. On the other hand, second proviso to section 48 provides the method of computing long-term capital gains in respect of any long-term capital assets acquired by any assessee irrespective of his status except the long-term capital gain arising to non-resident from the transfer of long-term capital asset specified in the first proviso to section 48. According to this method, the cost of acquisition and the cost of improvement mentioned in section 48(ii) shall be substituted by ‘the indexed cost of acquisition’ and ‘the indexed cost of improvement’ which shall be deducted from the sale consideration for computing the long-term capital gain. [Para 12]

Thus, the Legislature has provided two different categories for computing the long-term capital gain. The intention of the Legislature appears to be that no gain be taxed to the extent it relates to general inflation of price in the market. That is why, the Legislature has related ‘the indexed cost of acquisition’ and ‘the indexed cost of improvement’ to the ‘cost inflation index’ which is defined in clause (v) of the Explanation to section 48. Application of this method is restricted to the cases falling within the scope of the second proviso to section 48. A different method has been provided to the cases falling within the scope of first proviso to section 48 considering the rapid devaluation of Indian currency. Foreign investors represented that capital gain be computed in accordance with the increase in the value of asset in terms of foreign currency. Accepting such representations of non-residents, the Legislature has provided different methods for computing capital gain in the first proviso to section 48. The Legislature has also used the word ‘shall’ in the first and second proviso to section 48 vis-a-vis the computation of capital gain. On the other hand, the case of non-resident falling within the ambit of the first proviso has been specifically excluded from the computation of long-term capital gain in the second proviso. Thus, neither the assessee nor the Assessing Officer has any option in this matter. Therefore, the case of the assessee would fall within the ambit of the first proviso to section 48. Therefore, the proviso to section 112 could not be applied to the instant case. [Paras 13 and 14]

Section 115AD provides 10 per cent rate of tax on long-term capital gain arising/accruing to foreign institutional investors vis-a-vis securities falling under section 115-O, but sub-section (3) of section 115AD specifically provides that both the provisos to section 48 would not apply in computing the long-term capital gain. Similarly, section 115AB provides 10 per cent rate of tax on long-term capital gain arising/accruing to overseas financial organization vis-a-vis the units purchased in foreign currency, but sub-section (2) of this section specifically provides that the second proviso to section 48 would not apply for computing such capital gain. The first proviso to section 48 is not applicable to units purchased in foreign currency and, therefore, the Legislature has not mentioned about the first proviso to section 48 in sub-section (2) of section 115AB. So, the Legislature has provided concessional rate of 10 per cent on gross amount of long-term capital gain, i.e., computed without claiming any deduction/benefit provided in the first and second provisos to section 48. It is in this context that the Legislature thought that the assessee falling under the second proviso to section 48 should not be put to disadvantageous position as compared to the assessee falling under sections 115AB and 115AD. The Legislature has provided only the marginal relief under section 112(1) proviso in those cases where rate of 20 per cent on net long-term capital gain is more than 10 per cent rate of tax on gross amount of capital gain. The assessee had conveniently ignored the provisions of sub-section (2) of section 115AB and sub-section (3) of section 115AD while advancing the arguments. [Para 15]

On appeal by revenue:

■

From a plain reading of the provisions, the requirement of law is for the utilization of net consideration for acquiring another capital asset. The provision does not mandate a strict or direct one-to-one correlation between the exact funds received and the funds invested. The emphasis is on utilization in substance and not on the form or timing of such utilization. [Para 28.1]

■

In the present case, it is an admitted fact that the assessee's property was compulsorily acquired and compensation was received. It is also not in dispute that the assessee has invested substantial amounts in acquisition of immovable properties at Kothanur village. Therefore, the primary condition of reinvestment in capital assets stands satisfied. [Para 28.2]

■

The AO as well as the CIT(A) denied the claim mainly on two grounds. Firstly, one of the properties was purchased prior to the receipt of compensation on transfer of the property under compulsory acquisition. Secondly, the other property was acquired through loan taken against fixed deposits and therefore, according to them, there was no nexus with the sale consideration. [Para 28.3]

■

Both these objections are hyper-technical and not in consonance with the scheme of section 11(1A) of the Act. The law does not prescribe that the investment must be made only after receipt of consideration. Hence, it is held that even investments made prior to transfer can be considered, if the overall funds position establishes that the assessee has applied the consideration for acquiring capital assets. [Para 28.4]

■

Further, regarding the second property, the finding that the investment was made from borrowed funds ignores the substance of the transaction. The record shows that the loans were taken against fixed deposits which were made from the amount of compensation received. Therefore, in substance, the source of investment remains the compensation itself. The borrowing is only a financial mechanism and cannot be used to deny the benefit otherwise available under the statute. [Para 28.5]

■

Section 11(1A) does not require tracing of funds in a rigid manner. CBDT Circular No. 72 supports the view that utilization of funds should be understood in a practical and commercial sense. The approach of the AO in insisting on direct nexus is therefore misplaced. [Para 28.6]

■

The reliance placed by the CIT(A) on the decision in Al Ameen Educational Society v. DIT (Exemption) [2012] 26 taxmann.com 250/139 ITD 245 (Bangalore), in fact, supports the case of the assessee rather than the Revenue. The said decision clearly explains that what is relevant is utilization of net consideration, and even proportionate exemption is permissible where the entire consideration is not utilized. [Para 28.7]

■

In the present case, the assessee has demonstrated that substantial investment has been made in capital assets. Therefore, at the minimum, proportionate exemption u/s 11(1A)(a)(ii) ought to have been allowed. The outright denial of exemption by the lower authorities is therefore not sustainable. [Para 28.8]

■

On the above discussion, it is held that the assessee has substantially complied with the conditions prescribed u/s 11(1A) of the Act. The interpretation adopted by the AO and affirmed by the CIT(A) is too narrow and defeats the legislative intent of granting relief to charitable trusts reinvesting the consideration on transfer of property into capital assets. Accordingly, the AO is directed to allow exemption u/s 11(1A) in respect of the capital gains. The addition made by the AO and confirmed by the CIT(A) is hereby deleted. Hence, the ground of appeal of the assessee is allowed. [Para 28.9]

The assets on which tax is payable in respect of any income arising from the transfer are listed securities or unit or zero coupon bond. If the asset is not a share or debenture, the residents and non-resident assessees are allowed computation of capital gains on the basis of indexation. In respect of units and zero coupon bonds, which are other than shares or debentures, all the assessees, whether residents or non-residents, are eligible to the benefit of indexation in the computation of capital gains arising on their transfer. However, the 3rd proviso denies the benefit of indexation to bonds or debentures. While applying the proviso to section 112(1) to determine the tax payable, the computation mechanism includes such assets. There is, thus, no dichotomy in the proviso to section 112(1) and the 3rd proviso to section 48. Section 48 is a section which governs mode of computation of income whereas section 112 determines the tax payable on such income. It may be important to keep in mind that the application of the proviso is based on the capital asset to which the provisions of 2nd proviso to section 48 apply. If it is the case that it applies to the 1st proviso meant for a non-resident assessee, then the proviso would have made a mention of it. One cannot read anything more in the statute than what is stated therein. [Para 25]

It is averred that the mandate of the phrase in the proviso to section 112(1) is not to let the indexation formula enter into the computation process and is not a condition that unless an assessee is eligible to apply the indexation formula, only then the reduced rate of 10 per cent prescribed by the proviso to section 112(1) can be applied. In this regard, it may be stated that the indexation formula already enters into the computation in the first limb where it is mentioned that 'tax payable in respect of any income arising from the transfer of long-term capital asset' is to be determined. In fact, there is no issue on this part of proviso whether the 2nd proviso to section 48 enters into the said computation or not. The issue that arises lies in the second limb of the proviso starting with the phrase 'ten per cent of the amount of capital gains before giving effect to the provisions of the second proviso to section 48'. This cannot be read to mean 'deny the concessional rate of tax to the category of assessees who are not eligible to have the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition under the second proviso of section 48'. It only conveys how a particular amount is to be determined. Any other meaning would tantamount to rewriting this part of the proviso of section 112(1). [Para 26]

As the indexation on the zero coupon bond is available by virtue of 2nd proviso, it will affect the computation of capital gains under section 48 on which tax is payable under the first limb of the proviso and, thus would not go out of the purview of the proviso to section 112(1). The zero coupon bond on which indexation is available will get the benefit of the lower rate of tax at 10 per cent under the proviso. The exclusion from application of 1st and 2nd provisos to section 48 while calculating the amount of Income-tax on the income by way of long-term capital gains in the cases of non-residents and allow them the benefit of lower tax rates of 10 per cent also find mention in sections 115AC(3) and 115AD(3). The Act has taken care when, where, and how the 1st and the 2nd provisos to section 48 are to be excluded. The long-term capital gains on the sale of shares of the listed companies are otherwise exempt from tax under section 10(38) if the sale of the shares takes place through the recognized stock exchange on which security transaction tax is paid. However, in the instant case, such exemption is not available as the shares of the listed company CIL are sold in the off-market mode. [Para 27]

AE, 44B, 44BBA and 44BBB provide that notwithstanding anything contained in sections 28 to 43C/44, etc., (as the case may be as per the relevant section), a certain amount calculated on the basis of specified percentage of the specified base would be deemed to be income chargeable under the head 'Profits and gains of business or profession'.

Such deemed profits would be included in total income of the concerned company when its Normal TI is computed. Even in such cases, if Normal TI is less than 30% of book profits, section 115JA of the Act would apply and such book profits would constitute its total income.

This is because:

◆ Section 115JA of the Act affects total income computed under normal provisions of the Act which include the aforesaid sections.

◆ The field of operation of section 44AD, etc. is different and restricted. They deem a certain amount as profits chargeable under the said head and not total income.

1.14-6 Capital gains and rate of tax - In case of a company engaged in investment business, in respect of investments held as capital assets, under the Act, income on sale of such assets would be chargeable as capital gains. For the purpose of computing capital gains, prescribed method of arriving at cost of acquisition or cost of improvement are to be applied. As a result, the capital gains may be substantially lower then the profits which are booked in the accounts. Even, in such a case, provisions of section 115JA of the Act may apply and the company may be liable to pay tax on 30% of its book profits.

For the purpose of levy of tax on long term capital gains, section 112 prescribes a concessional rate, which, in the case of a company, with effect from assessment year 1997-98 is 20%.

In the above case, the issue is; what is the rate of tax chargeable ?

There could be two possible views, which are discussed hereinafter in little detail.

As per one view, the effect of section 115JA of the Act is as follows :

◆ Section 115JA deems a certain part of book profits as total income. Such computation is irrespective of the head. The provision does not prescribe any rate of tax.

◆ Sub-section (4) of section 115JA provides that save as otherwise provided in that provision, all other provisions of the Act would apply.

◆ Accordingly, the deemed total income is computed. Section 2(45) defines 'total income' to mean as total amount of income referred to in section 5, computed in the manner laid down in this Act. In the context of section 115JA, it would therefore mean income referred to in section 115JA and computed in the manner laid down in that section.

◆ Section 4 creates a charge on total income. The charge is to be determined with reference to rate or rates of tax as may be prescribed by a Central Act.

◆ The rate of tax is prescribed by a Finance Act. For assessment year 1997-98, the rates for the purpose of advance tax are prescribed by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1996. The provisions are contained in section 2(7) of the said Finance Act and Part III of the First Schedule to the said Act prescribes the rate of tax, which includes the rate of tax prescribed under Chapter XII of the Act in respect of any income chargeable to tax under Chapter XII. Section 112 forms part of Chapter XII and prescribes rate of tax on long term capital gains.

◆ The said provisions read as follows :

'Where the total income of an assessee includes any income..., chargeable under the head 'Capital gains", the tax payable by the assessee on the total income shall be the aggregate of,—

(a) …………..

(b) in the case of a domestic company—

(i) The amount of income-tax payable on the total income as reduced by ... such long term capital gains,....; and

(ii) The amount of income-tax calculated on such long term capital gains at the rate of twenty per cent.'

◆ As is evident from section 4 read with above provisions prescribing the rate, the tax is on total income. Section 112 of the Act lays down the manner in which tax is computed where total income includes any income arising from transfer of a long term capital asset. The said provision applies to section 115JA also.

◆ 30% of the books profit also includes the amount embedded in book profits, which are chargeable under the head 'Capital gains'. Accordingly, to the extent of profit which represents income chargeable under the head capital gains, it is taxable at the rate prescribed by section 112.

The other view could be :

The moment Normal IT is ignored, by applying section 115JA of the Act, manner of computation and charge under different heads, etc., are nullified.

◆ Accordingly, when 30% of book profits is total income on which tax is payable, this is a total income as computed under section 115JA of the Act and not the one computed as per normal provisions.

The assessee purchased National Saving Certificates of Rs. 15,000 on 18-4-1985 and of Rs. 20,000 on 13-2-1986 out of his deposits in bank and claimed deduction in respect of the said investments under section 8OCCA. From the entries in the bank pass book of the assessee, the ITO came to the conclusion that National Saving Certificates of Rs. 20,000 had been purchased from provident fund amount received by the assessee on leaving the job which had been credited to his account in the pass book and that National Saving Certificate of the balance amount of Rs. 15,000 had been purchased out of the amount received on maturity of CTD 10 years in respect of which Rs. 33,000 had been credited in the pass book of the assessee. He held that deduction under section 80CCA could be claimed only if the investments in question had been made out of the income chargeable to tax and that as the provident fund amount and CTD amount received by the assessee did not represent amount chargeable to tax either in the current year or in the earlier year, deduction under section 8OCCA was not available to the assessee. Accordingly, he disallowed the assessee’s claim. On appeal, the assessee contended that the amounts received by him by way of PF and CTD were out of the amounts chargeable to tax in the earlier years and as such, when investments were made in the National Saving Certificates from these amounts, conditions for allowability of deduction under section 8OCCA were satisfied. 3.7-1 Receiving gifts in the form of impermissible investments

A question that arises is whether a charitable institution can accept gift of impermissible investments. This is explained separately for shares and other assets.

3.7-1a Other impermissible assets

So far as assets other than shares are concerned, the relevant clause reads as follows:

"…any income thereof, if for any period during the previous year-

(i) any funds of the trust or institution are invested or deposited after the 28th day of February, 1983 otherwise than in any one or more of the forms or modes specified in sub-section (5) of section 11;

…

to the extent of such deposits or investments referred to in sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iii).

Thus, the clause applies in respect of funds invested or deposited otherwise than in permissible modes. It has been held in a series of decisions that when a charitable institution receives a gift, its funds are not invested or deposited within the meaning of the aforesaid sub-clause [Auditor Dasaradha Rami Reddy Charities v. CIT [1989] 44 Taxman 453 (Mad.); CIT v. Birla Charity Trust [1987] 34 Taxman 504 (Cal.); CIT v. Sir Shri Ram Foundation [2001] 116 Taxman 113 (Delhi)]. Hence, the amendment does not affect the taxation of other impermissible assets received as a gift. Incidentally, such assets could have been held by the institution even under the pre-amendment law without losing any exemption; however, after the amendment, if the income of the charitable institution is actually invested or deposited in impermissible modes (say, debentures of a private company) the amount of income so invested in making such investment will not enjoy exemption under section 11(1) and be liable to tax under section 13(1)(d).

3.7-1b Shares

So far as shares are concerned, under the pre-amended law, shares could not be held by a charitable institution, even if they were donated to the institution. After the amendment, the exact language of the amendment is "to the extent of such deposits or investments referred to in sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iii)". It is pertinent that sub-clause (iii), which deals with shares does not at all use the expression "such deposits or investments." On the other hand, income is not invested if shares are received as a gift and hence, on a plain reading, in such a case, no part of income can be regarded as invested.

The matter is not very clear, but it appears that:

(a)

income invested in shares is taxable under section 13 (1)(d)

(b)

shares received as gifts are not taxable.

As mentioned above, the aforesaid view is also supported by the Explanatory Memorandum, reproduced in para 3.7 above.

The law is silent on the income from such impermissible investment. It appears that such income (including capital gains) qualifies for exemption under section 11(1)(a) and is entitled to the benefit of the deemed application under Explanation 1(2) or secondary accumulation for 5 years under section 11(2). Further, the capital gains from investment should also qualify for benefit under section 11(1A).

Proviso (iia) to section 13(1)(d) provides that nothing in the section shall apply if the impermissible investment is not held beyond the expiry of one year from the end of the previous year in which such impermissible investment is acquired. This proviso continues to apply even after the amendment. Hence, income shall not be taxable under the amended section 13(1)(d) if the impermissible investment is liquidated on or before the expiry of the year subsequent to the year in which it is acquired. To illustrate, suppose an assessee buys preference shares in a company on 15th March 2023. If it transfers the shares on or before 31st March 2024, no part of its income will be taxable. On the other hand, if it transfers the shares on 4th April 2024, the income to the extent of the cost of shares will be taxable under section 13(1)(d).

The amount of taxable income is not liable to penalty under section 271AAE (please see para 11).

The Supreme Court in the case of India Cements Ltd. v. CIT [1966] 60 ITR 52 , has observed that there is a difference in capital raised in shape of shares and capital raised in shape of debentures which is not of enduring advantage. In the instant case, the assessee raised capital by floating bonds. The bonds were of limited period and after maturity of the period, the assessee had to repay the bond amount along with profit, as agreed upon by the assessee. The assessee had shown an earning out of raised capital through bonds in profit and loss account. It had obtained capital through bonds and not through shares. Bonds are like debentures, i.e., they are loans to the assessee and, therefore, they were not of enduring advantage as the ratio of the decision in case of India Cements Ltd. (supra) held. Thus, the amount received through Bonds was a stock-in-trade and expenditure incurred in obtaining this loan was revenue in nature. Therefore, the expenditure was deductible while computing the income of the assessee.

Treatment of fund transferred by employer to trustee [Rule 14 of Part A of the Fourth Schedule]
