Interpretation of Proviso

12. What then is the real purport, scope and meaning of the proviso to section 112(1)? Let us address ourselves to that question.

12.1 We are of the view that the benefit of the proviso to section 112(1) cannot be denied to the non-residents/foreign companies who are also entitled to a different relief in terms of first proviso to section 48. At the outset, while interpreting the proviso to section 112(1), it should be borne in mind that the said proviso is a special provision in relation to the transfer of certain long-term capital assets viz., listed securities, units and zero-coupon bonds. In our view, there is no warrant to limit the 10 per cent effective rate provided therein as against the normal rate of 20 per cent only to the three categories of resident assessees specified in clauses (a), (b) and (d ). Clear words would have been deployed in the proviso if one particular category i.e., non-residents are to be excluded. It is difficult to hold that such a result was intended to be achieved by means of the phraseology - ‘before giving effect to the second proviso to section 48’. Nor can it be said that the said phrase by necessary implication excludes clause (c) category of assessees who are, of course, entitled to another benefit conferred by the first proviso to section 48.

12.2 In plain and peremptory words, the proviso limits the rate of tax on the gains from the transfer of listed securities to 10 per cent, but, with an important rider that the quantum of capital gains should be arrived at without taking into account the formula laid down in the second proviso to section 48 based on the indexed cost of acquisition. In other words, while computing the capital gains on the listed securities held for more than 12 months, do not give effect to the calculation spelt out in the second proviso to section 48 wherever it is applicable, or to put it in a different language, let not the indexation formula enter into the computation process - that is the mandate of controversial phrase in the proviso to section 112(1). It does not say - deny the concessional rate of tax to the category of assessees who are not eligible to have the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition under the second proviso. In other words, the eligibility to avail the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition (under the second proviso to section 48) is not a sine qua non for applying the reduced rate of 10 per cent prescribed by the proviso to section 112(1). The second proviso to section 48 is only a mode of computation of capital gains. The crucial words relied upon by the Revenue cannot be construed as the words of exclusion of a category of assessees i.e., non-residents who cannot avail of indexation benefit.

Further, as per Rule 74(4), an abstract for the financial year or other applicable accounting period of the individual account of each employee participating in a provident fund shall be furnished by the trustees in Form No. 41 (only showing the totals of the various columns thereof for the financial year or other accounting period) to the AO of the area in which the accounts of the fund are kept. The assets on which tax is payable in respect of any income arising from the transfer are listed securities or unit or zero coupon bond. If the asset is not a share or debenture, the residents and non-resident assessees are allowed computation of capital gains on the basis of indexation. In respect of units and zero coupon bonds, which are other than shares or debentures, all the assessees, whether residents or non-residents, are eligible to the benefit of indexation in the computation of capital gains arising on their transfer. However, the 3rd proviso denies the benefit of indexation to bonds or debentures. While applying the proviso to section 112(1) to determine the tax payable, the computation mechanism includes such assets. There is, thus, no dichotomy in the proviso to section 112(1) and the 3rd proviso to section 48. Section 48 is a section which governs mode of computation of income whereas section 112 determines the tax payable on such income. It may be important to keep in mind that the application of the proviso is based on the capital asset to which the provisions of 2nd proviso to section 48 apply. If it is the case that it applies to the 1st proviso meant for a non-resident assessee, then the proviso would have made a mention of it. One cannot read anything more in the statute than what is stated therein. [Para 25]

It is averred that the mandate of the phrase in the proviso to section 112(1) is not to let the indexation formula enter into the computation process and is not a condition that unless an assessee is eligible to apply the indexation formula, only then the reduced rate of 10 per cent prescribed by the proviso to section 112(1) can be applied. In this regard, it may be stated that the indexation formula already enters into the computation in the first limb where it is mentioned that 'tax payable in respect of any income arising from the transfer of long-term capital asset' is to be determined. In fact, there is no issue on this part of proviso whether the 2nd proviso to section 48 enters into the said computation or not. The issue that arises lies in the second limb of the proviso starting with the phrase 'ten per cent of the amount of capital gains before giving effect to the provisions of the second proviso to section 48'. This cannot be read to mean 'deny the concessional rate of tax to the category of assessees who are not eligible to have the benefit of indexed cost of acquisition under the second proviso of section 48'. It only conveys how a particular amount is to be determined. Any other meaning would tantamount to rewriting this part of the proviso of section 112(1). [Para 26]

As the indexation on the zero coupon bond is available by virtue of 2nd proviso, it will affect the computation of capital gains under section 48 on which tax is payable under the first limb of the proviso and, thus would not go out of the purview of the proviso to section 112(1). The zero coupon bond on which indexation is available will get the benefit of the lower rate of tax at 10 per cent under the proviso. The exclusion from application of 1st and 2nd provisos to section 48 while calculating the amount of Income-tax on the income by way of long-term capital gains in the cases of non-residents and allow them the benefit of lower tax rates of 10 per cent also find mention in sections 115AC(3) and 115AD(3). The Act has taken care when, where, and how the 1st and the 2nd provisos to section 48 are to be excluded. The long-term capital gains on the sale of shares of the listed companies are otherwise exempt from tax under section 10(38) if the sale of the shares takes place through the recognized stock exchange on which security transaction tax is paid. However, in the instant case, such exemption is not available as the shares of the listed company CIL are sold in the off-market mode. [Para 27]

The case of revenue was that if an asset held by a trust was not used for charitable purpose, then capital gains arising on its transfer would not be entitled to exemption under section 11(1A). [Para 10]

It was not disputed that assessee was a trust of long standing, registered in 1896 and was granted registration under section 12A. Its objects were undisputedly charitable. Once a trust is existing for charitable purposes and it is registered under section 12A, then its income has to be computed in accordance with sections 11, 12 and 13 and other provisions of the Act would not be applicable. [Para 11]

Once it was undisputed that trust was existing for charitable purposes and was registered under section 12A then benefit of exemption under sections 11 and 12 could not be denied to the assessee-trust subject to conditions laid down under section 13. The assessing authority and Commissioner (Appeals) had not pointed out any violation of any provisions of section 13, therefore, question of rejecting the exemption on account of provisions of section 13 would not arise. [Para 12]

Now, it had to be seen whether the assessee-trust after holding certificate of registration under section 12A could be denied exemption available to it under section 11(1A).

The provisions of section 11(1A) provide exemption from capital gains on transfer of the capital asset by the trust. In addition to sub-section (1A) which deals with capital asset, sub-section (1) deals with income derived from property held under the trust.

A joint reading of sub-sections (1) and (1A) clearly reveals that sub-section (1) is applicable for providing exemption to income derived from property held for charitable or religious purposes subject to sections 60 to 63. Whereas section 11(1A) deals with gain arising from transfer of capital asset held by a charitable trust, it also provides exemption from capital gains if new capital asset is acquired and held for charitable purposes. Sub-section (5) of section 11 gives the list of capital assets which can be acquired out of net consideration received by the assessee on transfer of property held under the trust. Sub-section (1A) was inserted in section 11 by the Finance (No. 2) Act of 1971 with retrospective effect from 1-4-1962, the object and provision of this insertion was explained in the Departmental Circular No. 72, dated 6-1-1972.

Further Instructions were issued by the Government in Instruction No. 883, dated 24-9-1975.

From the above Circular and Instruction issued by the Government, following propositions emerged :—

(1)

Only the income derived from property held under trust for charitable or religious purposes is exempt under sub-section (1).

(2)

Because of certain amendments by the Finance Act, 1970, a charitable trust would forfeit exemption if trust funds/property in corpus are invested in prohibited categories.

(3)

In order to suitably modify the investment portfolio and to avail the benefit of exemption, it was provided that if trust acquires another capital asset for the use and benefit of the trust by utilizing capital gain from the transfer of property in the corpus then capital gains so utilized would be regarded as applied to charitable or religious purposes of the trust.

(4)

In order to give effect to this intention, sub-section (5) was inserted in section 11 thereby if net consideration is invested in specified categories as enumerated in sub-section (5) then to that extent, trust would continue to avail exemption from the capital gains.

(5)

Where if net consideration on transfer of property in the corpus of the trust is invested in F.D. in a bank for a period of six months or above then it would be regarded as utilization of consideration for acquiring another capital asset within the meaning of section 11(1). The department had not disputed the investment of net consideration on transfer of land to SMC.

(6)

Investment of sale proceeds of the asset held by the trust in F.D. is permissible.

The assessee-trust had invested a sum of Rs. 16.63 crores in IDBI Bank on 31-5-2006 and reinvested in F.D. with State Bank of India on 30-8-2006. Therefore, the conditions laid down in section 11(5) were satisfied. [Para 13]

Background

The extant income-tax provisions provide for substantial income-tax benefits to an employee at the time of withdrawal of retirement corpus from Provident Fund schemes held with the EPFO. Under this scheme, a specified sum (i.e. 12% of salary) is deducted from the salary of the employee as contribution towards the fund. The employer also contributes the matching sum to the fund. The contributions of the employer and the employee are invested in approved securities. Interest earned thereon gets credited to the account of the employee and the accumulated balance is paid to the employee at the time of his retirement or resignation, as the case may be.

The objective of such schemes are:

To encourage the habit of savings among the working class;

To enable them to have resources accumulated;

For their future needs in times of old age, sickness or other uncertainties of life.

Currently, the applicable interest rate on Employees Provident Fund is 8.5 percent for tax year 19/20, which is significantly higher than other savings schemes such as Public Provident Fund (PPF), fixed deposit, senior citizen savings scheme etc.

From an income-tax perspective as well it's a tax efficient option, since EPF falls under the Exempt-Exempt-Exempt (EEE) taxation regime. This means that no tax is levied at the time of contribution, on accrual of interest and at the time of withdrawal.

Fascinated by some of the benefits, many employees contribute beyond the mandated 12% of salary as per EPF regulations, under the voluntary provident fund scheme (VPF). VPF is an extension of EPF scheme and therefore provides similar interest rate and tax benefits. VPF is linked to EPF account and the deposit is made as employee's contribution to EPF.

Similar to this, self-employed individuals may subscribe to PPF scheme, which offers an interest rate of 7.1% (approximately) and can be opened either with a Post office or with any nationalized bank. A salaried employee may also contribute to PPF in addition to the fund operated by his employer. PPF comes with a minimum lock-in period of 15 years and one can invest up to a maximum of INR 1.5 lakhs annually. PPF investments also fall under the EEE tax category.

Proposal in Budget 2021:

Budget 2021 has proposed to levy tax on interest accrued on such portion of the contribution that exceeds INR 2.5 lakhs per annum. This restriction shall be applicable only for such contributions made on or after 01 April 2021. Although this will affect the taxability of interest income for employees drawing high salaries, people with comparatively lower salary might be impacted, if they are contributing to VPF or PPF. Such interest would be taxable under the head "Income from other sources", at the tax rate applicable to such individual.

It may be noted that the extant tax provisions provide exemption with respect to the accumulated balance payable to an employee participating in EPF/VPF. However, as per the Budget proposal, these provisions are to be amended to levy tax on interest accrued on such portion of the contribution that exceeds INR 2.5 lakh annually. Hence, a doubt arises as to whether the interest accrued on such portion of the contribution that exceeds INR 2.5 lakhs per annum, would be taxable at the time of withdrawal of EPF on retirement of the employee. It is suggested that considering tax would be levied on interest on excess contribution on accrual basis year on year, the same should not be taxed at the time of payment on retirement/resignation, as it would lead to double taxation and would be against the intention of the proposed amendment.

Contributing to EPF only

If an individual is contributing up to INR 20,833 per month under the EPF scheme, then the tax proposed to be imposed by this budget should not bring in any further adverse impact. Further, employees with current annual basic salary up to INR 2,083,333 are unlikely to be affected by the proposed amendment, if they are not contributing to VPF. This is because mandatory EPF contribution, i.e., 12% of INR 2,083,333 = 2.5 lakh is within the contribution limit above which interest will become taxable.

in what manner, delegation should be, is always a matter of great concern for political and management thinkers. Section 119 of Income-tax Act 1961 and Section 37B of the Central Excise Act, 1944 deal with power of delegation by parliament to Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) and Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC). But the scope of this power has always been surrounded in controversies. There are three aspect of this controversy which are discussed below : Some of the decisions are given below

In the case of Navnit Lal C. Javeri v. K. K. Sen, AAC [1965] 56 ITR 198, the legal effect of such circular is, inter alia, considered by a Bench of five judges of Supreme Court. Section 2(6A)(e) and section 12(1B) were introduced in the Income-tax Act by the Finance Act 15 of 1955, which came into force on April 1, 1955. The Government, however, realised that the operation of section 12(1B) would lead to extreme hardship because it would have covered the aggregate of all outstanding loans of past years and would impose an unreasonably high liability on the shareholders to whom the loans might have been advanced. The Minister, therefore, gave an assurance in Parliament that outstanding loans and advances which are otherwise liable to be taxed as dividends in the assessment years 1955-56 will not be subjected to tax if it is shown that they had been genuinely refunded to the respective companies before June 30, 1955. Accordingly, a circular was issued by the Central Board of Revenue on May 10, 1955, pointing out to all Income-tax Officers that it was likely that some of the companies might have advanced loans to their shareholders as a result of genuine transactions of loans, and the idea was not to affect such transactions and not to bring them within the mischief of the new provision. The officers, therefore, were asked to intimate to all the companies that if the loans were repaid before June 30, 1955, in a genuine manner, they would not be taken into account in determining the tax liability of the shareholders to whom they may have been advanced despite the new section. This circular was held by Supreme Court as binding on the Revenue, though limiting the operation of section 12(1B) or excluding certain transactions from the ambit of section 12(1B). It was so held because the circular was considered as issued for the purpose of proper administration of the provisions of section 12(1B) and the court did not look upon this circular as being in conflict with section 12(1B). This decision of Supreme Court became the landmark precedence, though it was interpretated in different manner by different benches of Courts and Tribunals.

A similar view of the Central Board of Direct Taxes circulars has been taken in the case of K. P. Varghese v. ITO [1981] 131 ITR 597/7 Taxman 13 (SC), by a Bench of two judges consisting of P. N. Bhagwati and E. S. Venkataramiah, JJ. The Bench has held that circulars of the Central Board of Direct Taxes are legally binding on the Revenue and this binding character is attached to the circulars even if they be found not in accordance with the correct interpretation of the section and they depart or deviate from such construction. Citing the decision of Navnit Lal C. Javeri case (supra), Supreme Court observed that circulars issued by the Central Board of Direct Taxes under section 119 of the Act are binding on all officers and persons employed in the execution of the Act even if they deviate from the provisions of the Act.

In Keshavji Ravji & Co. v. CIT [1990] 183 ITR 1/49 Taxman 87, a Bench of three judges of Supreme Court has also taken the view that circulars beneficial to the assessee which tone down the rigour of the law and are issued in exercise of the statutory powers under section 119 are binding on the authorities in the administration of the Act. The benefit of such circulars is admissible to the assessee even though the circulars might have departed from the strict tenor of the statutory provision and mitigated the rigour of the law. This court, however, clarified that the Board cannot preempt a judicial interpretation of the scope and ambit of a provision of the Act. Also a circular cannot impose on the taxpayer a burden higher than what the Act itself, on a true interpretation, envisages.

HEADNOTE: Section 2(13)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Adventure in nature of trade - Assessment years 1979-80 and 1981-82 - Assessee-company was an investment company - Assessee had received 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds on dissolution of a partnership firm as capital - After a retention for 13 months, 20 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold and surplus taken to capital reserve account - Then 5 Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased and 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold - Surplus realisation was again transferred to capital reserve account - Again 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased on 13-4-1979 and no sales were effected - It was on 11-7-1980 that entire balance holding of 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds was sold and surplus realisation transferred to capital reserve account - Whether, it could be said that sale of aforesaid bonds by assessee was an adventure in nature of trade and, therefore, excess realisation on sale of such bonds was assessable as assessee’s Income - Held, on facts, no

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1979-80 - Assessee-company made contributions to provident fund, which was a new account applied for - On asking Code No. Provident Fund Commissioner informed that it was not covered within definition of establishment - Aforesaid contributions made were returned and paid to employees as additional salary - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of such contributions to provident fund - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was earning income from rendering various kinds of services to certain companies and interest income on its investments and holdings. It maintained its accounts on mercantile system. It had received 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds on 1-8-1977 on dissolution of a partnership firm as capital. For the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee had claimed exemption in respect of the amount respresenting profit realised on sale of National Defence Gold Bonds worth 10 Kg. gold. This amount had been credited to the profit and loss account and therefrom transferred to the ‘capital reserve account’. The assessee had claimed exemption on the ground that the gold bonds sold were not capital assets under section 2(14)(iv ). The ITO held that the sale of 10 Kg. worth gold bonds by the assessee was an adventure in the nature of trade and, therefore, the excess realisation on the sale of aforesaid bonds was the assessee’s taxable income. He, therefore, proposed to include the aforesaid realisation in the total Income of the assessee and sought necessary directions under section 144B from the IAC. The IAC noted that prior to the sale of 10 Kg. of gold bonds the assessee possessed 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds out of which 20 Kg. worth of gold bonds had been purchased. The IAC held that during the year in question the assessee had become an investment trading company and the profit made by it on sale of 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds was required to be assessed as its income. He, therefore, accepted the proposal of the ITO and directed the ITO to add the aforesaid amount to the assessee’s total income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the addition.

On second appeal:

HELD: No hard and fast rule, principle or test may be laid down to determine the character of a transaction being adventure in the nature of trade or not. A number of factors like the income-earning regular activity of the assessee, the nature of the asset involved, the intention of the assessee of acquiring it, the treatment given to the profit on sale thereof, the period of retention thereof, the circumstances attending on and leading to the sale of the asset etc., are required to be taken into account before the transaction is held to be an adventure in the nature of trade. A capital investment on resale thereof would not lose its capital nature merely because resale was foreseen and contemplated by the assessee when investment was made and the possibility of enhanced value motivated the investment. Accretion to capital does not become income merely because the original capital was invested in the hope or expectation that it would in due course of time, rise in value. And if it does so rise, the realisation does not partake the character of income. The true character of the transaction would depend upon all the facts and circumstances of a’ case.

HEADNOTE: Section 11(1A)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Charitable or religious trust - Exemption of income from property held under - In accounting year relevant to assessment year in question, assessee-trust sold shares of certain companies held by it - Proceeds so realised were reinvested in fixed deposits with different parties - Whether ‘fixed deposits’ were property and would, therefore, constitute ‘capital asset’ within meaning of section 2(14) and, thus, utilisation of capital gain which arose on sale of said share by assessee was for charitable purpose - Held, yes

The proceeds so realised were invested in fixed deposits with different parties. The assessee claimed that the net consideration of capital gain arose out of the sale of shares deemed to have been applied for charitable purpose since it had acquired ‘another capital asset’ within the meaning of the aforesaid term occurring in section 11(1A). The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim and held that the capital gain arose on sale of shares was assessable as its income. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the order of the ITO.

On second appeal:

HELD: When money is placed in a fixed deposit, it is not the same as keeping the money idle at home because the money is given to the bank

for making a deposit for the benefit of the person who hands it over which benefit would not accrue to such person if the money is kept idle at home. The fixed deposits are considered by the public as investments and, therefore, from a commercial angle also fixed deposits are considered as property, i.e., income-yielding investments. It is so recognised by the statute in section 11 itself. Thus, the ‘fixed deposits’ are property and would, therefore, within the meaning of section 2(14) clearly constitute ‘capital asset’ and such capital asset is entirely different from the money deposited for getting the fixed deposit. The net consideration invested in the fixed deposit is, therefore, an investment for acquiring another capital asset.

Accordingly, no part of the capital gain as above could be brought to tax in the relevant assessment year.

Editorial Team

Section 11, read with Schedule IV, of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (ITA 2025), provides an exclusive list of income that does not form part of the total income of a non-resident or a foreign company. The Income-tax (Amendment) Ordinance 2026 inserts two new entries, 13D and 13E, into Schedule IV with effect from 01-04-2026.

Entry No. 13D provides the exemption for the interest on government securities (G-Sec) and capital gains from the sale, exchange or transfer of such securities to the Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs). Entry 13E extends a similar exemption to the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).

1. Existing tax treatment

The pre-amended ITA 2025 (or the repealed ITA 1961) did not provide any exemption to FIIs for interest income and capital gains arising from G-Secs. Such income was taxed under a special regime contained in Section 210 of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 115AD of the ITA 1961).

This provision prescribed special tax rates on the income from 'securities', and on capital gains arising from the transfer of such securities to FPIs and specified funds. The term 'securities' takes its meaning from Section 2(h) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956, which expressly includes Government securities along with shares, bonds, debentures and derivatives.

The rates under this regime in respect of G-Secs were as follows:

(a)

Interest income earned by an FPI on securities is taxable at a concessional rate of 20%, subject to any more beneficial treatment under the applicable tax treaty.

(b)

Long-term capital gains are taxable at 12.5%, while short-term capital gains are taxable at 30%.

Further, the payer was required to deduct tax at source, under Section 393(2) [Table S. No. 15] of the ITA 2025 (corresponding to Section 196D of the ITA 1961), before paying any income on securities to an FPI.

Similarly, the ITA 2025 or ITA 1961 did not provide any specific exemption for the 'Bank for International Settlements', an institution established at the Hague Conference in 1930 and headquartered in Basel, Switzerland. It is the world’s oldest international financial institution, and the Reserve Bank of India has been a member since 1996. BIS is often called the bank for central banks because it accepts deposits from central banks and manages a portion of their foreign exchange reserves. The founding documents of the BIS contemplate tax immunity for the Bank in member countries, and most member countries grant it. However, the ITA did not contain any specific exemption for the BIS.

2. Amendment by the Ordinance

The new entries 13D and 13E provide exemptions to FIIs and BIS from any interest on G-Secs, and any capital gains arising from the sale, exchange, or transfer of such G-Secs. The impact of these insertions in Schedule IV is discussed below.

2.1. Eligible Income

The exemption is available for the following incomes:

(a)

Interest on G-Secs

(b)

Capital gains from the sale, exchange or transfer of G-Secs

Note 4(c) to Schedule IV defines the term “government security” for the purposes of the exemption under this schedule. It provides that “Government security” shall have the same meaning as assigned to it in section 2(f) of the Government Securities Act, 2006 (‘GSA’).

Section 2(f) of the GSA provides that the "Government security" means a security created and issued by the Government for the purpose of raising a public loan or for any other purpose and subject to such terms and conditions as may be notified by the Government in the Official Gazette. Section 2(e) of the GSA defines "Government", in relation to any Government security, as the Central or State Government that issues the security.

2.1-1. Types of G-Secs

The G-Secs issued by the Central Government, State Government and Local Authorities can be classified into the following:

(a)

The second proviso to section 48 is only a mode of computation of capital gains. The crucial words relied upon by the Revenue cannot be construed as the words of exclusion of a category of assessees i.e., non-residents who cannot avail of indexation benefit. 12.3 We need not travel beyond the crucial provision [proviso to section 112(1)] to demonstrate the fallacy in the argument advanced on behalf of the revenue. The proviso itself shows the right path to interpretation. In the company of ‘listed securities’, Units and Zero-Coupon Bonds (‘ZCBs’) were also included by the Finance Acts of 2000 and 2005. We shall first turn our attention to ZCBs. The third proviso to section 48 which was introduced by the Finance Act, 1997, ordains "nothing contained in the second proviso shall apply to the long-term capital gains arising from the transfer of a long-term capital asset being bond or debenture other than capital indexed bonds issued by the Government". Thus, for computation of capital gains under section 48 in respect of ZCBs, the benefit of second proviso to section 48 is specifically excluded by the third proviso to section 48. When the second proviso to section 48 is thus excluded in relation to ZCBs, it should logically follow, if the revenue’s contention is accepted, that ZCBs should also go out of purview of the proviso to section 112(1) whereas ZCB was specifically included by way of amendment of the proviso admittedly with a view to extend the benefit of concessional rate of 10 per cent to such bonds. Otherwise, the amendment inserting ZCBs in the proviso to section 112(1) will be infructuous. It is nobody’s case that ZCBs answering the description of long-term assets should be subjected to the normal 20 per cent tax under the substantive provision of section 112. If the revenue’s interpretation of the phrase "before giving effect to the second proviso to section 48" has to be accepted, it would, in relation to ZCBs, lead to re-writing of the proviso and unintended results would follow. The resident assessee’s will have to pay tax at the normal rate of 20 per cent. The entire argument on the side of the Revenue will then break down as a self-effacing exercise. The provision [proviso to section 112(1)] cannot be read in one way insofar as the listed securities/shares are concerned and be read in a different way in relation to the ZCBs. No canon of interpretation would support such illogical interpretation of the said provision. The only answer of the Revenue in this regard is that ZCB is an investment and not an asset and therefore with a view to extend the concession of 10 per cent tax, it was specifically included in the proviso to section 112(1). We find it difficult to understand this line of distinction. Questions 2 and 3 are renumbered by us as questions 3 and 2 respectively. Nor is it a direct answer to the question of interpretation of the particular words used in the proviso. [Emphasis supplied]

12.4 Another point - Debentures are also included within the definition of ‘securities’ in section 2(h) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956. Debentures listed in a recognized stock exchange in India fall within the domain of the proviso to section 112(1) though such listing seems to be rare now-a-days. In view of the third proviso to section 48, indexation benefit under the second proviso will not apply to debentures. If the revenue’s interpretation is to be accepted the resident assessee will have to pay tax at 20 per cent on the capital gain arising from the transfer of such debentures held as long-term assets because the second proviso will not apply. This is obviously an unintended result, which even the Revenue would like to avoid.

12.5 The counsel appearing for the department argued that if the non-residents can also invoke the proviso to section 112, then, there will be a contradiction between the main section 112 as applicable to non-residents and the proviso thereto inasmuch as two rates 20 per cent and 10 per cent - would be in force after applying the first proviso to section 48. We see no such contradiction between the main provision and the proviso. Section 112(1) applies in general to the long-term capital assets whereas the proviso is specific and governs only the enumerated assets, viz, listed securities, units and zero coupon bonds answering the description of long-term capital assets. Obviously, in relation to those specified assets the Parliament wanted to reduce the tax rate. That is why the proviso was introduced.

10 Kg. worth gold bonds by the company in this year was an adventure in the nature of trade and, therefore, the excess realisation of Rs. 3,38,000 on the sale of the said gold bonds was taxable income of the company. Thus, proposing addition of Rs. 3,38,000 as aforementioned, to company’s total income the ITO sought necessary directions u/s 144B of the Act from the IAC, AR.IX, Ahmedabad. 4. The IAC examined the issues relating to the character of the company as an Investment Company and the nature of transaction of sale of 10Kg. worth gold bonds by it in this year. On applying the three tests, as mentioned by Sampath Iyengar in his book on Income Tax Act, 1961, to the case of the company in order to find out its true character, the learned IAC found that no doubt the main objects of the company stated that it would be an investment holding company and clause B(13) of the Memorandum of Association laid down that the profits, if any, realised on the sale of its capital asset would be carried over to "Capital Reserve Account" and would not be available for distribution but clause 16O(C) in Part XXI on Capitalisation of the Articles of Association lifted the prohibition made by clause B(13) of the Memorandum and gave an option to the Directors of the Company to distribute The profits made on sale of capital assets, or investments or the undistributed profits. He was thus of the opinion that the company was free to act both ways, i.e., as an Investment Company or Investment holding company and Investment dealing company. Next, he took note of the porportion in which the assets of the company were employed in ordinary trading and investments. He noted that prior to the sale of 10 kg. worth of gold bonds the company possessed 25 kg. worth of gold bonds out of which 20 kg. worth of gold bonds had been purchased for Rs. 8,20,000. The IAC was of the view that had 10 kg. worth of gold bonds not been sold off, the value of 25 kg. worth of gold bonds, at the price those were sold, would have been Rs. 18,50,000. On the other hand the company, after realisation of the profit on the sale of the gold bonds got itself enabled to make investments to the extent of the profit made. The IAC referred to the Balance Sheet of the company and pointed out that the assets of the company simply rose from Rs. 10,65,389 in last year to Rs. 14,16,178 this year. He further observed that alternatively it could also be said that had the gold bonds in question not been sold and valued at current market rate of Rs. 740 per 10 grams, the preponderant amount of asset would have been found as assets of the company. He pointed out that if the Gold Bonds, as shown in the balance sheet at Rs. 5,52,000, were revalued @ Rs. 740 per 10 gms. the value thereof would come to Rs. 11,22,000. Finally he examined the source of income of the company and came to the conclusion that in the year under consideration the preponderant source of income of the company had been the trading activity undertaken by it. Having thus tested the character of the company with reference to its object, preponderant employment of assets and preponderant proportion of its income the IAC held that during the year under consideration the company had become an investment trading company and the profit of Rs. 3,38,000 made by it on sale of 10 kg. worth of gold bonds was required to be assessed as its income. He, therefore, accepted and approved the proposal of the ITO in that behalf and accordingly directed him to add the aforesaid amount to company’s total income. The ITO duly complied with such directions u/s 144B.

5. The company had further claimed deduction of Rs. 7,385 being company’s contribution to Provident Fund, other funds and superannuation schemes. The ITO disallowed the claim on the ground that the funds, to which contributions had been made were not recognised by the department.

6. The ITO finally assessed the company at a positive income of Rs. 3,43,510 as against loss of Rs. 1,875 declared.

schedules pertain to profits and gains from business or profession, including two new schedules that address agricultural boards. One schedule explains deductions allowed under Section 123 (corresponding to Section 80C of the ITA), another outlines the rules related to recognised provident funds or approved superannuation funds or gratuity funds, and the final schedule details the forms and modes of investment or deposits permitted for charitable and religious trusts (corresponding to section 11(5) of the ITA). Both the ITA and ITB outline their respective definitions in Section 2. Under the ITB, the charging provisions are covered in Clause 15 (income from salary), Clause 20 (house property), Clause 26 (business or profession), Clause 67 (capital gains), and Clause 92 (other sources). Clubbing provisions are addressed in Clauses 96 to 100, while Clauses 108 to 121 govern the set-off and carry forward of losses. Deductions are explained in Clauses 122 to 154, and transfer pricing regulations are codified in Clauses 160 to 177. Special tax rates are stipulated under Clauses 190 to 198, and new tax regimes are introduced in Clauses 199 to 205. The taxability of non-residents and foreign companies is covered in Clauses 207 to 220, whereas Clauses 263 to 286 outline procedures for income returns and assessments, supplemented by search-related assessment provisions in Clauses 292 to 301. A newly introduced Chapter XVII-B (Clauses 332 to 355) specifically addresses the taxability of non-profit organisations. Appellate mechanisms are outlined in Clauses 356 to 374. Notably, while the ITA features over 65 provisions for Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) and Tax Collected at Source (TCS), the ITB consolidates these into nine Clauses (390 to 398). Lastly, penalties and prosecutions are detailed in Clauses 439 to 498 of the ITB.

A number of factors like the income-earning regular activity of the assessee, the nature of the asset involved, the intention of the assessee of acquiring it, the treatment given to the profit on sale thereof, the period of retention thereof, the circumstances attending on and leading to the sale of the asset etc., are required to be taken into account before the transaction is held to be an adventure in the nature of trade. A capital investment on resale thereof would not lose its capital nature merely because resale was foreseen and contemplated by the assessee when investment was made and the possibility of enhanced value motivated the investment. Accretion to capital does not become income merely because the original capital was invested in the hope or expectation that it would in due course of time, rise in value. And if it does so rise, the realisation does not partake the character of income. The true character of the transaction would depend upon all the facts and circumstances of a’ case.

In the instant case, it was not disputed that the assessee was an investment company. By its very nature of that character, the assessee, in normal course, might reasonably be looked at as acquiring various assets with a view to earn interest income therefrom. In that sense of matter, the number of purchases or the frequency in making investments could not be viewed with suspicion. Then, the assets involved were gold bonds, which did not fall within the categories of ‘capital asset’ as defined in section 2(14)(iv). Gold bonds are not items of trade and according to the scheme of the Act annual payments on them is not to be taxed as provided under section 10(15)(ia). It was also the established position that the department never treated the gold bonds as stock-in-trade of the assessee. The gold bonds were always projected as investments in the balance sheets from year to year. Surplus realisation on their sales was transferred to capital reserve account and was never made available for distribution. Annual payment for their holding and retention at one stage or the other of the relevant assessment proceedings, was treated by the department as exempt from tax under section 10(15)(ia).

The position of their sales was this that initially the assessee had received 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds on 1-8-1977 not as stock-in-trade but as capital. After a retention for about 13 months 20 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold on 31-8-1978 and the surplus taken to capital reserve account Then 5 Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased on 15-4-1978 and 10 Kg. worth of gold bonds were sold on 30-3-1979. The surplus realisation was again transferred to capital reserve account. 10Kg. worth of gold bonds were purchased on 13-4-1979 and no sales were effected in that year. It was on 11-7-1980 that the entire balance holding of 25 Kg. worth of gold bonds was sold and the surplus realisation transferred to capital reserve account. It might be noted that during the duration of three years there were two instances of sales. The frequency in sales was not such as might justify the conclusion that it was in the direction of undertaking adventures in the nature of trade. On each sales the surplus realisation was taken to capital reserve account and not distributed as income. The revenue had brought no evidence on record to prove that the profits earned by the assessee on the sales of gold bonds had not resulted in capital accretions and were revenue receipts of the assessee.

Therefore, the sales of the gold bonds by the assessee during the previous year relevant to the assessment year in question were not adventures in the nature of trade and as such did not bring taxable profits to the assessee.

IASC started issuing revised standards a couple of years ago. The revised standards do not permit alternative accounting treatments and instead zero in on one treatment as the ideal and best. The IAS-18 referred to above is one such reversed standard, which is all the more reason why it should be looked upon as an authority. The standards evolved by the ICAI, while following the broad pattern of the IASC, are tempered to suit Indian laws and practices.

Need of review of Supreme Court's decision 7. It is, therefore, humbly urged that the Supreme Court may review its judgment in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) in the light of the accounting authorities cited and discussed above. The Accounting Standard-13 of the ICAI has tremendous force when it says that interest/dividend relatable to the pre-acqitisition period must not be viewed as income but has recovery of cost and, therefore, should be viewed as a capital receipt. And capital receipts are not taxable for the simple reason that they do not constitute income. The Supreme Court rightly held where a bank purchased securities at a price with reference to their actual value as well as the interest accrued thereon till the date of purchase, the entire price paid would be in the nature of capital outlay. As a corollary, it follows that when this cost is recovered by way of interest, such recovery, far from being income, is an abatement against the cost originally incurred and should be reduced from the cost of purchase. It is this aspect urged in this article and buttressed by the accounting authorities that craves for reconsideration by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held the assessee (Vijaya Bank) to be liable for the entire interest including for the broken period, i.e., the pre-acquisition period. It is submitted that this is not correct. The broken period interest, it is reiterated, is a capital receipt and should be rightly reduced from the cost of securities. This accounting treatment is nothing new. Those familiar with preparing consolidated accounts of the holding company with the accounts of its subsidiary, would know that the proportionate part of pre-acquisition profits of the subsidiary relatable to the holding company's holding in the subsidiary is always reduced from the cost of investment and is never shown as part of reserves and surplus. This analogy should be sufficient to remove the mental block or the mind-set of those who are unable to come round to the view-point that broken period interest is a capital receipt.

Implications for shares

8. The Accounting Standard-13 applies to shares as much as it does to interest-bearing securities. In case of shares, the treatment propounded is likely to be even less palatable to tax administration because it will have the effect of converting dividend into capital gains, and if the holding period is more than 12 months, the investor is going to get away with a host of benefits that come with long-term capital gains - to be specific, a flat rate of 20 per cent tax irrespective of the quantum of gains and section 54F benefit which exempts long-term capital gains from tax if they are ploughed back in a residential house.

Implications for stock-in-trade

9. A dealer in securities is not going to be affected one way or the other, whether he is required to follow the law laid down by the Supreme Court in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) or the one propounded by the accounting standards and endorsed in this article. For, in any case, the entire transaction is revenue in nature. The cost of interest-bearing securities is going to be debited to the profit and loss account and the carrying amount at the end of the financial year, cost or market value, whichever is less, is going to be credited to such account. In the event, interest relating to the broken-period is not an issue at all in his case. It must be made clear that in Vijaya Bank Ltd. 's case (supra), the Supreme Court did not say that in case of a bank purchase of interest-bearing securities will invariably constitute investments. Nor did it say that they will invariably constitute stock-in-trade. This classification will, therefore, be governed by the RBI norms and other accounting considerations which are outside the scope of this article. What is relevant is the Supreme Court's verdict in Vijaya Bank Ltd.'s case (supra) has grave portents for investors.

Section 10(10D) provides for exemption with respect to any sum received under ULIP, including the sum allocated by way of bonus on such policy. However, if the premium is paid in excess of the limits prescribed, no exemption will be provided under this section except in case of the death of the policyholder.

Exemption under this section would not be allowed with respect to any sum received under the ULIPs, in case of following cases:

(a) If the premium payable for any of the years during the term of the policy exceeds 10% of the actual capital sum assured, then no exemption under this section would be allowed with respect to the sum received under the policy. Such a situation is hereinafter referred to as 'excess premium'.

(b)

Besides restricting the exemption under Section 10(10D) for payment of excess premium, the Finance Act, 2021 has inserted Fourth and Fifth Proviso to Section 10(10D) that no exemption shall be available under this provision in respect of ULIPs issued on or after 01-02-2021, if the amount of premium payable for any of the previous year during the term of the policy exceeds Rs. 2,50,000 ('high premium ULIPs').

As per Section 2(14) of the Income-tax Act, only those ULIPs shall be considered as a capital asset to which exemption under Section 10(10D) does not apply, on account of the applicability of the fourth and fifth proviso thereof. In other words, only the high-premium policies will be covered within the meaning of capital asset. It is not clear whether excess-premium policies (where premium is more than 10% of the sum assured) shall be considered as a capital asset. This does not seem to be logical but seems to be an inadvertent error. If this aspect is ignored, the proceeds from the excess premium policies shall also be taxable under the head capital gains.

Since the Income-tax Act does not contain any guidance on the taxability of excess premium ULIPs, it can be argued that the income arising from excess premium ULIPs should also be taxable under the head capital gains. The reasoning behind this is that when a person takes an insurance policy, he gets the right to receive the sum due against his insurance policy either on maturity or on its surrender or mishappening. Therefore, the right to receive a sum from the insurance policy is a capital asset within the meaning of Section 2(14), and any income or losses arising on its transfer shall be chargeable to tax under the head capital gains.

It is recommended that the upcoming Finance Act bring necessary amendments to clarify this aspect.

14. Section 54B exemption should be allowed even if the new agricultural land is purchased before the sale of agricultural land

Section 54B provides an exemption to an Individual or HUF from the capital gains arising from the transfer of agricultural land. The exemption is allowed if capital gains are invested in a new agricultural land within the prescribed time limit.

The provisions of Section 54B provide relief when the capital gain arising from the transfer of agricultural land is invested in another agricultural land within two years after the date of transfer. Sections 54 and 54F also allow capital gain exemption if the assessee purchases a residential house either within one year before the date of the transfer or within two years after the date of transfer of the original asset.

Unlike Section 54/54F, Section 54B does not allow the capital gain exemption if the assessee purchases agricultural land before the date of transfer of old agricultural land. It is recommended that the deduction under Section 54B should be allowed even if the assessee purchases the new agricultural land before selling the original agricultural land.

It is important to have a look at the definition of 'zero coupon bond' as it appears in the Act. A 'zero coupon bond' is defined under section 2(48). As per the definition introduced in the Finance Act, 2005, a zero coupon bond would mean a bond in which no benefit is received or receivable before the maturity or redemption and which are issued on or after 1-6-2005, by an infrastructure capital company or infrastructure capital fund or public sector company and specified by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. The definition came into effect from 1-4-2006. The Finance Ministry has also come up with the guidelines to be followed for recognition of the zero coupon bonds issued by an infrastructure capital company or an infrastructure capital fund or a public sector company. The tax treatment of zero coupon bonds has also been rationalized. It had specified that income on transfer of a zero coupon bond would be treated as capital gains, except the income arising from business of dealing in zero coupon bonds. Introduction

Accounting for employers provident fund plans, which require interest shortfalls to be recompensed (Exempt Provident Funds), has been a contentious issue ever since AS 15 Employee Benefit was issued. Under AS 15, employer's established provident funds are to be considered as defined benefit plans with a requirement to apply actuarial techniques and the Projected Unit Credit method for accounting for such plans. While the accounting standard requires such plans to be treated as defined benefit plans, two pain points arise in its implementation, the first being the lack of any guidance to the actuarial profession in valuing interest rate guarantees on exempt provident funds and the second being the increase in mandated rates of interest on provident funds by the Ministry of Finance. The recommended rates of interest, particularly for financial year 2010-11, were at variance from what the employer's set-up provident funds were earning on their investment portfolio, leading to an interest deficit. The Institute of Actuaries of India recently issued a "Guidance Note on Valuation of Interest Rate Guarantees on Exempt Provident Funds under AS 15 (Revised)" (GN 29). The Guidance Note provides guidance to actuaries in performing actuarial valuations and preparing actuarial reports related to interest guarantee on Exempt Provident Funds.The same is effective for the financial years ending March 31, 2012 onwards.

In accordance with the bye-laws of the assessee-co-operative society its employees had to make some contributions towards provident fund. The co-operative society had to make investments in accordance with the resolution passed by the executive committee of the co-operative society. The assessee was obliged to keep funds invested in Government securities. From the course of conduct actually adopted by the society it appeared that the interest earned by the investment of the provident fun d amount in Government securities was in its turn, credited by the assessee in the individual account of the employees' provident fund proportionately. In other words, the assessee-society did not retain any part of the interest so earned for itself.

In this factual background it was difficult to see how the assessee could claim to have 'borrowed money' for purposes of claiming deduction within the meaning of section 19(ii). 'Borrowed money' is a phrase well known to the commercial world. The money must belong to the person who lends the same to a borrower, on an understanding as to the time when it is to be returned and on payment of interest. Here the assessee which had the custody of the provident fund which belonged to its employees, invested it in accordance with the resolution of its executive committee in Government securities. The entire interest earned by the society was credited in the accounts of the individual employees. In fact, the assessee acted only as an investing agent. There was no relationship of lender and borrower between the assessee-society and its employees. It was, therefore, difficult to uphold the conclusion of the Tribunal that the moneys of the provident fund invested in Government securities constituted 'borrowed money' within the meaning of section 19(ii) .

The phrase 'money borrowed' used in section 19(ii ) has been used in its ordinary sense known to the commercial world. There was, no justification for expanding its meaning to include transactions which are not intrinsically of that nature.

Therefore, the Tribunal was legally not correct in upholding the AAC's order allowing the assessee' claim of deduction from its income from interest on securities of sums being interest paid or payable by it to its employees on account of provident fund amounts standing to the credit of their provident fund accounts in the books of the assessee.

15. Amount to be deposited under the Capital Gain Account Scheme should be the actual sale consideration and not the stamp duty value

Section 86 of the ITA 2025 [Corresponds to Section 54F of the ITA 1961] of the Income-tax Act allows exemption to an Individual and HUF from the long-term capital gains arising from transferring a capital asset other than a residential house property.

The exemption is allowed if the amount of net consideration is invested in a new house property within the prescribed time limit. If such net consideration is not invested by the due date of filing the income-tax return, then the assessee is required to deposit the amount in the capital gain account scheme.

'Net Consideration' is the full value of the consideration received or accruing from the transfer of the capital asset, as reduced by any expenditure incurred wholly and exclusively in connection with such transfer. However, it ignores a few situations where the net consideration to be invested will fall short of the money available in hand, such as:

(a)

Where the stamp duty value is higher than the full sales consideration;

(b)

Deduction of tax at source (TDS) by the purchaser while remitting sales consideration; and

(c)

Receipt of consideration in instalments.

In all of the situations mentioned above, the actual amount received by the person is less than the sales consideration used for the computation of capital gains. Thus, there would be a shortfall in the amount required to be invested in the capital gain account scheme to claim the Section 86 exemption. The Assessing Officer often challenges the Section 86 exemption by concluding that the assessee was required to deposit sales consideration, which was taken into consideration for computing capital gains.

It is recommended that the Government revisit the definition of 'net consideration' to bring clarity under the law so as to avoid any litigation.

16. Taxability of capital gains in case of a JDA entered into by assessees other than an Individual or HUF

Section 67(14) of the ITA 2025 [Corresponds to Section 45(5A) of the ITA 1961] provides that capital gains arising in the case of JDAs shall be chargeable to tax in the year in which the competent authority issues a completion certificate.

This provision applies only in cases where the owner of immovable property is an Individual or an HUF. The law does not provide taxability if any other assessee has entered into JDAs. Thus, it is recommended that the Govt provide clarity on the taxability of capital gains arising from JDAs entered into by any assessees other than Individuals or HUFs.

Q33. I have earned profit from the sale of listed shares which were kept for more than 12 months. Will it be treated as capital gain or business profit?

Vide Circular No. 6/2016, dated 29-2-2016 , the CBDT has instructed the Assessing Officers to consider the following while deciding whether surplus generated from the sale of listed shares or other securities is taxable as capital gains or business income:

1.

Where the assessee himself, irrespective of the period of holding of listed shares and securities, opts to treat them as stock-in-trade, the income arising from the transfer of such shares/securities would be treated as its business income.

2.

In respect of listed shares and securities held for more than 12 months immediately preceding the date of its transfer, if the assessee desires to treat the income arising from the transfer thereof as capital gains, the same shall not be put to dispute by the Assessing Officer. However, once taken by the assessee in a particular Assessment Year, this stand shall remain applicable in subsequent Assessment Years. The taxpayer shall not be allowed to adopt a different/contrary stand in this regard in subsequent years.

The CBDT has formulated the above principles to reduce litigation and maintain consistency in the treatment of income derived from the transfer of shares and securities. All the relevant provisions of the Act shall continue to apply to the transactions involving the transfer of shares and securities.

The CBDT10 has decided that the income arising from the transfer of unlisted shares would be considered under the head 'Capital gains', irrespective of the holding period, to avoid disputes/litigation and maintain a uniform approach.

Q34. I have earned a profit from intra-day trading. Is it taxable as business profit or capital gain?

Intra-day trading is considered a speculative business, and the resultant gain or loss would be a speculative gain or speculative loss. Speculative gain is taxed at normal rates, and speculative losses can only be set off against speculative profit.

As a result, the capital gains may be substantially lower then the profits which are booked in the accounts. ◆ Sub-section (4) of section 115JA provides that save as otherwise provided in that provision, all other provisions of the Act would apply.

Section 37(1)  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of - Assessment year 1979-80 - Assessee-company made contributions to provident fund, which was a new account applied for - On asking Code No. Provident Fund Commissioner informed that it was not covered within definition of establishment - Aforesaid contributions made were returned and paid to employees as additional salary - Whether assessee was entitled to deduction in respect of such contributions to provident fund - Held, yes

FACT: During the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1979-80, the assessee- company had made contributions to the provident fund, which was a new account. The assessee had asked for its Code No. The Provident Fund Commissioner, however, held that the assessee was not covered by the definition of ‘establishment’ so as to have a Code No. and contribute to a provident fund. The contribution amount was thereafter returned and paid to the employees as additional salary. The assessee claimed deduction in respect of the aforesaid contributions made to the provident fund. The ITO disallowed the assessee’s claim. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) also upheld the disallowance.

On second appeal:

HELD: The circumstances under which the claim for deduction of contribution to provident fund as business expenditure was advanced by the assessee justified its allowability under section 37(1) . Therefore, the Commissioner ( Appeals) was not justified in disallowing the assessee’s claim.

Accumulation of income under section 11(2). Does the amendment apply if the impermissible investment is retained only for a short period? On a literal reading, the amendment, on a standalone basis, applies even in such a situation. However, on a combined reading along with proviso (iia) to section 13(1)(d), no income will be liable to tax (see para 3.7-1b).

3.7-1 Receiving gifts in the form of impermissible investments

A question that arises is whether a charitable institution can accept gift of impermissible investments. This is explained separately for shares and other assets.

3.7-1a Other impermissible assets

So far as assets other than shares are concerned, the relevant clause reads as follows:

"…any income thereof, if for any period during the previous year-

(i) any funds of the trust or institution are invested or deposited after the 28th day of February, 1983 otherwise than in any one or more of the forms or modes specified in sub-section (5) of section 11;

…

to the extent of such deposits or investments referred to in sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iii).

Thus, the clause applies in respect of funds invested or deposited otherwise than in permissible modes. It has been held in a series of decisions that when a charitable institution receives a gift, its funds are not invested or deposited within the meaning of the aforesaid sub-clause [Auditor Dasaradha Rami Reddy Charities v. CIT [1989] 44 Taxman 453 (Mad.); CIT v. Birla Charity Trust [1987] 34 Taxman 504 (Cal.); CIT v. Sir Shri Ram Foundation [2001] 116 Taxman 113 (Delhi)]. Hence, the amendment does not affect the taxation of other impermissible assets received as a gift. Incidentally, such assets could have been held by the institution even under the pre-amendment law without losing any exemption; however, after the amendment, if the income of the charitable institution is actually invested or deposited in impermissible modes (say, debentures of a private company) the amount of income so invested in making such investment will not enjoy exemption under section 11(1) and be liable to tax under section 13(1)(d).

3.7-1b Shares

So far as shares are concerned, under the pre-amended law, shares could not be held by a charitable institution, even if they were donated to the institution. After the amendment, the exact language of the amendment is "to the extent of such deposits or investments referred to in sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iii)". It is pertinent that sub-clause (iii), which deals with shares does not at all use the expression "such deposits or investments." On the other hand, income is not invested if shares are received as a gift and hence, on a plain reading, in such a case, no part of income can be regarded as invested.

The matter is not very clear, but it appears that:

(a)

income invested in shares is taxable under section 13 (1)(d)

(b)

shares received as gifts are not taxable.

As mentioned above, the aforesaid view is also supported by the Explanatory Memorandum, reproduced in para 3.7 above.

The law is silent on the income from such impermissible investment. It appears that such income (including capital gains) qualifies for exemption under section 11(1)(a) and is entitled to the benefit of the deemed application under Explanation 1(2) or secondary accumulation for 5 years under section 11(2). Further, the capital gains from investment should also qualify for benefit under section 11(1A).

Proviso (iia) to section 13(1)(d) provides that nothing in the section shall apply if the impermissible investment is not held beyond the expiry of one year from the end of the previous year in which such impermissible investment is acquired. This proviso continues to apply even after the amendment. Hence, income shall not be taxable under the amended section 13(1)(d) if the impermissible investment is liquidated on or before the expiry of the year subsequent to the year in which it is acquired. To illustrate, suppose an assessee buys preference shares in a company on 15th March 2023. If it transfers the shares on or before 31st March 2024, no part of its income will be taxable. On the other hand, if it transfers the shares on 4th April 2024, the income to the extent of the cost of shares will be taxable under section 13(1)(d).

The amount of taxable income is not liable to penalty under section 271AAE (please see para 11).

3.7-1 Receiving gifts in the form of impermissible investments

A question that arises is whether a charitable institution can accept gift of impermissible investments. This is explained separately for shares and other assets.

3.7-1a Other impermissible assets

So far as assets other than shares are concerned, the relevant clause reads as follows:

"…any income thereof, if for any period during the previous year——

(i) any funds of the trust or institution are invested or deposited after the 28th day of February, 1983 otherwise than in any one or more of the forms or modes specified in sub-section (5) of section 11;

…

to the extent of such deposits or investments referred to in sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iii).

Thus, the clause applies in respect of funds invested or deposited otherwise than in permissible modes. It has been held in a series of decisions that when a charitable institution receives a gift, its funds are not invested or deposited within the meaning of the aforesaid sub-clause [Auditor Dasaradha Rami Reddy Charities v. CIT [1989] 44 Taxman 453 (Mad.); CIT v. Birla Charity Trust [1987] 34 Taxman 504 (Cal.); CIT v. Sir Shri Ram Foundation [2001] 116 Taxman 113 (Delhi)]. Hence, the amendment does not affect the taxation of other impermissible assets received as a gift. Incidentally, such assets could have been held by the institution even under the pre-amendment law without losing any exemption; however, after the amendment, if the income of the charitable institution is actually invested or deposited in impermissible modes (say, debentures of a private company) the amount of income so invested in making such investment will not enjoy exemption under section 11(1) and be liable to tax under section 13(1)(d).

3.7-1b Shares

So far as shares are concerned, under the pre-amended law, shares could not be held by a charitable institution, even if they were donated to the institution. After the amendment, the exact language of the amendment is "to the extent of such deposits or investments referred to in sub-clauses (i), (ii) and (iii)". It is pertinent that sub-clause (iii), which deals with shares does not at all use the expression "such deposits or investments." On the other hand, income is not invested if shares are received as a gift and hence, on a plain reading, in such a case, no part of income can be regarded as invested.

The matter is not very clear, but it appears that:

(a)

income invested in shares is taxable under section 13 (1)(d)

(b)

shares received as gifts are not taxable.

As mentioned above, the aforesaid view is also supported by the Explanatory Memorandum, reproduced in para 3.7 above.

The law is silent on the income from such impermissible investment. It appears that such income (including capital gains) qualifies for exemption under section 11(1)(a) and is entitled to the benefit of the deemed application under Explanation 1(2) or secondary accumulation for 5 years under section 11(2). Further, the capital gains from investment should also qualify for benefit under section 11(1A).

Proviso (iia) to section 13(1)(d) provides that nothing in the section shall apply if the impermissible investment is not held beyond the expiry of one year from the end of the previous year in which such impermissible investment is acquired. This proviso continues to apply even after the amendment. Hence, income shall not be taxable under the amended section 13(1)(d) if the impermissible investment is liquidated on or before the expiry of the year subsequent to the year in which it is acquired. To illustrate, suppose an assessee buys preference shares in a company on 15th March 2023. If it transfers the shares on or before 31st March 2024, no part of its income will be taxable. On the other hand, if it transfers the shares on 4th April 2024, the income to the extent of the cost of shares will be taxable under section 13(1)(d).

The amount of taxable income is not liable to penalty under section 271AAE (please see para 11).

ITAT’s decision 14. Now we shall turn our attention to the order of the ITAT, "H" Bench, Mumbai in ITA No. 2552 of 2005 on which strong reliance has been placed by Revenue. The learned Members of the Tribunal held that the Legis- lature never intended to give the benefit of proviso to section 112(1) to those cases where long-term capital gain is required to be computed under the first proviso to section 48. The Tribunal purported to reach the con- clusion on a literal construction of the proviso, the language of which, the Tribunal acknowledges, is unambiguous. With due respect to the lear- ned Members of Tribunal, we find it difficult to appreciate the observation that the literal construction of proviso leads to the meaning it has attributed to the provision. The Tribunal failed to note that there are no words of exclusion of the assessees like the applicant governed by the first proviso to section 48. Nor can they be inferred by necessary implication. It appears that the Tribunal’s views is based on the premise that the legislature did not intend to provide two reliefs to a non-resident assessee - one under the proviso to section 48 and another under the proviso to section 112(1). As already discussed in the preceding para, no such legislative intention can be imputed to the legislature except by way of some guess work or a priori reasoning. The assumption of the Tribunal that it was giving effect to literal construction as well as legislative intent is incorrect. The further observation of the Tribunal that if the legislature intended to cover the cases falling under the first proviso to section 48, it would not have used the words ‘second proviso to section 48’ [in the proviso to section 112(1)] is based on a wrong premise. One does not follow from the other. The second proviso to section 48 should necessarily be mentioned in the proviso to section 112(1) as the tax rate of 10 per cent should be calculated without reference to the indexation formula that is applicable to the resident assessees. Hence, the reference to 2nd proviso to section 48 cannot be avoided. The only question is about the connotation of the expression "before giving effect to the second proviso to section 48" - whether those words have the effect of excluding those who cannot avail of the indexation benefit under the 2nd proviso, that is to say, the non-residents including foreign companies. We are of the considered opinion, for the reasons already set out, that the crucial phrase in the proviso to section 112(1) does not have such effect.

14.1 The learned Members of the Tribunal placed much reliance on sub-section (3) to section 115AD by way of contrast with the language of the proviso to section 112(1). Section 115 AD, inter alia, provides that where the total income of a foreign institutional investor includes income by way of capital gain arising from the transfer of securities, the amount of income-tax calculated on the said income shall be at the rate of 10 per cent. Sub-section (3) says nothing contained in the first and second provisos to section 48 shall apply for the computation of capital gains arising out of the transfer of securities...’. After referring to sub-section (3), the Tribunal makes an observation that "if the legislature had intended to give benefit of marginal relief of tax to all non-residents, it could have easily used the words ‘first and second provisos of section 48’. The Tribunal missed to note that by adding the words ‘first proviso’, the intended result will not be achieved. On the other hand, the position of non-resident will be worse. For these reasons, we have no hesitation in differing with the view taken by the Tribunal.

21. Money in bank accounts is a property liable for provisional attachment under Section 281B: HC

Assistant Commissioner of Income-tax v. Mohammed Salih [2025] 171 taxmann.com 23 (Kerala)

The police seized a huge amount of cash from a car in which the assessee was riding. After recording reason to believe that income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment, proceedings were initiated in relation to the same by the issuance of notice under Section 148.

The expected demand on assessment, including penalty, would be a substantial amount exceeding two crores. The competent authority of the Department ordered provisional attachment of the Bank accounts of the assessee under section 281B.

The matter reached the Kerala High Court.

The High Court held that the word 'property' is a word of very wide connotation. It is relevant to note that section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of 'any property'. The prefix 'any' to the word 'property' has much significance. It indicates that the word 'property' occurring therein is not to be comprehended in a restricted sense.

Therefore, 'any property' mentioned in section 281B(1) would take within its sweep, money lying in the bank account also. Section 281B(1) provides for the provisional attachment of any property belonging to the assessee in the manner provided in the Second Schedule to the Act. The Second Schedule to the Act is titled, 'Procedure for Recovery of Tax'. Evidently, except for the property exempted from attachment under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), other properties are liable to attachment.

Section 60 CPC provides the property liable to attachment. Noticeably, section 60(1) CPC specifically states that money is an attachable property. Properties that are not liable to attachment have been specified in the proviso to the section. Therefore, money in a bank account is property liable to attachment.

There could be instances where the assessee does not own immovable property sufficient enough to secure the likely demand, but there are sufficient funds in the bank account. The power for provisional attachment is provided to protect the interest of the revenue. There is no warrant to hold that money lying in a bank account is not liable to attachment.
